Detection Engineering: Stop Drowning in Alerts and Start Catching Bad Guys
items.summary: Detection engineering is both a role and an activity. It’s the discipline of building and maintaining the logic that identifies malicious or risky behavior within your organization. It’s where security analysis meets software engineering, turning raw logs and telemetry into actionable detections that defenders can rely on. Detection engineers bridge the gaps between security operations, threat intelligence, and infrastructure. They understand how attackers operate, how defenders respond, and how systems generate the data that supports those detections. A well-built detection can mean the difference between an alert that matters and one that drowns in noise. Precision and Recall: The Balancing Act Every detection faces a trade-off between precision and recall. Precision measures how much you can trust your alerts: of everything that fired, how much was actually malicious? High precision = fewer false positives = analysts trust the tool. Recall measures how much you’re catching: of everything malicious that happened, how much did you detect? High recall = fewer blind spots = threats don’t slip through. Detection engineering lives in the tension between the two: too much precision risks missing subtle threats; too much recall floods analysts with false positives. The goal is calibration through testing, iteration, and feedback. Core Components of Detection Engineering 1. Scoping and Prioritization Start with intent. What are you trying to detect, and why? Define the threats, behaviors, or assets that matter most, then align your work with frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK®. Evaluate risk and value to determine which detections provide the highest impact for the effort required. Prioritize based on business importance and available telemetry. 2. Data and Telemetry Great detections rely on great data. Keep inventory of your logs. Validate that each contains the data you need. Normalize and enrich your logs so detections remain consistent across tools and environments. Understanding how logs are generated is essential to writing logic that fits your environment. 3. Detection Logic Development This is where hypothesis meets code. Write queries or rules that detect behaviors, not just static indicators. Combine multiple approaches: Signatures for known indicators of compromise (IoCs) Behavioral logic for Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) and patterns Anomaly models for statistical outliers 4. Testing and Validation Use adversary emulations or frameworks like Atomic Red Team to verify that your detections actually fire and your logging is working. Measure quality through precision, recall, and additional factors like confidence (how certain you are it’s malicious) and criticality (how severe the impact would be). 5. Deployment and Tuning Monitor performance, including trigger frequency, false positive rates, and analyst response time. Detection engineering is iterative and ongoing, not “write once and done.” 6. Documentation and Knowledge Transfer Good detections come with context. Record what the detection looks for, why it matters, what data it uses, and how it was tested. Version control your rules using Git and promote collaboration so analysts, hunters, and engineers can learn from one another. Playbooks and detection libraries ensure institutional knowledge does not disappear when staff change roles. 7. Metrics and Continuous Improvement Track measurable outcomes such as coverage across ATT&CK® techniques, number of validated detections, false positive rates, and mean time to detect. Regularly retire stale detections, update ones that drift, and automate validation wherever possible. Detection-as-Code practices keep everything maintainable and scalable. Building the Skillset Detection engineering requires a strong foundation in logging, security tooling, and incident response. You should understand when it’s best to detect, when to block, and how to use data sources effectively. Whether you’re building your first rule or managing hundreds, the mindset remains the same: test everything, learn constantly, and make each detection better than the last. Get Started Explore resources like: detectionengineering.net and SigmaHQ. Follow community leaders like: Zack Allen (Detection Engineering Weekly) and Haider Dost (Threat Detection Maturity Framework). Study detections and see how others approach logic design at: research.splunk.com Read: Practical Threat Detection Engineering. For more resources check out: https://bit.ly/notlogic
items.summary_html:
Detection engineering is both a role and an activity. It’s the discipline of building and maintaining the logic that identifies malicious or risky behavior within your organization. It’s where security analysis meets software engineering, turning raw logs and telemetry into actionable detections that defenders can rely on.

Detection engineers bridge the gaps between security operations, threat intelligence, and infrastructure. They understand how attackers operate, how defenders respond, and how systems generate the data that supports those detections. A well-built detection can mean the difference between an alert that matters and one that drowns in noise.

Precision and Recall: The Balancing Act

Every detection faces a trade-off between precision and recall.

Precision measures how much you can trust your alerts: of everything that fired, how much was actually malicious? High precision = fewer false positives = analysts trust the tool.

Recall measures how much you’re catching: of everything malicious that happened, how much did you detect? High recall = fewer blind spots = threats don’t slip through.

Detection engineering lives in the tension between the two: too much precision risks missing subtle threats; too much recall floods analysts with false positives. The goal is calibration through testing, iteration, and feedback.

Core Components of Detection Engineering1. Scoping and Prioritization

Start with intent. What are you trying to detect, and why? Define the threats, behaviors, or assets that matter most, then align your work with frameworks such as MITRE ATT&CK®. Evaluate risk and value to determine which detections provide the highest impact for the effort required. Prioritize based on business importance and available telemetry.

2. Data and Telemetry

Great detections rely on great data. Keep inventory of your logs. Validate that each contains the data you need. Normalize and enrich your logs so detections remain consistent across tools and environments. Understanding how logs are generated is essential to writing logic that fits your environment.

3. Detection Logic Development

This is where hypothesis meets code. Write queries or rules that detect behaviors, not just static indicators. Combine multiple approaches:

  • Signatures for known indicators of compromise (IoCs)
  • Behavioral logic for Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) and patterns
  • Anomaly models for statistical outliers
4. Testing and Validation

Use adversary emulations or frameworks like Atomic Red Team to verify that your detections actually fire and your logging is working. Measure quality through precision, recall, and additional factors like confidence (how certain you are it’s malicious) and criticality (how severe the impact would be).

5. Deployment and Tuning

Monitor performance, including trigger frequency, false positive rates, and analyst response time. Detection engineering is iterative and ongoing, not “write once and done.”

6. Documentation and Knowledge Transfer

Good detections come with context. Record what the detection looks for, why it matters, what data it uses, and how it was tested. Version control your rules using Git and promote collaboration so analysts, hunters, and engineers can learn from one another. Playbooks and detection libraries ensure institutional knowledge does not disappear when staff change roles.

7. Metrics and Continuous Improvement

Track measurable outcomes such as coverage across ATT&CK® techniques, number of validated detections, false positive rates, and mean time to detect. Regularly retire stale detections, update ones that drift, and automate validation wherever possible. Detection-as-Code practices keep everything maintainable and scalable.

Building the Skillset

Detection engineering requires a strong foundation in logging, security tooling, and incident response. You should understand when it’s best to detect, when to block, and how to use data sources effectively.

Whether you’re building your first rule or managing hundreds, the mindset remains the same: test everything, learn constantly, and make each detection better than the last.

detectionengineering.net and SigmaHQ.

Zack Allen (Detection Engineering Weekly) and Haider Dost (Threat Detection Maturity Framework).

Study detections and see how others approach logic design at:

research.splunk.com

Practical Threat Detection Engineering.

items.title: Addressing PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: upgrade guidance and Azure WAF mitigations
items.summary: Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​ Introduction Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities.
items.summary_html:
Written in collaboration with yuvalpery​ and Gunjan Jain​  Introduction

Today, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities were disclosed in PHP. We strongly recommend that customers upgrade to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading is the only way to fully remediate these vulnerabilities. Read more on the PHP official website.

Microsoft has been part of the coordinated industry response to these vulnerabilities, working alongside the PHP Foundation, Wiz, security researchers, and other industry partners to help protect customers. Azure Web Application Firewall (WAF) has developed mitigations against known exploitation patterns to provide an additional layer of protection while customers apply the PHP security updates. These protections are intended to complement patching and are not a replacement for it. 

About the vulnerabilities: 
  1. CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via OOM corruption
  2. CVE-2026-109619- RCE via stale global state  

Both vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network without privileges or user interaction, with a high potential impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. 

The vulnerabilities relate to PHP handling of memory when a request terminates abnormally, for example due to memory exhaustion or a fatal error. Under certain conditions, improper memory handling could allow an attacker to achieve remote code execution. 

Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, 8.2.35. 

Refer to vendor guidancefor patching of different versions of PHP.

Recommended action: upgrade PHP 

We recommend that customers: 

  1. Upgrade all PHP deployments to a patched version, including virtual machines, containers, base images, and platform runtimes. We suggest prioritizing internet-facing workloads. 
  2. Rebuild and redeploy container images that include their own PHP runtime, since updating the host does not update PHP inside an image. 
  3. Migrate to a supported PHP branch if the branch currently in use no longer receives security fixes. 
  4. Treat the Azure WAF mitigations below as a temporary, supplementary measure. They address a specific technique and do not remediate the underlying vulnerabilities. 
Azure WAF protection

If you are unable to upgrade PHP to a patched version immediately, apply the following mitigations in the interim -

  • Azure Front Door WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the managed rule for response-side mitigation.
  • Application Gateway WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation and enable the rewrite rule for response-side mitigation.
  • Application Gateway for Container WAF: Apply the mitigation using custom rules for request-side mitigation.

See below sections for details.

Mitigation using custom rules

These custom rules can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities. Depending on application traffic, the rules may result in false positives and affect legitimate requests. They are intended as temporary mitigations and do not replace the need to upgrade PHP.  Learn more: Azure WAF custom rules for PHP2Shell mitigation. 

Request-side signals alone may not be sufficient to reliably identify certain exploitation attempts. Signals in the server response can provide additional evidence that malicious activity has occurred, enabling more targeted mitigation with higher confidence and lower false positives.  For this vulnerability, Azure WAF identifies known malicious patterns in the session and removes the potentially malicious elements from the response before it reaches the client. This provides an additional layer of protection for supported exploitation scenarios, while patching PHP remains necessary to fully address the underlying vulnerability.  

Azure Front Door WAF: managed rule 

A managed rule to handle potential attack vector in response is currently rolling out for Azure Front Door WAF, expected to complete October 28. Once the rule is available, its details are as follows: 

  • Rule group: MS-ThreatIntel-Response-CVEs 
  • Rule ID: 99006001 
  • Default state: disabled. Customers need to enable the rule. 

Supported rulesets: DRS 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2. Unlike other WAF rules, this rule does not block or challenge any traffic. When the rule identifies malicious signals in the session that provides strong evidence of exploitation, it removes the potentially malicious elements from the response while leaving the remainder of the response unchanged. Mitigation for this rule takes effect only when the rule action is set to Block on anamoly. Please note that the response side mitigation does not generate WAF log entries or hit counts.   

Application Gateway WAF: rewrite rule

Customers can apply an interim mitigation now using the HTTP header rewrite capability of Application Gateway, which is available on v2 SKUs. A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway is expected to roll out at a later date. Until then, we recommend the following rewrite rule: 

       1. Create a rewrite rule in a rewrite set associated with your routing rule(s). 

       2. Add a condition that evaluates the Set-Cookie response header against the following regular expression: 

^PHPSESSID=(?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]|%2[Cc])*(?:[^a-zA-Z0-9;%-]|%(?!2[Cc]))+[a-zA-Z0-9-]*[^;]+;

  

          3. Set the action to delete the matching Set-Cookie response header. Alternatively, the header can be set to a replacement value of your choice.                     Please note that setting a value overwrites the entire header, including attributes such as Path=/;. 

 

 Additional considerations: 

  • The rule applies only to a Set-Cookie header that matches the pattern. Other Set-Cookie headers in the same response are not affected. 
  • We recommend validating the rule on a non-production gateway before broader deployment. 

For further information, see Rewrite HTTP headers and URL with Azure Application Gateway. 

Application Gateway for Containers (AGC): A WAF managed rule for Application Gateway for Containers is expected to roll out at a later date. In the interim, customers can apply the custom rules. Application Gateway for Containers does not support regex-based rewrite rules on HTTP response. Summary 

Service 

Available protection 

Recommended action 

Azure Front Door WAF 

Custom rules, managed rule 99006001 rolling out, expected to complete by 28 October 2026; mitigation using high confidence signals without blocking traffic. 

Upgrade PHP to a patched version. If you are unable to patch, apply custom rules in the interim.

Application Gateway WAF 

Custom rules, header rewrite mitigation available now; managed rule expected to roll out later. 

Upgrade PHP to a patched version. If you are unable to patch, apply custom and rewrite rule in the interim.

Application Gateway for Containers 

Custom rules, managed rule expected to roll out later. 

Upgrade PHP to a patched version. If you are unable to patch, apply custom rules.

 

Conclusion 

Following PHP security guidance and upgrading to a patched version is the recommended and complete remediation. Azure WAF mitigations can help reduce exposure during the upgrade period, and we encourage customers to upgrades at the earliest opportunity. 

Changelog
  • 10/21/2026 9:00 PM PST – Updated with additional guidance around custom rules 
  • 10/22/2026 9:00 AM PST – Updated rule rewrite regular expression

WorkNest Secure Gains The Cyber Scheme Accreditation
items.summary: UK cybersecurity specialist WorkNest Secure has achieved Accredited Organisation status under The Cyber Scheme, providing further independent recognition of the technical expertise and professional standards maintained across its services. The accreditation recognises organisations that demonstrate professional competence, quality and alignment with established cybersecurity industry standards. It also places particular emphasis on the qualifications and capabilities of the professionals delivering those services. For WorkNest Secure, the latest recognition builds on its existing technical accreditations and reflects its continued investment in developing and maintaining a highly skilled cybersecurity workforce. Independent Recognition of Cybersecurity Expertise The Cyber Scheme is a Licensed Body of the UK Cyber Security Council and works to assess and recognise cybersecurity professionals against established industry standards. Its Accredited Company Programme is designed to give businesses greater confidence when selecting cybersecurity service providers by linking organisational accreditation to independently verified workforce capabilities. Unlike certifications focused primarily on processes or technical controls, the programme places significant importance on the people delivering cybersecurity services and their professional competence. WorkNest Secure already has a number of penetration testing consultants who hold individual accreditations through The Cyber Scheme, making company-wide recognition a natural progression. Jordan Constantine, Head of Offensive Security at WorkNest Secure, said the accreditation provides customers with independent evidence of the team’s capabilities. “Becoming accredited under The Cyber Scheme felt like a natural step for WorkNest Secure. It’s one thing to say our team meets a high standard; it’s another to have that verified independently, and many of our penetration testing consultants are accredited under their scheme.” He added: “Their assessments are respected across government and industry, and that gives our clients real confidence in the people testing their systems. It’s proof, not just a claim.” Building Trust in Cybersecurity Services The accreditation comes as organisations increasingly rely on external cybersecurity specialists to help identify vulnerabilities, assess risks and strengthen their defences. With businesses placing considerable trust in third-party providers, independently verified qualifications and professional standards can provide an important measure of assurance. Kirsty Fowler , Managing Director of WorkNest Secure, believes the expertise of cybersecurity professionals remains central to delivering effective security services. “Cybersecurity is a people business. Technology is incredibly important, but customers also need to know that the people testing their systems, advising their teams and helping them respond to risk have the right expertise behind them.” She added that the accreditation also reflects the company’s commitment to supporting professional development. “Achieving the Cyber Scheme accreditation gives our customers another level of independent assurance and reflects the investment we continue to make in our people.” Supporting Continued Growth WorkNest Secure was formed following the integration of Pentest People and Bulletproof under the WorkNest Group, bringing together expertise across penetration testing, red teaming, attack simulation, information security, data protection and compliance. The company also provides GuardNest , its proprietary vulnerability management platform, which combines vulnerability visibility, threat intelligence and compliance capabilities. WorkNest Secure holds CREST and CHECK accreditations for penetration testing and recently achieved CREST STAR-FS accreditation for intelligence-led red teaming within financial services. The latest accreditation adds to these credentials as the company continues to develop its technical capabilities and strengthen its position in the UK cybersecurity services market. WorkNest Secure forms part of WorkNest Group, which employs more than 800 people and supports over 50,000 customers across ten countries.

items.title: Field Notes: Reconstructing an Attacker’s Workflow
items.summary: Introduction During a recent incident, we recovered several PowerShell scripts the attacker had left behind on disk. Instead of reconstructing every action from individual event log entries, file-system artefacts, and EDR telemetry, we could read some parts of the attacker’s workflow directly from their own code. The scripts covered several stages of post-compromise activity: command execution, credential harvesting, Active Directory reconnaissance, remote-access testing, and SMB share discovery. Parts of this tradecraft overlap with activity Microsoft documented in its analysis of the TerminalFix campaign, a ClickFix variant that ultimately deploys a reverse tunnel into the victim network. Among other things, Microsoft described a persistent PowerShell loop that watches a local file for commands, executes them, and writes the results to another file.

items.title: Facebook’s misleading privacy claims land Meta a $25 billion penalty
items.summary: Facebook’s Cambridge Analytica scandal may feel like very old news . But the consequences are still arriving, and the latest comes with a $25 billion price tag. Reuters reports that a New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in civil penalties after a jury found that Facebook misled consumers about its data practices and its handling of hate speech and misinformation. Meta says it expects to win on appeal. This case is about more than information ending up in the wrong hands. It concerns what Facebook told people about who could access their information, how much control users had, and how the company enforced its own rules. What Facebook told its users In September, jurors found that the company and its leadership made 26 misleading statements on data privacy, hate speech, and other subjects. For example , Mark Zuckerberg’s 2010 statement that: “We do not share your personal information with people or services you don’t want.” That assurance appeared in a statement the jury found misleading. The judge found that choosing who could see a Facebook post did not necessarily control what outside app developers could access. That access was governed by separate settings that many users did not know existed. New Mexico’s attorney general filed the lawsuit in 2021, following revelations that Cambridge Analytica obtained personal information from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app. But New Mexico’s case went beyond Cambridge Analytica. The state challenged Facebook’s representations to consumers about its data practices and its efforts to address misinformation and hate speech. The case centered on misleading consumers under New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act , the state’s consumer protection law. The state argued that third parties had broad access to users’ information and that Facebook tolerated harmful content when doing so benefited its business. Meta disputed the allegations, denied selling users’ information, and said the state had taken statements out of context. New Mexico’s Department of Justice says the jury found 43,899,725 violations of state law. That does not mean nearly 44 million individual New Mexicans had their data taken. The count reflected the estimated audience for each misleading statement, rather than the number of individual people affected. State law allows penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. Judge Francis Mathew found that a penalty exceeding $219 billion was warranted under the law but reduced the amount to $25 billion. The judge said earlier penalties had failed to stop Meta from misleading consumers, including a $5 billion FTC penalty in 2019 . The money is not earmarked for compensation payments to individual Facebook users. According to Attorney General Raúl Torrez, state law directs the penalties to New Mexico’s school system. Meta’s chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the company is confident it will prevail on appeal and characterized the lawsuit as an attempt to impose “a tax on speech.” Meta has also argued that a multibillion-dollar penalty risks violating constitutional protections concerning due process and excessive fines. How to stay safe on social media The case illustrates why privacy is not just a matter of choosing who can see a post. In a separate 2019 case , the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) alleged that Facebook had shared users’ information with third-party apps used by their friends, even when those users had chosen restrictive privacy settings. A few precautions can help you limit what you share, although settings alone cannot guarantee privacy: Share selectively. Leave optional profile details blank, limit who can see your posts, and avoid publishing sensitive details such as your address or live location. Ask permission before posting information or photos involving other people. Check app permissions. Does a social media app really need your contacts, precise location, or entire photo library? Turn off unnecessary access in your device settings. Review tracking and advertising settings. Look for controls covering personalized ads, activity outside the platform, and data sharing. Restrict what you can, but don’t assume opting out of personalized ads stops all collection. Be selective about connected apps. Before connecting a quiz, game, or other service to your account, check what information it requests. Decline access that seems excessive for what the service does. Remember what “private” means. Restricting your audience helps control who sees your posts. It does not stop the platform itself from collecting or using information about your activity. Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once. Malwarebytes Identity Theft Protection catches suspicious activity before it becomes a problem.

Facebook’s Cambridge Analytica scandal may feel like very old news. But the consequences are still arriving, and the latest comes with a $25 billion price tag.

Reuters reports that a New Mexico judge has ordered Meta to pay $25 billion in civil penalties after a jury found that Facebook misled consumers about its data practices and its handling of hate speech and misinformation. Meta says it expects to win on appeal.

This case is about more than information ending up in the wrong hands. It concerns what Facebook told people about who could access their information, how much control users had, and how the company enforced its own rules.

What Facebook told its users

In September, jurors found that the company and its leadership made 26 misleading statements on data privacy, hate speech, and other subjects. For example, Mark Zuckerberg’s 2010 statement that:

“We do not share your personal information with people or services you don’t want.”

That assurance appeared in a statement the jury found misleading. The judge found that choosing who could see a Facebook post did not necessarily control what outside app developers could access. That access was governed by separate settings that many users did not know existed.

New Mexico’s attorney general filed the lawsuit in 2021, following revelations that Cambridge Analytica obtained personal information from as many as 87 million Facebook users through a third-party app.

But New Mexico’s case went beyond Cambridge Analytica.

The state challenged Facebook’s representations to consumers about its data practices and its efforts to address misinformation and hate speech. The case centered on misleading consumers under New Mexico’s Unfair Practices Act, the state’s consumer protection law.

The state argued that third parties had broad access to users’ information and that Facebook tolerated harmful content when doing so benefited its business. Meta disputed the allegations, denied selling users’ information, and said the state had taken statements out of context.

New Mexico’s Department of Justice says the jury found 43,899,725 violations of state law. That does not mean nearly 44 million individual New Mexicans had their data taken. The count reflected the estimated audience for each misleading statement, rather than the number of individual people affected.

State law allows penalties of up to $5,000 per violation. Judge Francis Mathew found that a penalty exceeding $219 billion was warranted under the law but reduced the amount to $25 billion.

The judge said earlier penalties had failed to stop Meta from misleading consumers, including a $5 billion FTC penalty in 2019.

The money is not earmarked for compensation payments to individual Facebook users. According to Attorney General Raúl Torrez, state law directs the penalties to New Mexico’s school system.

Meta’s chief legal officer, C.J. Mahoney, said the company is confident it will prevail on appeal and characterized the lawsuit as an attempt to impose “a tax on speech.” Meta has also argued that a multibillion-dollar penalty risks violating constitutional protections concerning due process and excessive fines.

How to stay safe on social media

The case illustrates why privacy is not just a matter of choosing who can see a post. In a separate 2019 case, the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) alleged that Facebook had shared users’ information with third-party apps used by their friends, even when those users had chosen restrictive privacy settings.

A few precautions can help you limit what you share, although settings alone cannot guarantee privacy:

  • Share selectively. Leave optional profile details blank, limit who can see your posts, and avoid publishing sensitive details such as your address or live location. Ask permission before posting information or photos involving other people.
  • Check app permissions. Does a social media app really need your contacts, precise location, or entire photo library? Turn off unnecessary access in your device settings.
  • Review tracking and advertising settings. Look for controls covering personalized ads, activity outside the platform, and data sharing. Restrict what you can, but don’t assume opting out of personalized ads stops all collection.
  • Be selective about connected apps. Before connecting a quiz, game, or other service to your account, check what information it requests. Decline access that seems excessive for what the service does.
  • Remember what “private” means. Restricting your audience helps control who sees your posts. It does not stop the platform itself from collecting or using information about your activity.

Scammers don’t need to hack you. They just need you to click once.

items.summary: Key Takeaways Healthcare zero trust requires phased implementation that protects patient safety and clinical availability while reducing implicit trust. Legacy clinical systems can be protected through gateways and compensating controls when upgrades or agents are impractical. Strong identity controls, time-bound vendor access, and least privilege help reduce unauthorized access to critical systems. Healthcare network segmentation should follow traffic mapping, clinical engineering reviews, and carefully tested pilots. Network visibility, threat detection, and deception complement preventive controls by identifying suspicious activity across legacy systems and connected medical devices. Healthcare zero trust works when it’s phased, ranked by risk, and tested against how care is actually delivered. A hospital can’t pause an imaging suite to try a new access policy, and it can’t swap out a clinical application because a framework prefers newer infrastructure. What it can do is remove implicit trust a piece at a time. Verify identity more carefully, limit which systems may talk to each other, watch what really crosses the network, and treat clinical availability as a design requirement. NIST describes the transition the same way. Its zero trust architecture publication [1] calls it a journey that can’t be completed by wholesale technology replacement, and it expects most organizations to run a hybrid of zero trust and perimeter controls for an indefinite period. Hospitals have extra reason to move carefully. FDA notes [2] that cyber incidents have rendered medical devices and hospital networks inoperable, with delayed diagnosis or treatment as a possible result. This article covers where legacy healthcare systems and connected medical devices complicate zero trust in healthcare, how to phase the work, and where network visibility and threat detection fit. Why Zero Trust Is Different in Healthcare NIST’s definition centers on dropping trust based on network location, so every request is judged on identity, device condition, and context. In an office, a misfired policy means a help desk ticket. In a hospital, it can cut a clinician off from a record or separate a device from the system collecting its readings. A healthcare zero trust architecture has to account for that, which is why patient data security and clinical availability get weighed together. Hospitals also share the problem with manufacturers. FDA’s February 2026 guidance is directed at medical device manufacturers and FDA staff. Its recommendations are generally nonbinding, although Section 524B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act establishes statutory cybersecurity requirements for qualifying cyber-device submissions. The guidance calls cybersecurity a shared responsibility among facilities, patients, providers, and manufacturers, and it gives manufacturers an example threat-modeling assumption: hospital networks are hostile and an adversary may control them. Device makers already plan for an untrusted network. A hospital reducing implicit trust inside that network is heading the same way, and what the guidance asks manufacturers to publish becomes useful input for the hospital’s own decisions. One distinction matters across healthcare cybersecurity guidance. HHS’s HICP [3] and its performance goals [4] are voluntary and recommend zero trust and network segmentation. The current HIPAA Security Rule remains in effect. HHS’s 2024 proposal [5] would strengthen requirements for MFA, network segmentation, and asset inventories, but no final rule has been issued, so it shouldn’t be treated as current law. FDA’s guidance acknowledges the endgame for manufacturers: when a device stays in service past end of support, the maker should have a process for transferring risk to the user, and that risk grows over time. Where design fixes aren’t possible, it recommends compensating controls. That’s the opening zero trust security in healthcare needs. If the asset can’t change, the paths to it can. NIST describes an enclave model, with a gateway at the edge of a group of resources, for legacy applications that can’t talk to a gateway themselves. The cost is coarser protection, since the gateway guards the group rather than each system. Around an aging clinical application, that’s often a reasonable first step for clinical system security. Connected medical devices and IoMT security A connected device isn’t an island. FDA treats it as one piece of a system that includes the facility network, other devices, and update servers, and it asks manufacturers to consider attacks that could affect many patients at once, such as bedside monitors restarting together. That’s why medical device cybersecurity and IoMT security depend on the surrounding network as much as on the device. Identity and access management beyond the clinician login NIST counts applications and other non-human entities as subjects alongside people, and it flags automated agents as an open problem because they may authenticate with something weaker than MFA. Healthcare adds shared workstations, contractors, and vendors who maintain devices remotely. CISA’s April 2026 OT zero trust guidance [6] , which is general OT guidance rather than healthcare-specific, lists supply chain risk and identity and access management among its focus areas. MFA shows the tension: NIST warns that over-prompting users creates usability problems, and at a clinical workstation that friction has to be designed deliberately. Encrypted traffic adds opacity, though NIST notes metadata and machine learning can still help flag malicious activity. Closing these network visibility gaps comes first. Healthcare network segmentation limits lateral movement , and HHS lists it as an enhanced goal. It’s also the change most likely to collide with clinical work. NIST says early deployments often deny requests that should succeed, so expect a tuning phase, and CISA’s guidance stresses applying zero trust without disrupting the systems themselves. How to Build Healthcare Zero Trust Without Disrupting Clinical Operations NIST’s migration outline runs from identifying actors, assets, and key processes, through risk and policy for a candidate workflow, to deployment with monitoring, then expansion. Healthcare IT security teams can use it as the backbone of their own zero trust implementation. Sequence varies. Weak remote access might put vendor access first, a flat device network might put segmentation first, and a team with decent controls but little insight might start with monitoring. Map workflows and dependencies, not just devices For each workflow, record the systems it relies on, the accounts that touch them, the network paths between them, and what happens clinically if one goes down. Rank by patient-safety impact, exposure, and how exploitable the weaknesses are. Manufacturer labeling helps here: FDA says it may list network ports and destinations, a software bill of materials, and end-of-support information. A hospital can request those documents and treat them as inputs. NIST suggests starting by use case, so pick one workflow with a defensible scope. Tighten identity where change is possible Start with the most privileged and exposed access: administrator accounts, remote access, and service accounts. Give shared and service credentials owners, and retire the ones nobody can explain. Apply least privilege access where the workflow can absorb it, and test the login experience with clinical staff first. Where a legacy application can’t handle modern authentication, put the control in front of it. Treat vendor access as its own project Vendor reach tends to be broader and longer-lived than the task needs. Define what each vendor requires, route access through a controlled path with named accounts and MFA, and make it time-bound where operations allow. Segment by function, then validate with clinical engineering Begin with coarse zones, such as device networks apart from user and administrative networks, and tighten only where evidence supports it. Some devices need their connections to do their job, so isolation is a joint decision, not a security ticket. Imagine an older imaging archive running an unsupported operating system, a connected scanner, a few viewing workstations, and a vendor who services the scanner remotely. The team first lists those systems and gathers the manufacturer’s documented ports and update paths. Next it maps which systems must talk to which: scanner to archive, workstations to archive, vendor to scanner. Vendor access then moves behind a controlled path with named accounts and MFA, and the archive gets a gateway in front of it because it can’t be changed itself. NIST’s tenets include monitoring asset posture and collecting as much data as possible on assets, traffic, and access requests to improve policy. NIST also says a well-built architecture reduces risk without eliminating it, because someone holding valid credentials can still reach what that account is allowed to reach. Detection is how misuse inside permitted access gets noticed, and behavior-aware approaches are likelier to catch stolen credentials. Detection also tests the controls. Traffic between segments that shouldn’t communicate means a rule is too loose, a device is compromised, or a dependency went undocumented. It doesn’t replace prevention, though. Watching an unsegmented network with shared administrator credentials leaves the exposure in place, and no healthcare zero trust program is complete without both layers. Where Network Detection and Deception Fit Zero trust is assembled from many tools, and NIST’s 2025 practice guide [7] built 19 example architectures with 24 vendors to show it. Fidelis products sit in the detection and verification layer. They don’t set access policy, manage identities, or enforce segmentation, and they don’t make an organization HIPAA compliant. Fidelis Network ® gives teams visibility into traffic that access controls can’t explain on their own. It collects more than 300 metadata attributes of protocols and files, inspects sessions deeply, and profiles TLS traffic to help separate human from machine activity. It detects lateral movement, correlates alerts against MITRE ATT&CK, and applies new threat intelligence to stored history. Sensors cover internal as well as inbound and outbound traffic, with on-premises, VM, and cloud options. Fidelis Deception ® covers the places where installing software isn’t possible. It places decoys that resemble real assets, so any interaction is suspicious, and it works without agents on endpoints. A Fidelis customer, a university children’s hospital with nearly 5,000 staff and volunteers, deployed it out of line and agentless, with no network performance impact, and it surfaced scanning from an associate organization and unauthorized tools. That example shows a detection use case, not a full zero trust program. For identity, Fidelis Active Directory Intercept adds AD-aware detection, deception, and log monitoring to the directory service at the center of many environments. Useful indicators include: Inventory: systems and devices with a known owner and communication profile, checked against observed traffic. HHS’s proposal would require inventories and network maps reviewed at least every 12 months, but that remains proposed. Privilege: administrative and vendor accounts reviewed, and how many were narrowed or removed. Visibility: whether the paths for the highest-risk workflows are monitored and understood. Excessive access: how much was found and how long closing it took. Detection coverage: which segments and system types sit inside monitoring and which don’t. Segmentation validation: rules tested after each change, with clinical workflow checks recorded. Response time: time to investigate relevant events, tracked as a trend, not a target. The current Security Rule remains in effect, and the 2024 proposal hasn’t been finalized. Confirm legal obligations with counsel. Does network detection replace segmentation or access controls? Build a workflow-based inventory of high-impact systems, strengthen remote, administrative, and vendor access, and make critical communication paths visible before segmenting in stages. items.title: PHP2Shell: Early Attack Activity Through Imperva’s Lens
items.summary: Following the public disclosure of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), Imperva Threat Research observed a sharp increase in scanning and exploitation attempts across protected environments. What had been a small number of unsuccessful probes before disclosure quickly grew into widespread automated activity targeting sites across industries and regions. Before public disclosure, Imperva participated in the coordinated disclosure process with Wiz, OpenAI, and Calif. The researchers shared confidential vulnerability details, enabling us to assess existing protections, develop dedicated detection and mitigation rules, and prepare diagnostic testing against proof-of-concept exploits. Our involvement began with a confidential briefing from Wiz on October 12. We deployed dedicated monitoring rules that same day and refined them as our analysis progressed. When PHP announced the lifting of the embargo on October 21 at 13:38 UTC, Imperva immediately enabled the full set of PHP2Shell protection rules. Existing protections had already covered the early probing attempts. Below, we trace the disclosure and attack timeline, then examine the scale, targeting, and client behavior observed during the first 24 hours of activity. The First 24 Hours in Numbers During the first 24 hours of observed activity, Imperva recorded: 482,342 requests 122,311 attack sessions 21,998 targeted sites 103 targeted countries The activity was broad but relatively shallow: each attack session contained approximately 3.9 requests, and targeted sites received an average of nearly 22 requests during the observation period. This pattern is consistent with opportunistic spray-and-pray scanning, in which attackers probe many sites for potentially vulnerable deployments. These figures describe observed traffic and targeting. They do not represent confirmed successful exploitation or compromised sites. How the Activity Developed The aggregate figures show the scale of targeting, while the hourly distribution shows how quickly activity intensified. The chart below traces observed request volumes alongside key disclosure and patch-release milestones. Figure 1: PHP2Shell-associated requests by hour, with disclosure and patch-release milestones. All times are UTC. Following the initial increase, request volume rose sharply and reached a pronounced peak before declining. Activity continued after the peak, with several smaller spikes during the remaining observation period. This pattern is consistent with an initial burst of automated scanning and exploitation attempts followed by continued activity at lower volumes. The timing alone does not establish what triggered each spike or whether the requests came from the same tools or actors. Targeting Concentrated in the United States Sites in the United States accounted for 64.5% of targeted sites, making it the clear center of the observed activity. Indonesia was the second-most targeted country, followed by Australia, Germany, and the Brazil. Despite this concentration, associated activity reached sites across 103 countries within 24 hours. The geographic distribution shows how quickly scanning and exploitation attempts spread beyond a single region once vulnerability details became public. These percentages reflect the distribution of targeted sites within Imperva’s observations. They do not, by themselves, establish a deliberate attacker preference for particular countries. Education and Financial Services Lead Industry Targeting The activity reached organizations across a wide range of industries. Business accounted for the largest share of targeted sites at 34.3%, followed by Education and Financial Services. The distribution shows that targeting was not limited to sectors traditionally associated with high-value financial or government data. Instead, activity extended across industries likely to operate large or publicly accessible PHP environments. Automation Drives Early Activity The clients associated with the traffic further support an assessment of heavily automated activity. Almost half of the observed activity came from clients classified as browser impersonators, which present themselves as legitimate browsers. Most of the remaining activity was split between known bots and clients using the Go HTTP library. The prominence of browser impersonation suggests that many of the tools generating this traffic were designed to blend into normal web activity. At the same time, the substantial use of Go-based clients is consistent with purpose-built, high-speed tooling used to scan large numbers of targets. Imperva Customers Remain Protected As detailed in our initial analysis , Imperva Cloud WAF customers are protected against PHP2Shell out of the box. Elastic WAF customers receive protection following the applicable software update. WAF Gateway customers receive protection following the applicable software and ADC security-content updates. Existing protections covered the early unsuccessful probing attempts. Imperva also developed and refined dedicated PHP2Shell rules before public disclosure, enabling the full set immediately after the embargo was lifted. items.summary_html:
Following the public disclosure of PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619), Imperva Threat Research observed a sharp increase in scanning and exploitation attempts across protected environments. What had been a small number of unsuccessful probes before disclosure quickly grew into widespread automated activity targeting sites across industries and regions. 

Before public disclosure, Imperva participated in the coordinated disclosure process with Wiz, OpenAI, and Calif. The researchers shared confidential vulnerability details, enabling us to assess existing protections, develop dedicated detection and mitigation rules, and prepare diagnostic testing against proof-of-concept exploits. 

Our involvement began with a confidential briefing from Wiz on October 12. We deployed dedicated monitoring rules that same day and refined them as our analysis progressed. When PHP announced the lifting of the embargo on October 21 at 13:38 UTC, Imperva immediately enabled the full set of PHP2Shell protection rules. Existing protections had already covered the early probing attempts. 

Below, we trace the disclosure and attack timeline, then examine the scale, targeting, and client behavior observed during the first 24 hours of activity. 

The First 24 Hours in Numbers 

During the first 24 hours of observed activity, Imperva recorded: 

  • 482,342 requests 
  • 122,311 attack sessions 
  • 21,998 targeted sites
  • 103 targeted countries 

The activity was broad but relatively shallow: each attack session contained approximately 3.9 requests, and targeted sites received an average of nearly 22 requests during the observation period. This pattern is consistent with opportunistic spray-and-pray scanning, in which attackers probe many sites for potentially vulnerable deployments. 

These figures describe observed traffic and targeting. They do not represent confirmed successful exploitation or compromised sites. 

How the Activity Developed 

The aggregate figures show the scale of targeting, while the hourly distribution shows how quickly activity intensified. The chart below traces observed request volumes alongside key disclosure and patch-release milestones. 

Figure 1: PHP2Shell-associated requests by hour, with disclosure and patch-release milestones. All times are UTC. 

Following the initial increase, request volume rose sharply and reached a pronounced peak before declining. Activity continued after the peak, with several smaller spikes during the remaining observation period. 

This pattern is consistent with an initial burst of automated scanning and exploitation attempts followed by continued activity at lower volumes. The timing alone does not establish what triggered each spike or whether the requests came from the same tools or actors.  

Targeting Concentrated in the United States 

Sites in the United States accounted for 64.5% of targeted sites, making it the clear center of the observed activity. Indonesia was the second-most targeted country, followed by Australia, Germany, and the Brazil. 

Despite this concentration, associated activity reached sites across 103 countries within 24 hours. The geographic distribution shows how quickly scanning and exploitation attempts spread beyond a single region once vulnerability details became public. 

These percentages reflect the distribution of targeted sites within Imperva’s observations. They do not, by themselves, establish a deliberate attacker preference for particular countries. 

Education and Financial Services Lead Industry Targeting 

The activity reached organizations across a wide range of industries. Business accounted for the largest share of targeted sites at 34.3%, followed by Education and Financial Services. 

The distribution shows that targeting was not limited to sectors traditionally associated with high-value financial or government data. Instead, activity extended across industries likely to operate large or publicly accessible PHP environments. 

Automation Drives Early Activity 

The clients associated with the traffic further support an assessment of heavily automated activity. Almost half of the observed activity came from clients classified as browser impersonators, which present themselves as legitimate browsers. Most of the remaining activity was split between known bots and clients using the Go HTTP library. 

The prominence of browser impersonation suggests that many of the tools generating this traffic were designed to blend into normal web activity. At the same time, the substantial use of Go-based clients is consistent with purpose-built, high-speed tooling used to scan large numbers of targets. 

Imperva Customers Remain Protected 

As detailed in our initial analysis, Imperva Cloud WAF customers are protected against PHP2Shell out of the box. Elastic WAF customers receive protection following the applicable software update. WAF Gateway customers receive protection following the applicable software and ADC security-content updates. 

Existing protections covered the early unsuccessful probing attempts. Imperva also developed and refined dedicated PHP2Shell rules before public disclosure, enabling the full set immediately after the embargo was lifted. 

Organizations should apply the relevant PHP security updates to remediate affected deployments. WAF protections provide a compensating control while that remediation takes place. 

Imperva Threat Research continues to monitor PHP2Shell activity and refine protections as scanning tools, exploitation techniques, and attacker behavior evolve. These findings capture the first 24 hours of observed activity; the volume and distribution may change as further activity emerges.

items.title: Gcore Makes Enterprise Security Bundle Free for Public Agencies Until End of the Year
items.summary: Contern, Luxembourg, October 22nd, 2026, CyberNewswire Gcore is offering its WAAP Enterprise plan free of charge to any government body or public agency until December 31, 2026. The offer follows the php2shell vulnerabilities that forced public websites offline across Europe earlier this week. Gcore WAAP blocks the php2shell attack path (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) by default for all customers. Sites taken offline can be placed behind the service and brought back online while patching continues. The two PHP vulnerabilities, rated CVSS 9.2, allow unauthenticated remote code execution before any application code runs. Government portals in the Netherlands, Finland, Denmark, and France, along with hospitals, schools, and commercial sites, were taken offline this week on the advice of CERT-EU and national agencies. Going offline was the right call while no fix existed. Patching large estates takes days. A filtering layer that blocks the attack pattern lets a site run while that work is done. If new variants appear, Gcore updates the rule centrally and operators do not need to repeat the patching cycle. Gcore’s Enterprise plan covers domains and websites, custom rules, IP reputation, bot management, threat intelligence, API security, and SIEM integration. Public-sector organizations can apply here with an official government domain. Gcore advises all PHP operators to update to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35; restart PHP-FPM and long-running workers after updating; and restrict origin access so traffic reaches the server only through a protection layer. PHP 8.1 and older receive no official fix; operators should obtain a vendor backport or upgrade. About Gcore Gcore connects the world to AI, anywhere, anytime. items.title: Job Seekers Who Use AI for Applications Need to be on the Lookout for Scams
items.summary: Researchers at Malwarebytes warn that job seekers are increasingly vulnerable to scams as AI enables them to take a “spray-and-pray” approach to job applications. Users who have automated their job application process are more likely to forget where they’ve applied, and an unsolicited message from a recruiter may seem more plausible. Job seekers can also be more willing to overlook or ignore red flags associated with scams, since they’re anxious to avoid missing an opportunity.

items.summary: Earlier this year, I showed how to break encrypted USB drives with time-travel debugging ( slides ) at RE//verse . After having a lot of recent success with AI-assisted reverse engineering and vulnerability research, I wanted to see how well AI could handle the same tasks. The results exceeded my expectations. For one encrypted USB drive, the investigation uncovered a backdoor that let me decrypt files with alternative passwords. AI also reproduced my earlier research in seven minutes using static analysis. I tried it on two more USB-protection products I had not studied before, and it broke those too. A copy-protected USB drive The first drive was YutianDun (御天盾), sold by SecZure . It hides encrypted files from Windows Explorer and opens them through bundled readers that claim to block copying, screenshots, and printing. Fun fact: I had studied this drive before. In “Examining USB Copy Protection” in Paged Out! , issue 5 (November 2024) , I showed that a DLL injected into its PDF reader process could read a protected file that another process could not read. That broke its copy protection. I used time-travel debugging (TTD) with the help of AI to analyze it. The TTD trace revealed that the software hooks NtCreateFile and NtReadFile inside the PDF reader, supplying decrypted data. My injected DLL ran inside the same process, so it could transparently read the decrypted bytes, even though I did not know the exact mechanism back then. The cryptosystem at a glance This time, I decided to examine the security of its cryptosystem. Simply put, the Administrator password is hashed, and the hash is used to unwrap a value the code calls an “identifier.” The identifier is then used to derive the AES key that encrypts the file bytes. In simplified pseudocode: credential = MD5 ( b " [SECZURE] " + password ). hexdigest (). upper (). encode ( " ascii " ) wrap_key = HMAC_MD5 ( credential , credential ). hexdigest (). upper ()[: 16 ]. encode ( " ascii " ) identifier = AES_128_ECB_decrypt ( wrap_key , hex_decode ( administrator_record . wrapped_identifier )). rstrip ( b " \0 " ) file_key = HMAC_MD5 ( identifier , identifier ). hexdigest (). upper ()[: 16 ]. encode ( " ascii " ) plaintext = AES_128_ECB_decrypt ( file_key , ciphertext ) There are a few obvious weaknesses. First, it uses fast MD5/HMAC-MD5, not PBKDF2. Second, taking 16 hex characters for each AES key limits it to at most 64 bits of entropy. But brute-forcing 2^64 possibilities is still impractical. So far, the encryption appeared to be secure. Other mysterious users Upon closer examination of the trace, I noticed a backend login as Buffer using the password 123456 before I typed in the Administrator password. This account is hidden from the user-management screen. Its record holds some bookkeeping fields, but I did not dig into the account’s exact purpose. More importantly, its record contains another wrapped copy of the same content identifier, and its default password, as seen in the code, is 123456 . I confirmed that I could unwrap Buffer ’s identifier with 123456 and use the derived AES key to decrypt the files. Further code analysis revealed another built-in account, System , with the fixed password SECZURE.COM . On two tested drives, both accounts opened each drive’s identifier. Administrator password ──→ Administrator's wrapped identifier ──┐ Buffer / 123456 ──→ Buffer's wrapped identifier ──┼─→ content identifier → AES file key System / SECZURE.COM ──→ System's wrapped identifier ──┘ I call this a backdoor from a technical perspective: the fixed passwords decrypt files without the user’s password. That does not imply malicious intent. However, it points to a problem with opaque crypto products: a backdoor can be hard to detect, even when the main cryptosystem appears secure. Breaking NetacFileLock again I started with NetacFileLock , which I had previously analyzed using time-travel debugging (TTD) to trace the ciphertext back to its AES key. I only did one prompt: This is a file encryption utility. Analyze its crypto system and see if it is secure. You can use Binary Ninja MCP to help you. Within seven minutes, Codex reached the main flaw: the program initialized AES-256 with a fixed 32-byte key embedded in the executable. The user password was checked separately and did not determine the encryption key. This means anyone can decrypt the file without knowing the user password. During those seven minutes, the agent also made the following findings, some of which were not discussed in my talk: NetacFileLock wrote the user’s password into diagnostic logs. It encrypted independent 16-byte blocks without an IV or chaining, giving it ECB-style behavior. It used MD5 for password verification. It used an unkeyed MD5 digest as a file “signature.” Its SM4 option used another fixed key. One open question in my research was why only one-third of my test file was encrypted. That is now solved too: the behavior is not limited to PDF files; it applies to any file over 1,024 bytes when fast mode is enabled. Fast mode covers the following file formats: PNG, JPEG, GIF, TIFF, DWG, PSD, PST, DBX, Office, MDB, WPD, PDF, ZIP, RAR, WAV, AVI, RAM, RM, MPEG, MOV, ASF, and MIDI I did not bother asking AI why anyone would choose to do this. I had mixed feelings after this. On the one hand, I was surprised and even a bit worried that AI could do it so quickly. On the other hand, this is an excellent time to become much more productive with AI’s help. KakaSoft USB Copy Protection From there, I wanted to test AI against something new. After a little searching, I found a seemingly promising product category: “copy-protected” USB drives. The vendors claim that files copied onto these drives can be viewed only through their software and cannot be extracted from the device. I was immediately suspicious. If a client can display a file, it must decrypt that file; when the user controls the computer doing the decryption, preventing extraction is extremely difficult. I started with KakaSoft USB Copy Protection 5.6.0.299. I was working on macOS, while the tool runs only on Windows. This was hardly a problem: I asked the AI to handle the installer and analyze the extracted Windows binaries. The program offered three security strengths: Normal: “Hide and Lock Files.” This does not encrypt the file. High: “Scramble and encrypt file headers.” The program XORs at most the first 16,385 bytes with a byte-sized key derived from the password. There are only 256 possible keys, known file signatures reveal the key immediately, and everything after the scrambled prefix remains plaintext. Highest: “256-bit Blowfish Encryption.” This was the safest-looking option and the one I selected. The first two were obviously insecure. What caught my eye was the AI’s suggestion that it might recover a file encrypted at the Highest level without the password. When I asked for details, however, it appeared uncertain. To confirm the weakness, I ran the software and let it protect a small text file. When I inserted the protected drive, it appeared to contain only USBCopyProtect.exe , which was required to view the file. This did not bother the AI. It first located the protected data, which KakaSoft had hidden inside an unusual directory tree on the exFAT volume. Parsing the raw directory entries produced this tree: USB root └── HPSafeBox [hidden + system] ├── desktop.ini [hidden + system] ├── con.{d3e34b21-9d75-101a-8c3d-00aa001a1652} └── Important Folder └── Com1.{d3e34b21-9d75-101a-8c3d-00aa001a1652} └── \x7f\x7f\uE347.. [unusual UTF-16 name] ├── Info.bd ├── Daily.db └── NLLastF [hidden + system] └── test.txt.txt [667 bytes] HPSafeBox and NLLastF had the exFAT hidden and system attributes. The Com1.{...} component combines the reserved Windows device name COM1 with a shell CLSID-style suffix. The next directory’s on-disk name begins with two 0x7f DEL characters, followed by the private-use Unicode character U+E347 and two dots. These names confuse normal Windows path handling and help keep the tree out of Explorer. Here is a shortened hexdump of the hidden 667-byte test.txt.txt : 00000000: a0 ea 96 ca 0e 03 f0 98 0b 3e ad 18 99 a7 e3 9d .........>...... 00000010: 08 b2 f6 55 b7 2f 47 3c 0e 66 2b a9 1f 82 97 c8 ...U./G<.f+..... 00000020: b5 47 c4 22 09 08 30 2c 7a 65 9b b8 b3 1e 87 25 .G."..0,ze.....% 00000030: 45 35 49 a4 58 1c 63 5b 4e e3 ee 0a 05 48 b3 56 E5I.X.c[N....H.V ... 00000250: 20 32 34 31 38 35 36 35 37 33 31 34 32 41 44 38 241856573142AD8 00000260: 38 32 30 36 43 45 31 42 46 38 33 35 46 41 38 46 8206CE1BF835FA8F 00000270: 37 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 7............... 00000280: 00 00 00 0e 6b 61 6b 61 65 6e 63 72 79 70 74 69 ....kakaencrypti 00000290: 6f 6e 08 42 6c 6f 77 46 69 73 68 on.BlowFish The first eight bytes are a random salt, the next eight are the Blowfish CBC IV, and the ciphertext begins at offset 0x10 . The final 75 bytes start at 0x250 . This trailer contains a 32-character verifier followed by the readable strings kakaencryption and BlowFish : 8-byte salt | 8-byte IV | Blowfish ciphertext | 75-byte trailer The client was a 32-bit Delphi program. The AI followed its TBlowfishEncryption class to learn how those bytes were decrypted. Each file had its own salt and IV. The fatal problem was how the key was derived: internal password = modified MD5 of an embedded seed file key = RIPEMD-128(salt || internal password) plaintext = Blowfish-CBC-Decrypt(file key, IV, ciphertext) The first hash was recognizably based on MD5, but it was not standard MD5. Here are the first eight operations of the third round in a vanilla implementation: HH ( a , b , c , d , x [ 5 ], 4 , 0xfffa3942 ); HH ( d , a , b , c , x [ 8 ], 11 , 0x8771f681 ); HH ( c , d , a , b , x [ 11 ], 16 , 0x6d9d6122 ); HH ( b , c , d , a , x [ 14 ], 23 , 0xfde5380c ); HH ( a , b , c , d , x [ 1 ], 4 , 0xa4beea44 ); HH ( d , a , b , c , x [ 4 ], 11 , 0x4bdecfa9 ); HH ( c , d , a , b , x [ 7 ], 16 , 0xf6bb4b60 ); HH ( b , c , d , a , x [ 10 ], 23 , 0xbebfbc70 ); The rotation counts repeat 4, 11, 16, 23 . KakaSoft kept the same constants and message order, but its corresponding calls use 4, 11, 16, 16, 4, 11, 11, 4 . The changed arguments are visible in the decompiled client: Vanilla digest rendering normally looks like this: static const char hex [] = "0123456789ABCDEF" ; out [ i * 2 ] = hex [ digest [ i ] >> 4 ]; out [ i * 2 + 1 ] = hex [ digest [ i ] & 0x0f ]; KakaSoft performs the same lookup with 1903642857ACBEDF instead: This second change is only character substitution; the altered rotations are what make the raw digest differ from standard MD5. Rather than reimplementing this custom hash by hand, the AI emulated the relevant code in the client and produced the fixed internal password: AEF33093...DA1E With this value, it decrypted the file with Blowfish and restored its original bytes. In other words, the product not only failed to prevent copying; its files could be recovered without knowing the password. The static work took about two minutes to unpack the installer and another seven minutes to analyze its cryptography, requiring two prompts from me. Once I supplied the protected drive, the AI needed about 26 minutes and six short prompts–mostly confirmations about the mounted drive, test password, and analysis direction–to extract the hidden file, recover KakaSoft’s modified MD5 construction, and prove passwordless decryption. Nexcopy The second new target was Nexcopy Copy Secure , provisioned with Drive Wizard 1.0.81. The drive included both Windows and macOS viewers. The Mac viewer retained useful Objective-C method names, making its design particularly easy to follow. After plugging the protected drive into my Mac, those two viewers were all Finder showed: The protected content was encrypted this time with three-key Triple-DES in CBC mode. The problem was again how the key was stored. The drive contained an encrypted configuration file. The viewer opened it with this fixed 32-byte certificate embedded in the application: 83E89F19...A56F Both the 324-byte configuration and the 140-byte protected test.txt began with the same 36-byte ASCII marker. Here is the complete encrypted test.txt container: 00000000: 31 42 46 37 41 38 41 30 2d 36 45 42 46 2d 34 36 1BF7A8A0-6EBF-46 00000010: 42 38 2d 38 46 31 44 2d 35 35 41 44 42 36 41 46 B8-8F1D-55ADB6AF 00000020: 42 35 44 32 3b 2f 7e af c0 8f 84 c4 7f 45 fc d6 B5D2;/~......E.. 00000030: f8 68 27 bc 73 7a 3b 7a 33 c7 9e f0 46 da 70 04 .h'.sz;z3...F.p. 00000040: 53 44 46 4e 61 aa ea b9 aa d4 75 19 e8 32 b7 06 SDFNa.....u..2.. 00000050: 29 d0 3c f8 04 d7 af da c3 ab ae 46 87 a1 68 fd ).<........F..h. 00000060: 1e 9c 04 18 3c be 27 51 72 82 de 8b 5d 5c 49 98 ....<.'Qr...]\I. 00000070: c3 97 97 91 d0 10 b0 01 e1 1c 38 49 9a fc e2 6b ..........8I...k 00000080: 72 8d 45 8b 58 48 8f e6 9b 4f f6 02 r.E.XH...O.. The first 36 bytes are the marker; the remaining 104 bytes are padded 3DES-CBC ciphertext. The encrypted configuration used the same marker followed by 288 ciphertext bytes. Decrypting it with the embedded certificate produced: vid=FA6E pid="8598" prefix="7015A1496E" error_msg="Please contact [company information here] for an XXXXXXX." key="6CF96891F31A329CED2B33171D6518740AD1212B687CDACE892962F7C59F7172" password="123456" start=\Mac Viewer.app\Data The key field was the content certificate: a 24-byte 3DES key followed by an 8-byte IV. The password was a separate UI setting. fixed value in viewer ↓ encrypted configuration ↓ content key + IV ──→ protected-file decryption UI password ──→ string comparison in the viewer USB identifiers ──→ software device check The password and device checks only controlled whether the official viewer continued. They were not inputs to the file key. In fact, the Mac viewer retrieved the stored password and compared it directly with the entered text using isEqualToString: . With the content key and IV, the AI decrypted the ciphertext and restored its original contents. Nexcopy also attempted to enforce copy protection in the viewers. The code enumerated processes, intercepted screenshot-related keys, used clipboard APIs, and looked for applications such as ScreenFlow, Camtasia, Debut, Grab, and QuickTime. Those checks may discourage casual copying, but they do not protect the content key from someone who can inspect the viewer and reproduce its decryption. Altogether, the AI took about ten minutes and five prompts from me to unpack the installer, trace the cryptography, and identify the key-management failure. Conclusion I did not follow the conventional coordinated disclosure process for these bugs. If an adversary already has a device, it cannot be recalled or updated easily. I am publishing these findings directly so potential users know about these limitations and understand that their passwords may not protect their files. AI is improving rapidly, and in my experience, it has already accelerated reverse engineering and vulnerability research significantly. These examples show that, with minimal prompting, AI can independently produce valuable research results in remarkably little time. I am especially impressed by how quickly it locates the relevant code—a task that often consumes a substantial part of a human reverse engineer’s time. If you have not tried this workflow, you should. One easy way to get started is to download Binary Ninja Free and set up its MCP server —or ask your AI agent to do it for you!
