  3. It used MD5 for password verification.
  4. It used an unkeyed MD5 digest as a file “signature.”
  5. Its SM4 option used another fixed key.

One open question in my research was why only one-third of my test file was encrypted. That is now solved too: the behavior is not limited to PDF files; it applies to any file over 1,024 bytes when fast mode is enabled. Fast mode covers the following file formats:

PNG, JPEG, GIF, TIFF, DWG, PSD, PST, DBX, Office, MDB, WPD,
PDF, ZIP, RAR, WAV, AVI, RAM, RM, MPEG, MOV, ASF, and MIDI

I did not bother asking AI why anyone would choose to do this.

I had mixed feelings after this. On the one hand, I was surprised and even a bit worried that AI could do it so quickly. On the other hand, this is an excellent time to become much more productive with AI’s help.

KakaSoft USB Copy Protection

From there, I wanted to test AI against something new. After a little searching, I found a seemingly promising product category: “copy-protected” USB drives. The vendors claim that files copied onto these drives can be viewed only through their software and cannot be extracted from the device. I was immediately suspicious. If a client can display a file, it must decrypt that file; when the user controls the computer doing the decryption, preventing extraction is extremely difficult.

I started with KakaSoft USB Copy Protection 5.6.0.299. I was working on macOS, while the tool runs only on Windows. This was hardly a problem: I asked the AI to handle the installer and analyze the extracted Windows binaries.

The program offered three security strengths:

  • Normal: “Hide and Lock Files.” This does not encrypt the file.
  • High: “Scramble and encrypt file headers.” The program XORs at most the first 16,385 bytes with a byte-sized key derived from the password. There are only 256 possible keys, known file signatures reveal the key immediately, and everything after the scrambled prefix remains plaintext.
  • Highest: “256-bit Blowfish Encryption.” This was the safest-looking option and the one I selected.

The first two were obviously insecure. What caught my eye was the AI’s suggestion that it might recover a file encrypted at the Highest level without the password. When I asked for details, however, it appeared uncertain.

To confirm the weakness, I ran the software and let it protect a small text file. When I inserted the protected drive, it appeared to contain only USBCopyProtect.exe, which was required to view the file.

This did not bother the AI. It first located the protected data, which KakaSoft had hidden inside an unusual directory tree on the exFAT volume. Parsing the raw directory entries produced this tree:

USB root
└── HPSafeBox                              [hidden + system]
    ├── desktop.ini                        [hidden + system]
    ├── con.{d3e34b21-9d75-101a-8c3d-00aa001a1652}
    └── Important Folder
        └── Com1.{d3e34b21-9d75-101a-8c3d-00aa001a1652}
            └── \x7f\x7f\uE347..           [unusual UTF-16 name]
                ├── Info.bd
                ├── Daily.db
                └── NLLastF                [hidden + system]
                    └── test.txt.txt        [667 bytes]

HPSafeBox and NLLastF had the exFAT hidden and system attributes. The Com1.{...} component combines the reserved Windows device name COM1 with a shell CLSID-style suffix. The next directory’s on-disk name begins with two 0x7f DEL characters, followed by the private-use Unicode character U+E347 and two dots. These names confuse normal Windows path handling and help keep the tree out of Explorer.

Here is a shortened hexdump of the hidden 667-byte test.txt.txt:

00000000: a0 ea 96 ca 0e 03 f0 98 0b 3e ad 18 99 a7 e3 9d  .........>......
00000010: 08 b2 f6 55 b7 2f 47 3c 0e 66 2b a9 1f 82 97 c8  ...U./G<.f+.....
00000020: b5 47 c4 22 09 08 30 2c 7a 65 9b b8 b3 1e 87 25  .G."..0,ze.....%
00000030: 45 35 49 a4 58 1c 63 5b 4e e3 ee 0a 05 48 b3 56  E5I.X.c[N....H.V
...
00000250: 20 32 34 31 38 35 36 35 37 33 31 34 32 41 44 38   241856573142AD8
00000260: 38 32 30 36 43 45 31 42 46 38 33 35 46 41 38 46  8206CE1BF835FA8F
00000270: 37 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  7...............
00000280: 00 00 00 0e 6b 61 6b 61 65 6e 63 72 79 70 74 69  ....kakaencrypti
00000290: 6f 6e 08 42 6c 6f 77 46 69 73 68                 on.BlowFish

The first eight bytes are a random salt, the next eight are the Blowfish CBC IV, and the ciphertext begins at offset 0x10. The final 75 bytes start at 0x250. This trailer contains a 32-character verifier followed by the readable strings kakaencryption and BlowFish:

8-byte salt | 8-byte IV | Blowfish ciphertext | 75-byte trailer

The client was a 32-bit Delphi program. The AI followed its TBlowfishEncryption class to learn how those bytes were decrypted. Each file had its own salt and IV. The fatal problem was how the key was derived:

internal password = modified MD5 of an embedded seed
file key          = RIPEMD-128(salt || internal password)
plaintext         = Blowfish-CBC-Decrypt(file key, IV, ciphertext)

The first hash was recognizably based on MD5, but it was not standard MD5. Here are the first eight operations of the third round in a vanilla implementation:

HH(a, b, c, d, x[ 5],  4, 0xfffa3942);
HH(d, a, b, c, x[ 8], 11, 0x8771f681);
HH(c, d, a, b, x[11], 16, 0x6d9d6122);
HH(b, c, d, a, x[14], 23, 0xfde5380c);
HH(a, b, c, d, x[ 1],  4, 0xa4beea44);
HH(d, a, b, c, x[ 4], 11, 0x4bdecfa9);
HH(c, d, a, b, x[ 7], 16, 0xf6bb4b60);
HH(b, c, d, a, x[10], 23, 0xbebfbc70);

The rotation counts repeat 4, 11, 16, 23. KakaSoft kept the same constants and message order, but its corresponding calls use 4, 11, 16, 16, 4, 11, 11, 4. The changed arguments are visible in the decompiled client:

Vanilla digest rendering normally looks like this:

static const char hex[] = "0123456789ABCDEF";
out[i * 2]     = hex[digest[i] >> 4];
out[i * 2 + 1] = hex[digest[i] & 0x0f];

KakaSoft performs the same lookup with 1903642857ACBEDF instead:

This second change is only character substitution; the altered rotations are what make the raw digest differ from standard MD5.

Rather than reimplementing this custom hash by hand, the AI emulated the relevant code in the client and produced the fixed internal password:

AEF33093...DA1E

With this value, it decrypted the file with Blowfish and restored its original bytes. In other words, the product not only failed to prevent copying; its files could be recovered without knowing the password.

The static work took about two minutes to unpack the installer and another seven minutes to analyze its cryptography, requiring two prompts from me. Once I supplied the protected drive, the AI needed about 26 minutes and six short prompts–mostly confirmations about the mounted drive, test password, and analysis direction–to extract the hidden file, recover KakaSoft’s modified MD5 construction, and prove passwordless decryption.

Nexcopy

The second new target was Nexcopy Copy Secure, provisioned with Drive Wizard 1.0.81. The drive included both Windows and macOS viewers. The Mac viewer retained useful Objective-C method names, making its design particularly easy to follow.

After plugging the protected drive into my Mac, those two viewers were all Finder showed:

The protected content was encrypted this time with three-key Triple-DES in CBC mode. The problem was again how the key was stored.

The drive contained an encrypted configuration file. The viewer opened it with this fixed 32-byte certificate embedded in the application:

83E89F19...A56F

Both the 324-byte configuration and the 140-byte protected test.txt began with the same 36-byte ASCII marker. Here is the complete encrypted test.txt container:

00000000: 31 42 46 37 41 38 41 30 2d 36 45 42 46 2d 34 36  1BF7A8A0-6EBF-46
00000010: 42 38 2d 38 46 31 44 2d 35 35 41 44 42 36 41 46  B8-8F1D-55ADB6AF
00000020: 42 35 44 32 3b 2f 7e af c0 8f 84 c4 7f 45 fc d6  B5D2;/~......E..
00000030: f8 68 27 bc 73 7a 3b 7a 33 c7 9e f0 46 da 70 04  .h'.sz;z3...F.p.
00000040: 53 44 46 4e 61 aa ea b9 aa d4 75 19 e8 32 b7 06  SDFNa.....u..2..
00000050: 29 d0 3c f8 04 d7 af da c3 ab ae 46 87 a1 68 fd  ).<........F..h.
00000060: 1e 9c 04 18 3c be 27 51 72 82 de 8b 5d 5c 49 98  ....<.'Qr...]\I.
00000070: c3 97 97 91 d0 10 b0 01 e1 1c 38 49 9a fc e2 6b  ..........8I...k
00000080: 72 8d 45 8b 58 48 8f e6 9b 4f f6 02              r.E.XH...O..

The first 36 bytes are the marker; the remaining 104 bytes are padded 3DES-CBC ciphertext. The encrypted configuration used the same marker followed by 288 ciphertext bytes. Decrypting it with the embedded certificate produced:

vid=FA6E
pid="8598"
prefix="7015A1496E"
error_msg="Please contact [company information here] for an XXXXXXX."
key="6CF96891F31A329CED2B33171D6518740AD1212B687CDACE892962F7C59F7172"
password="123456"
start=\Mac Viewer.app\Data

The key field was the content certificate: a 24-byte 3DES key followed by an 8-byte IV. The password was a separate UI setting.

fixed value in viewer
        ↓
encrypted configuration
        ↓
content key + IV ──→ protected-file decryption
UI password       ──→ string comparison in the viewer
USB identifiers   ──→ software device check

The password and device checks only controlled whether the official viewer continued. They were not inputs to the file key. In fact, the Mac viewer retrieved the stored password and compared it directly with the entered text using isEqualToString:.

With the content key and IV, the AI decrypted the ciphertext and restored its original contents.

Nexcopy also attempted to enforce copy protection in the viewers. The code enumerated processes, intercepted screenshot-related keys, used clipboard APIs, and looked for applications such as ScreenFlow, Camtasia, Debut, Grab, and QuickTime. Those checks may discourage casual copying, but they do not protect the content key from someone who can inspect the viewer and reproduce its decryption.

Altogether, the AI took about ten minutes and five prompts from me to unpack the installer, trace the cryptography, and identify the key-management failure.

Conclusion

I did not follow the conventional coordinated disclosure process for these bugs. If an adversary already has a device, it cannot be recalled or updated easily. I am publishing these findings directly so potential users know about these limitations and understand that their passwords may not protect their files.

AI is improving rapidly, and in my experience, it has already accelerated reverse engineering and vulnerability research significantly. These examples show that, with minimal prompting, AI can independently produce valuable research results in remarkably little time. I am especially impressed by how quickly it locates the relevant code—a task that often consumes a substantial part of a human reverse engineer’s time.

If you have not tried this workflow, you should. One easy way to get started is to download Binary Ninja Free and set up its MCP server—or ask your AI agent to do it for you!

items.title: Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Spark Global Security Alert: Industry Experts React
items.summary: Two critical PHP vulnerabilities, the widely used programming language underpinning millions of websites and web applications, have prompted urgent warnings from cybersecurity authorities worldwide. Following reports on the 20th October that details of the vulnerabilities had leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure, PHP developers released emergency security updates on 21 October. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) urged organisations to identify affected systems and apply updates immediately, while Amazon’s threat intelligence team reported evidence of exploitation attempts dating back to 17 October. With the vulnerabilities highlighting the potential consequences of security flaws in widely used web infrastructure, The IT Security Guru has gathered reactions from cybersecurity industry experts on the risks, implications and lessons for organisations. Samuel Hassine, CEO and co-founder, Filigran : “Taking a website offline for a day is a far cheaper decision than explaining a breach for a year. The agencies asking organisations to do exactly that are giving sound advice, and the speed of the coordinated response shows how much the discipline has matured. These flaws sat in code that dates back to 2004 and were found with AI. The same tools will help attackers move just as fast, and early attacks are already being reported. The job is simple to state and hard to do. Find every system running PHP , including the ones hidden inside third-party products. Update to a supported version or take it offline. Then check that nothing got in while the window was open. Patching is the easy part. Knowing what you run is the real test.” Sai Molige, senior manager of threat hunting at Forescout : “PHP2Shell has the potential to become a Log4Shell-scale event, but for a different reason. With Log4j, the main problem was finding a library you didn’t know you had. With PHP, much of the forgotten infrastructure will be found, but won’t have an upstream fix. “The durable lesson from Log4j is that organisations should treat “How quickly can we identify where we run X” as a measurable capability separate from patching speed. “Discovering vulnerable infrastructure, however, is only the first step. When older systems have no available fix or depend on a vendor update, organisations need to reduce exposure, restrict unnecessary connections, and isolate affected systems while planning remediation. “AI is very good at performing variant analysis when it has a reference point, lowering the effort and expertise required. That could increase the volume of attempts we see with these critical vulnerabilities, even if many never turn into full exploits. “Common places where forgotten PHP tends to live include: Vendor appliances whose admin UIs are PHP: NAS devices, some firewalls and VPN portals, printers, building-management panels, and OT/ICS HMIs with web front ends. Organisations cannot patch them directly and have to wait for vendors which introduces lag. Bundled runtimes. Control panels and commercial packages often ship their own PHP binary, invisible to the OS package manager. Containers pinned to old base images. The host is current; the image from 2021 isn’t. Marketing microsites, campaign pages, and acquired-company infrastructure, often on hosting accounts paid by credit card outside IT. Admin tools on dev or jump boxes: phpMyAdmin, Roundcube, Nextcloud. Origins behind a CDN or WAF that are still directly reachable, which quietly defeats your edge rules. “Organisations concerned about exposure should prioritise identifying affected systems, reducing unnecessary external exposure, and follow vendor guidance for remediation or compensating controls. Teams should use a combination of external exposure scanning, host-level package managers, container or SBOM scans and network behavior to identify all implementations of PHP in their environment. Organisations who believe they are compromised should rotate secrets on exposed hosts, filter multipart at the edge, restrict agree from web workers, isolate EOL hosts. Look for classic web-shell patterns: php-fpm, httpd, or apache2 spawning sh, bash, curl, wget, or base64, new or modified .php files in web roots and outbound connections from web worker processes.” Oliver Simonnet, Lead Cybersecurity Researcher at CultureAI : “PHP2Shell is a clear example of how little time we now have as defenders to secure our environments in the age of AI. In a world where these types of vulnerability discoveries may become commonplace, and details being leaked before formal disclosure, exploits created exceptionally fast, and attackers exploiting the issue in the wild rapidly before fixes are even available. It’s almost impossible to justify a traditional maintenance window in this situation and what can you do if you know for a fact you’re vulnerable and you need to decide if you even can apply a temporary mitigation, or need take exposed systems offline. Its a nightmare scenario for security teams. AI may play a part in making this worse as it helps attackers develop exploits faster, but its also what gives us the power to discover these issues so they can finally be fixed. So the challenge is now to arrive at a balance where we have the capability to not only identify exposed systems, but also develop effective mitigations and get them deployed before active exploitation can cause these types of disruptions.” Charlotte Wilson, head of enterprise at Check Point : “The scale of this is enormous. We’re talking about two serious security flaws in technology that underpins around three-quarters of the internet, potentially allowing criminals to access vulnerable systems remotely without even needing a password. We’ve become so dependent on digital services that we rarely stop to consider how much of our everyday lives relies on the same underlying technology. Governments, businesses, banks and public services are all connected through an increasingly complex web of systems, and when a weakness like this is discovered, huge numbers of organisations can find themselves exposed at once. It’s a bit like discovering that millions of buildings have been fitted with the same faulty lock. Suddenly, everyone is racing to change it before someone works out how to open the door. We’ve already seen how disruption involving major technology providers can have consequences across the world, and there are growing questions about our reliance on a handful of companies to keep essential services running. Regulators are now looking much more closely at the role these providers play in our critical infrastructure. The timing is particularly concerning given the NCSC’s warnings that artificial intelligence will increase the frequency and intensity of cyberattacks. Criminals are becoming faster at identifying weaknesses and exploiting them, leaving organisations with less time to respond. When governments are choosing to take their own websites offline rather than risk leaving them exposed, it gives you a pretty clear indication of how seriously this is being taken. The immediate priority is getting systems updated, but the bigger question is whether we’ve become too dependent on technology that can leave so many organisations vulnerable at exactly the same time.” Ben Ronallo, director of cybersecurity operations at Black Duck : “This is a genuine drop-everything moment for anyone running PHP. The flaws are in the PHP engine itself, so a perfectly secure application on top of a vulnerable runtime is still exposed. Updating WordPress or your framework won’t fix it. You have to update PHP itself and restart the services that run it. It’s understandable that people are confused about how this unfolded. Word of the vulnerabilities leaked on Y Combinator’s Hacker News forum two days before the planned disclosure, and PHP moved its security release up a day in response. The source of the leak hasn’t been identified, but there’s no evidence a threat group was involved, and no exploit code was released. A screenshot of the researchers’ exploit tool did circulate, which added to the alarm. In the end, the early reports were largely accurate. The main difference is severity: PHP officially rates both flaws 9.2 rather than the 10.0 some reports cited. That’s still critical, and it doesn’t change the advice. The organizations I’m most concerned about are the ones that don’t know where PHP is running in their environment. Older versions sitting in containers, appliances, or legacy sites won’t receive an official fix. Nobody wants to be building a software inventory in the middle of an emergency. You need that visibility before the next one hits.” Tim Mackey, head of software supply chain risk strategy at Black Duck : “Preventing leaks of any vulnerability data for a CVE prior to an embargo for the patch being published is precisely what coordinated vulnerability disclosure processes are designed to protect against. When a leak, or advance knowledge, of a vulnerability occurs the entire ecosystem surrounding the vulnerability is placed at risk. As details of the leak are published, security defenders are faced with the real risk that malicious actors could use the absence of an official patch to supply their own malicious patches. Defenders should pay extra attention to the origin of their patches and validate functional changes against official release notes. After all, a malicious patch could implant a backdoor for future use and a rush to patch might present the right opportunity for malicious actors.” Jamie Akhtar, CEO and Co-founder of CyberSmart : “The NCSC advises identifying PHP across your infrastructure, prioritising internet-facing systems, and not limiting the search to outdated versions. That includes appliances and services that bundle PHP, so keep monitoring for updates from third-party vendors. Update to the latest version of PHP and apply the additional hardening steps from the PHP Team. If you cannot update, the PHP Team has provided temporary mitigations. If those cannot be applied, or would take too long, the NCSC suggests considering taking the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.” The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities serve as a reminder of how quickly weaknesses in widely used software can become a global cybersecurity concern. As organisations work to secure affected systems, the incident reinforces the importance of timely patching, continuous monitoring and maintaining visibility across the software powering critical services.

items.title: How Generative AI is Scaling Transnational Repression
items.summary: Kate Pundyk, Siena Anstis, and Marcus Michaelsen write about the rise of AI-enabled digital transnational repression in their piece for Just Security . The use of AI models to identify, monitor, and target diaspora activists and exiled dissidents around the world demonstrates how the misuse of technology produced by companies like Anthropic can have an adverse impact on human rights. Read the article

items.title: Major U.S. Banks Detect Unauthorized AI Agents Operating Inside Customer Accounts
items.summary: Major U.S. banks are detecting third-party AI agents inside customer accounts, raising concerns that automated tools could act beyond the instructions customers give them. Some agents have contacted call centers or appeared to attempt independent actions, according to an Axios report published October 22, citing people familiar with the matter. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo are among the institutions working to contain these risks. However, the report does not establish that every named bank detected unauthorized agents. Reuters also reported the findings but said it could not immediately verify them. The reported access generally starts with customers sharing their banking usernames and passwords with an AI assistant. Customers may approve that access, but the bank may not. Axios reported that such arrangements conflict with rules at most banks requiring customers to log in themselves. That distinction matters. Unauthorized AI access does not automatically mean hackers stole passwords or broke through a bank’s security systems. In these cases, customers may have opened the door themselves, creating a gap between what they allow and what their bank permits. The concern grows when agents receive permission to make purchases or move money. Bank executives fear that tools with these powers could take steps customers did not intend. Axios described attempted actions and concerns, not confirmed widespread theft or a disclosed total of financial losses. The central technical problem is linking account activity to clear human intent. A valid login can show that an account was accessed, but banks still need to determine whether the customer, an approved tool, or an agent acting beyond instructions initiated the activity. That separate report, based on Arrakis Security research, found that many inactive agents still held working credentials. It does not establish a connection to the banking incidents, but highlights the broader problem of permissions outlasting active use. A Morgan Stanley spokesperson told Axios that the bank had not observed “rogue AI agents accessing our platforms.” A Chase spokesperson warned customers not to share usernames and passwords with anyone. Those comments should not be presented as confirmation of successful autonomous account takeovers. Most banks have approved, or are moving toward, read-only access, Axios reported . This approach lets third-party tools view financial information without making transactions. Banks already support similar connections for services such as Quicken, offering a possible route for useful automation without direct control over funds. That activity is different from customers granting assistants account access. Keeping those cases separate avoids confusing deliberate cybercrime with unsafe or poorly controlled automation. For customers, the message is to follow their bank’s access rules and avoid giving banking passwords to outside AI tools. For banks, the challenge extends beyond blocking bots. They need ways to identify agents, limit permissions, and establish when a customer approved an action. Axios also reported that banks are preparing recovery plans to secure or restore customer access if incidents occur. The emerging issue is not simply whether AI can enter an account, but whether banks can reliably control what happens next. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Huntress Expands Ingram Micro Partnership Across Canada and Latin America
items.summary: Cybersecurity company Huntress has expanded its distribution partnership with Ingram Micro into Canada, Latin America and the Caribbean, strengthening its channel presence across the Americas. Building on its existing relationship in the United States, the agreement gives Huntress a single distribution route across the region, making it easier for managed service providers (MSPs) and value-added resellers (VARs) to access and deliver its cybersecurity services. The expansion comes as Huntress continues to grow internationally, following increased investment in its channel operations across Europe , Africa, Australia and New Zealand. Simplifying Cybersecurity Distribution Across the Americas By extending its relationship with Ingram Micro, Huntress aims to reduce the complexity of working across multiple markets while taking advantage of the distributor’s established local infrastructure and partner relationships. For MSPs and resellers, the agreement provides a more straightforward route to sourcing Huntress products and services through a familiar distribution partner. Kevin Hallmark, Head of Global Distribution at Huntress, said the move would help the company reach more businesses through its channel partners. “Partners are central to scaling our mission to protect all businesses, and expanding our relationship with Ingram Micro across the Americas gives more partners a simple, familiar path to Huntress.” He added: “With coverage across the U.S., Canada, and Latin America through a single distributor, we can move faster to deliver stronger security to the businesses targeted by cybercrime.” New Opportunities for Canadian MSPs In Canada, the expanded agreement will allow MSPs and VARs to access Huntress through Ingram Micro’s existing distribution network. The partnership is designed to help Canadian partners strengthen their cybersecurity portfolios without adding unnecessary complexity to their operations. Alistair Edmondson, Director of Advanced Solutions at Ingram Micro Canada, said the addition of Huntress would support partners looking to expand their managed security offerings. “Canadian partners are looking for security solutions that strengthen the protection they deliver without adding unnecessary complexity to their businesses.” He added that bringing Huntress into Ingram Micro’s cybersecurity portfolio would help partners deliver managed security services while building businesses that can scale. Supporting Growth Across Latin America The agreement also extends Huntress’ reach across Latin America and the Caribbean, where differing legal, commercial and regulatory requirements can make regional expansion challenging. Through Ingram Micro’s export division, Huntress will be able to work with a single distribution partner rather than establishing separate agreements in individual countries. Daniela Rosa, Vice President and Country Chief Executive for Latin America at Ingram Micro, said the expansion would provide partners with greater access to cybersecurity technology. “Our partners in Latin America are looking for technology relationships that can scale across borders while supporting the realities of doing business locally.” She added that the agreement would help partners extend enterprise-grade cybersecurity protection to more customers across the region. Access to Huntress’ Agentic Security Platform Under the expanded partnership, Ingram Micro channel partners will gain access to the Huntress Agentic Security Platform, supported by the company’s 24/7 AI-centric Security Operations Centre (SOC). The platform combines protection across endpoints, identities, logs, security posture and employee behaviour with human-led security expertise. It also incorporates Athena, Huntress’ agentic investigation system, which uses AI to investigate suspicious activity at machine speed while working alongside security analysts to identify and respond to complex threats. Huntress currently protects more than 280,000 businesses globally, with MSPs and resellers playing a central role in delivering its managed cybersecurity services. The latest agreement strengthens the company’s distribution network across the Americas as it looks to make managed security more accessible to partners and the organisations they support.

items.title: How to Export systemd Journal Logs with journalctl
items.summary: Run journalctl with a time window and -o json, and you get one JSON object per line with every field the journal stored: sudo journalctl --since "2026-10-19 00:00" --until "2026-10-20 00:00" -o json --no-pager > web-03_journal.jsonl For a syslog-style text file instead, use -o short-iso. Without sudo, or membership in systemd-journal, adm or wheel, you see only your own user journal, not the system’s. On most modern distros, the journal is where everything lands first: services, the kernel, sudo, cron, logins. On Debian 12 and later, Fedora and Arch, it’s often the only place, because rsyslog isn’t installed. Prime Core has {N} detection rules for Linux system logs, mapped to {M} MITRE ATT&CK techniques, among them cron persistence (T1053.003), malicious systemd services (T1543.002) and sudo abuse (T1548.003). Get Started for Free Before you start Permissions. Same rules as for any system log: root, or the groups above. Our [Linux log permissions guide] has the details. Does the journal survive reboots? If /var/log/journal doesn’t exist, logs live in memory under /run/log/journal and disappear on reboot. journalctl –list-boots shows how many boots you actually have. If it lists only the current one, older history is gone. How much is there? journalctl –disk-usage tells you before you dump it all into a file. By default, a persistent journal can grow to 10% of its filesystem, capped at 4 GB. That’s far more than you want to upload in one piece. Time zones. The journal stores timestamps in UTC, but journalctl prints local time unless you add –utc. JSON output carries the raw UTC microsecond timestamp (__REALTIME_TIMESTAMP) either way. Step 1: Narrow it down Pick the filters that match your question. They combine: Filter What it does –since / –until Time window; accepts “2026-10-19 14:00”, yesterday or “2 hours ago” -b, -b -1 Current boot, previous boot -u nginx -u ssh One or more systemd units -p warning That priority and anything more severe -k Kernel messages only _COMM=sudo, _UID=0 Match any journal field exactly Step 2: Pick the output format -o json : one JSON object per line, with every field. This is the default choice for LogTotal, because nothing gets lost. -o json –output-fields=MESSAGE,_HOSTNAME,_COMM,_PID,SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER,PRIORITY : the same, trimmed. A few fields, such as the timestamps and the boot ID, are always included. This cuts file size dramatically. -o short-iso : syslog-style text with full ISO timestamps. Smaller and easy to read by eye. [PROOF: confirm LogTotal parses short-iso] Don’t use -o export. Despite the name, it’s a serialization format for shipping journals between systemd machines, not something to analyze. We recommend you a typical scoped export: sudo journalctl -b -1 -p info -u ssh -u cron \ -o json --no-pager > web-03_prevboot.jsonl Step 3 (optional): Read journal files from another machine In incident work, you often have a disk image or a copied /var/log/journal folder rather than a live system. journalctl reads those directly: journalctl -D /mnt/evidence/var/log/journal -o json --no-pager > evidence_journal.jsonl Use –file to point at individual .journal files. A journal from a crashed or uncleanly shut down system may print corruption warnings. Most entries usually still come out. Upload, sanitize and review in LogTotal Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the .jsonl file. [PROOF: upload screen, size limit] Sanitize. [PROOF: what gets masked in journal JSON: hostnames, usernames, IPs, machine and boot IDs]. Look it over before you continue. Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows] What this looks like on real data. We exported a day of journal from [PROOF: sample source, e.g. a throwaway test VM after adding a cron job, a new user and a suspicious systemd service]. LogTotal flagged [PROOF: actual findings]. [PROOF: link to the sample file] When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix Hint about not seeing messages from other users Not root, and not in the journal groups sudo, or add the account to systemd-journal — No entries — Time window or unit name doesn’t match; local vs. UTC confusion Widen the window; try –utc; check systemctl list-units Only the current boot exists Volatile journal Older logs are gone; check your log forwarder or SIEM Output looks binary or garbled -o export was used Use -o json The file is gigabytes No filters Add units, priority, –output-fields FAQ JSON or text? JSON for analysis, because it keeps PID, unit, boot ID and exact timestamps as separate fields. Text when a person will read it, or when size matters. Is the journal the same as /var/log/syslog? No. When rsyslog is installed, it copies messages from the journal into text files, so you may have both. When it isn’t, the journal is all there is.

  3. Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows]

items.title: PHP2Chaos
items.summary: Wow, this whole PHP ( PHP2Shell ) situation is pure chaos. Everyone seemingly wants credit for it, the disclosure process was apparently botched , ( attempted ) exploitation is being observed in the wild (though there’s a big difference between a PoC and an actual working, reusable, reliable exploit), and oh , it seems like official patches might also not fully mitigate the vulnerability. Wow , where to begin… Let’s focus on what I think the funniest aspect of this whole thing is (y’know, besides the fact that PHP is still a thing), and that’s the whole who’s-taking-credit-for-finding-the-vuln situation. According to the PHP foundations press release , Quarkslab conducted a security audit of PHP in 2024 and seemingly discovered the underlying issue ( OOM ) at that time, though this was more of a theory at that point, and no actual exploit was ever cooked up. Fast-forward to 2026, where PHP brought in Calif to conduct yet another audit. During that exercise, Ryan A at Calif discovered the same underlying OOM problem and perhaps an actual workable RCE to go with it! According to the PHP press release, OpenAI and Wiz also independently reported the same root cause issue days apart. (Here they also mention that Trail of Bits had been recently reviewing PHP, but I guess they didn’t find this?). This all happened around August 11th-ish. From that point, they started working on mitigation and coordinated disclosure. (Which was also very publicly botched .) Wiz get’s directly credited by the PHP Foundation, and they of course have a published post stating as much. They discovered it (so they say). They also give a teeny-tiny mention of OpenAI and Calif, though not worded as if those firms also independently discovered the same issue, but rather that they merely have posts detailing the vuln. Pretty weak sauce from Wiz there imo. A much bigger and heartier shoutout from Wiz went to Google, specifically for their Gemini 4 Argon model which Wiz supposedly used to discover the vuln and develop the exploit. So yeah , then comes Google with their own patting of the back and tooting of the horn. They too have a nice little press release where they credit Gemini for making an “invaluable contribution to finding the vulnerability”, etc… Everyone clap for Google! They credit Wiz here, but zero mention of Calif or OpenAI (hmm wonder why? ) Now according to OpenAI , they “led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP”. You read that right. They alone led the coalition. In their opening paragraph though, they state that Calif identified the flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol. (They also throw some credit Wiz’s way here in the opening paragraph — good on them!). My question is… did OpenAI security researchers actually find this bug? Did they do so as part of their Patch the Planet initiative? Or are they merely glomming some credit because Calif used Sol in their own research? They also write quite a bit about their “key” role in coordinating the global response to the vuln. OK … maybe? 🤷‍♂️ So now on to Calif , who seemed to be universally credited for finding and reporting the bug, and who obviously had the best (and most awesomely creative) writeup . They readily credit OpenAI and Wiz in their opening statement, and then jump right into a rather thorough chronology of the bug. An important point from Calif to mention here too — they used a public model to assist with the discovery, not a private or frontier model. Finally , to spice things up even more, this site was published in the wake of all the high-fiving and such by Wiz, Google, OpenAI, etc… Seems theres more to learn about who found what… Honestly… I just don’t know who to believe (though I do have a strong hunch). It seems everyone and their mom has come out in the aftermath to say they had some part to play in the discovery, or the weaponization, or the disclosure process… blah , blah . It’s really unlike anything I’ve ever seen. Everyone wants a piece of this very particular pie. And for what?? Yes, PHP is everywhere , and a true noauth RCE against PHP would/could be quite devastating to the Internet at large. But has it amounted to much thus far? Reports suggest… not really . Time will tell of course, and folks (both good and bad) are undoubtedly working around the clock to produce a reliable exploit for this, but I haven’t seen any reports of real impacts — just that attempted exploitation is being lobbed over the Internet at scale. If there’s any actual impacts to speak of thus far, it’s merely site outages as a result of admins simply shutting sites off to prep for patching. I’ve also seen a smattering of posts across social media about how the patches don’t fully address the bug, or that they address only specific things, but adjacent issues are still readily exploitable, or that the underlying OOM issue itself simply cannot be fixed at all. I can’t speak to the accuracy of any of these posts, but I find the idea that all this jostling for credit has happened for a bug that either A. doesn’t end up being that impactful and/or B. is quickly superseded by other, similar bugs, to be pretty hilarious. Stay tuned. There’s obviously more to come on all things PHP2Shell / PHP3Shell / phpbleed / PHP-in-general… er …, y’know what, let’s just call this what it is… PHP2Chaos .

I’ve also seen a smattering of posts across social media about how the patches don’t fully address the bug, or that they address only specific things, but adjacent issues are still readily exploitable, or that the underlying OOM issue itself simply cannot be fixed at all. I can’t speak to the accuracy of any of these posts, but I find the idea that all this jostling for credit has happened for a bug that either A. doesn’t end up being that impactful and/or B. is quickly superseded by other, similar bugs, to be pretty hilarious.

Stay tuned. There’s obviously more to come on all things PHP2Shell / PHP3Shell / phpbleed / PHP-in-general…er…, y’know what, let’s just call this what it is… PHP2Chaos.

items.title: eMudhra Exits Global SSL/TLS Certificate Business Following the Vulnerability Disclosure
items.summary: eMudhra Limited has announced it is exiting the global SSL/TLS certificate business after disclosing weak private keys in eight intermediate certificate authority certificates. The October 22, 2026, decision follows emergency browser protections and growing questions about the company’s certificate issuance controls. eMudhra said its other digital trust services remain unaffected. In its official announcement , the company said its board approved the voluntary exit after reviewing the incident and the business outlook. Chairman V. Srinivasan said eMudhra revoked the affected CA certificates within 14 hours of discovery and promptly disclosed the issue. The company said none of the affected intermediate CAs had issued end-entity certificates, which websites or software publishers use. It also said its infrastructure was not compromised, no data was breached, and all physical and logical security controls remained intact. Weak Private Keys Triggered Emergency Action The incident began with an October 17 report from a researcher identified as Wayne. According to Mozilla’s public incident record , the researcher supplied proof of control over eight private keys. Mozilla independently recovered the keys, confirming that their generation process was seriously flawed. Six affected certificates supported TLS, while two supported code signing. The technical problem was a lack of randomness. CERT-In said the affected P-384 elliptic-curve private keys had values smaller than 256, allowing them to be recovered almost instantly from their public keys. The failure was in key generation, not in the P-384 algorithm itself. eMudhra’s preliminary explanation pointed to an April 30, 2025, key-generation ceremony. A flawed script used during a key wrap and unwrap step created a second, weak set of keys. Similar key labels then led staff to use those weak keys in certificate signing requests instead of the original strong keys. As covered in CybersecurityNews’ earlier report on the eMudhra certificate authority compromise , the issue prompted emergency blocking measures. Anyone recovering these keys could potentially issue false certificates. Where affected chains remained trusted, an attacker able to intercept network traffic could impersonate websites or alter communications. Google and Mozilla blocked the affected TLS keys on October 17. Both also moved toward removing trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3, protecting clients that do not reliably receive or enforce intermediate certificate revocation information. CERT-In said Chrome’s root-store change was expected to reach relevant devices on October 27. eMudhra estimated that about 30,000 certificates required migration. Those certificates should not be confused with certificates issued by the eight weak intermediates. CERT-In said public disclosures had not established confirmed malicious exploitation as of October 21. The response reflects the wider consequences of certificate authority failures, also seen in Google’s removal of two certificate authorities from Chrome . Browser trust decisions can force website operators to replace otherwise valid certificates to keep services accessible. eMudhra said global SSL/TLS contributes about 1% of its revenue. Rising data sovereignty requirements, compliance costs and competition from free certificate providers have reduced the business’s returns. Srinivasan also argued that social media scrutiny was out of proportion to the segment’s size. The company plans to keep its G1 RSA roots serving customers during the transition and provide replacement certificates through partners at no cost. Revocation and certificate status services will continue until issued certificates expire or are replaced. It also committed to completing browser-program obligations, including a full root-cause report. Meanwhile, CERT-In’s advisory urges administrators to update browsers and trust stores, review certificate chains, and replace affected certificates. Teams should also check separate certificate bundles in applications, containers, and network devices, rather than assuming browser updates protect every system. items.title: Claude Security Now Scans Repositories Continuously to Find Flaws and Track Fixes
items.summary: Anthropic has updated Claude Security so it can keep checking connected code repositories as they change, rather than waiting for a person to start each scan. The service also tracks reported vulnerabilities after developers make changes, marks them fixed when a correction is detected, and reopens them if they return. The updated product is in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers. Anthropic says thousands of organizations have used Claude Security since its public beta began in April, finding more than one million vulnerabilities. That figure comes from the company and has not been independently confirmed. The update aims to help security and development teams keep findings closer to the current state of their software, where new code can introduce risks and older fixes can stop working. Claude Security Continuous Scans Teams start by creating a project, connecting repositories, and choosing the branches and code areas to scan. The service supports the Claude GitHub app, including GitHub Enterprise Server, and access tokens for GitLab and other Git providers. It first performs a deep scan to set a baseline. After that, it checks code changes at intervals based on their risk and complexity. Anthropic says there is no fixed scan schedule. A project can include multiple repositories. This matters because a security problem may involve how two services work together, rather than a flaw in one file. For example, a backend service may trust that a client has already checked user input. Looking across connected code can help Claude Security assess such relationships and trace how data moves through an application. Anthropic describes the tool as using its Claude models, including Claude Mythos, for security analysis. It says customers do not need access to the Cyber Verification Program to use the product. Findings include a severity rating based on the project’s threat model, an explanation of how the vulnerable code may be reached, and, in some cases, a diagram showing the path through the application. The company says its updated service builds on an earlier security-scanning effort. Cyber Security News previously reported on Anthropic’s launch of Claude Code Security , which focused on finding and reviewing code flaws. Its coverage of Claude Code vulnerabilities also highlights why teams need to consider security boundaries when AI tools work with project files and development settings. Finding a problem is only one part of vulnerability management. Teams still need to decide whether a finding applies to their environment, assign it, make a change, and confirm the issue is gone. Claude Security checks open findings against changed code and can mark them fixed when a correction lands, even if the work happened outside Claude Code. If a later scan detects the same issue again, the finding reopens. The service also lets teams add knowledge that code alone cannot show. A project can include details about how software is deployed, which security rules apply, and what controls already protect a system. Claude Security generates a threat model from the code, which the team can review and edit. Later scans use that model to help judge which issues matter and how severe they are. This context can reduce attention on risks that the organization has already addressed, though teams still need to check that the information is correct. To fit existing security work, Anthropic has added an API, webhooks, and an MCP connector for Claude.ai and Claude Code. Teams can use the API to read findings, manage projects, and resolve or reopen issues. Webhooks can send alerts when new findings appear. The MCP connector lets engineers discuss a finding and work on a fix from a Claude session. Role-based access controls let administrators set who can view projects, review findings, or create projects. The service remains in beta, so organizations should treat its findings and fix status as useful signals, not a replacement for human review. Anthropic’s help documentation says scan results can vary between runs and that proposed fixes should be reviewed before use. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: A New Extortion Gang Is Naming Companies on the Dark Web and Counting Down to Data Leaks
items.summary: ScarlettGroup, a newly observed cyber extortion gang, is naming companies on a dark web leak site and using countdown timers to threaten the release of allegedly stolen data. The operation puts public pressure on organizations before their breach claims have been independently verified. The group began appearing in threat monitoring records around September 2026 and became more visible during October. Its listings span technology, education, government, and entertainment, but available evidence does not show a clear focus on one industry or confirm the scale of its activity. Researchers from Foresiet documented ScarlettGroup’s activity in a report published on October 21, 2026. Foresiet’s threat intelligence research describes an emerging extortion operation, not a confirmed malware family. The researchers have not established how the attackers gain access or whether they deploy ransomware that encrypts files. A New Extortion Gang Is Naming Companies on the Dark Web ScarlettGroup’s Tor leak site displays alleged victims alongside publication dates, industry labels, disclosure status, and countdown timers. These details turn an unverified breach claim into a visible deadline. The aim appears to be pushing targeted organizations toward contact before the group releases the information it claims to hold. The approach resembles pressure seen in Everest’s alleged BMW breach , where a leak site countdown accompanied claims about stolen internal records. That comparison concerns the public pressure tactic only; it does not establish any connection between Everest and ScarlettGroup or prove either group’s claims. Criminal leak sites (Source – Foresiet) ScarlettGroup describes a process with three stages: public listing, a negotiation window, and closure or disclosure. During negotiations, an organization can communicate with the operators. The group claims a settlement leads to removal of the listing and deletion of the data, while failure to settle may trigger publication. Those promises remain claims made by criminals. Foresiet notes there is no independent guarantee that information will be deleted after a settlement. A removed listing therefore should not be treated as proof that copies no longer exist or that any possible network access has ended. What Researchers Have Actually Observed Foresiet documented ScarlettGroup activity on PwnForums, including alleged breach announcements and data offerings. Reported links involving BreachForums and DarkForums still require verification. Forum posts can spread allegations beyond a single leak site, increasing attention while also giving defenders leads for further checks. The lack of confirmed encryption is important. In the separate PAYLOAD attack without encryption , attackers used Windows domain policies and stolen data to create pressure. ScarlettGroup’s known activity is different: its public threats are documented, but comparable technical details about its intrusion methods have not been established. The report does not identify an exploited vulnerability, a malware payload, or a verified route into victim networks. It also provides no confirmed victim count. Treating those gaps as evidence of a particular attack method would go beyond the findings and could mislead security teams investigating an alert. Foresiet recommends checking criminal claims against independent evidence, preserving forensic material, and monitoring unusual downloads and data transfers. A company named on the site should investigate possible unauthorized access without presenting the listing itself as confirmation that a breach occurred. Access controls remain central to prevention. Coverage of Pink’s cloud credential theft shows how another extortion operation targeted accounts and cloud files. That case is separate from ScarlettGroup, but it underlines the value of Foresiet’s advice to strengthen multifactor authentication, limit account permissions, and review exposed credentials. Organizations should also assess internet facing systems and keep incident response procedures ready. Monitoring leak sites and underground discussions can help identify claims early, but useful intelligence requires context. The priority is to establish what happened, which information may be affected, and whether unauthorized activity is continuing. For now, the clearest evidence concerns the gang’s public extortion process, not its tools. That distinction matters for defenders: a timer can force urgent decisions, but it cannot establish the origin, age, or ownership of the advertised records. Investigators need evidence from their own systems before judging the claim’s scope or linking it to a wider security incident and planning a response. The deadline itself is not forensic evidence. Indicators of compromise (IoCs):- Type Source disclosure SHA or other file hashes Not published Malware filenames or samples Not published IP addresses or domains Not published Tor leak site address Not published Threat actor name ScarlettGroup Forum activity PwnForums documented; other associations unverified Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: DOQEX Achieves Cyber Essentials Certification to Strengthen Security Standards
items.summary: UK-based secure data exchange specialist DOQEX has achieved Cyber Essentials certification, adding another recognised security standard to its existing portfolio of accreditations. The York-based company, which specialises in protecting sensitive information shared between organisations, already holds ISO 27001, ISO 27017 and ISO 27018 certifications. The latest achievement reflects its continued focus on maintaining strong security controls and protecting customer information. Cyber Essentials is a UK Government-backed scheme designed to help businesses defend themselves against common cyber threats. It assesses five fundamental areas of cybersecurity: firewalls, secure configuration, security update management, user access control and malware protection. Getting the Cybersecurity Basics Right While DOQEX already operates under established international security standards, the company said completing the Cyber Essentials certification process provided a valuable opportunity to revisit its existing controls. Nick Case, Director and Co-Founder of DOQEX, admitted that the company had initially underestimated the process. “Having already achieved ISO 27001, ISO 27017 and ISO 27018, I’ll admit we initially underestimated Cyber Essentials. We thought we had the fundamentals well covered, but going through the process reminded us why they matter.” He explained that the certification’s emphasis on practical security measures provided an important reminder that even organisations with mature cybersecurity programmes need to regularly assess their defences. “Cyber Essentials has a clear focus on practical, verifiable security controls, and that has genuine value. It’s easy to concentrate on more complex security challenges, but the basics still need attention.” The certification comes as organisations face increasing pressure to demonstrate that appropriate security measures are in place, particularly when handling sensitive business information or working with external suppliers. Strengthening Trust Across the Supply Chain As businesses become more reliant on third-party technology providers and external partners, cybersecurity certifications are playing a growing role in procurement decisions and supplier assurance. Recognised standards can help organisations demonstrate that they have implemented appropriate safeguards, providing customers and partners with greater confidence in how their information is managed. Case believes improving baseline security across UK businesses is particularly important as supply chains become more interconnected. “We fully support what Cyber Essentials is trying to achieve. Raising the baseline of cybersecurity across UK businesses is important, particularly as organisations become increasingly dependent on suppliers and third parties. Stronger security across the supply chain benefits everyone.” Supporting Secure Data Exchange Founded in 2013, DOQEX helps organisations securely manage and exchange sensitive information between employees, customers, suppliers and business partners. Its services combine security technology with managed support, helping businesses maintain control over information as it moves between organisations. The Cyber Essentials certification builds on the company’s existing ISO standards and reinforces its approach to security governance, accountability and data protection. For DOQEX, the achievement also highlights a wider message for businesses: while cybersecurity threats continue to become more sophisticated, maintaining effective fundamental controls remains an essential part of protecting sensitive information.

items.title: Where to Find Linux auditd Logs and How to Export Them
items.summary: auditd writes to /var/log/audit/audit.log, readable only by root. The quickest export of a time window in the original format is: sudo ausearch --raw -ts yesterday > web-03_audit.log If /var/log/audit doesn’t exist, auditd isn’t installed. That’s the default on Debian and Ubuntu. The kernel’s audit events then go to the journal, where journalctl _TRANSPORT=audit finds them. auditd is Linux’s answer to “who ran what, and touched which file”: process execution, file access, permission changes and account changes, down to the syscall. Prime Core has 1350 detection rules for auditd data, mapped to 440 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: malicious shell use (T1059.004), planted SSH keys (T1098.004) and permission changes on sensitive files (T1222.002). Get Started for Free Before you start Is it running, and what is it recording? systemctl is-active auditd sudo auditctl -l Red Hat-family systems install auditd by default; Debian and Ubuntu need the auditd package. If auditctl -l prints No rules, you still get a baseline of logins, authentication and SELinux denials. You won’t get command execution or file-access records, though, because nobody asked for them. Root only. /var/log/audit is locked down tightly, so plan on sudo. Rotation is auditd’s own. auditd rotates its log itself, based on max_log_file and num_logs in /etc/audit/auditd.conf, into audit.log.1, audit.log.2, and so on. Older history sits in those files. The format takes getting used to. One event is often several lines (SYSCALL, EXECVE, CWD, PATH, PROCTITLE) sharing the same msg=audit( : ) stamp. Values with spaces are hex-encoded. That’s normal. Step 1: Export with ausearch ausearch filters by time, record type or rule key, and –raw keeps the original format: # a day, raw sudo ausearch --raw -ts yesterday -te today > web-03_audit.log The keywords today, yesterday, this-week and recent (last ten minutes) save you from date formats. Explicit dates follow your locale, 10/19/2026 00:00:00 in en_US, which is where most “no matches” surprises come from. For an upload, keep –raw: the original records carry more than the interpreted view. auditd writes to /var/log/audit/audit.log, readable only by root. The quickest export of a time window in the original format is:

sudo ausearch --raw -ts yesterday > web-03_audit.log

If /var/log/audit doesn’t exist, auditd isn’t installed. That’s the default on Debian and Ubuntu. The kernel’s audit events then go to the journal, where journalctl _TRANSPORT=audit finds them.

auditd is Linux’s answer to “who ran what, and touched which file”: process execution, file access, permission changes and account changes, down to the syscall. Prime Core has 1350 detection rules for auditd data, mapped to 440 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Among them: malicious shell use (T1059.004), planted SSH keys (T1098.004) and permission changes on sensitive files (T1222.002).

Get Started for Free

Before you start

Is it running, and what is it recording?

systemctl is-active auditd

sudo auditctl -l

Red Hat-family systems install auditd by default; Debian and Ubuntu need the auditd package. If auditctl -l prints No rules, you still get a baseline of logins, authentication and SELinux denials. You won’t get command execution or file-access records, though, because nobody asked for them.

Root only. /var/log/audit is locked down tightly, so plan on sudo.

Rotation is auditd’s own. auditd rotates its log itself, based on max_log_file and num_logs in /etc/audit/auditd.conf, into audit.log.1, audit.log.2, and so on. Older history sits in those files.

The format takes getting used to. One event is often several lines (SYSCALL, EXECVE, CWD, PATH, PROCTITLE) sharing the same msg=audit(:) stamp. Values with spaces are hex-encoded. That’s normal.

Step 1: Export with ausearch

ausearch filters by time, record type or rule key, and –raw keeps the original format:

# a day, raw

sudo ausearch --raw -ts yesterday -te today > web-03_audit.log

The keywords today, yesterday, this-week and recent (last ten minutes) save you from date formats. Explicit dates follow your locale, 10/19/2026 00:00:00 in en_US, which is where most “no matches” surprises come from.

For an upload, keep –raw: the original records carry more than the interpreted view.

If you’d rather just take everything, concatenate the files oldest-first:

sudo cat $(ls -tr /var/log/audit/audit.log*) > web-03_audit_all.log
Step 2 (no auditd): Get audit events from the journal

Without auditd, the kernel’s audit records still reach journald:

sudo journalctl _TRANSPORT=audit --since yesterday -o json --no-pager > web-03_audit.jsonl

With no rules loaded, expect mostly logins and SELinux or AppArmor messages, but it’s better than nothing.

  2. Sanitize. [PROOF: what gets masked in auditd records: usernames, hostnames, IPs, paths]. Look it over before you continue.
  3. Review.

items.title: Scammers are finding new ways to target your phone. Here are 5 ways to protect yourself
items.summary: The warnings are everywhere these days. Don’t click this. Don’t open that. Don’t scan this. Don’t download that. These messages of caution, however well-intended, are so ubiquitous and constant that it should come as no surprise that some people have started to tune them out. How many people? About one in three, according to our recent study . Keeping up with every warning can feel exhausting. Meanwhile, scammers are finding new ways to target people and phones give them plenty of opportunities. Mobile phones give scammers multiple ways to reach people, from text messages and calls to social media posts. According to a 2022 Federal Communications Commission report cited by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), texting is a more common communication method than voice or email. Criminals appear to be taking advantage of that fact. Consumers reported losing $470 million to text scams in 2024, up 26% from $373 million the year before and more than five times the amount reported in 2020. The FTC cites estimates that text message open rates run as high as 98%, compared to just 20% for email. People’s tendency to open and read their texts helps explain their appeal to scammers. Meanwhile, AI is making scams harder to detect, but better at impersonating people and companies to steal money, passwords, and identities. Voice phishing , or “vishing,” was a vanishingly small category of crime just a few years ago, but AI has made it considerably more convincing. Vishing doubled in the first half of 2026, according to CrowdStrike’s 2026 Threat Hunting Report. Meanwhile, 16% of adults in the Malwarebytes survey said they had received a voice-cloned phone call impersonating someone they knew in the past year. Our data also shows how difficult people find it to recognize scams: 85% of survey respondents said it’s hard to tell a scam from the real thing, up from 66% a year ago. And 84% said convincing video evidence no longer feels like the rock-solid proof it once was. Here are five ways to protect yourself 1. Treat unexpected texts and social media posts with suspicion Legitimate institutions generally won’t ask for payment or personal information through unsolicited texts. And if the message is marked “urgent,” all the more reason to pause. Instead, go directly to the company’s official website and inquire there. AI-generated images and videos are making it harder to tell what’s real online, so don’t rely on what you see as proof that a request is legitimate. If the content involves someone you know, contact them directly using a number you already trust. 2. Keep your operating system updated This is one of the most effective things you can do to keep your phone safe. Security updates patch vulnerabilities that malware takes advantage of. Malwarebytes’ threat research found Android malware detections rose 151% in the first half of 2025. On both iPhone and Android, automatic updates help decrease risk. 3. Protect your accounts Use a strong, unique password for every account. A password manager can create and store them for you. Where available, use a passkey—a way to sign in using your device, often with your fingerprint, face, or PIN—that resists phishing. Turn on two-factor authentication, also called 2FA, for all your apps that allow it. This one step makes it harder for criminals who have your password to gain access to accounts on your phone. 4. Be skeptical of voice calls, even from your mom This can be the hardest one to get your head around, but also one of the most dangerous and fastest-growing. AI-synthesized audio fraud has made it easier for scammers to sound convincingly like a loved one in trouble. Agree on a private code word with family members and friends in case of doubt or emergency. If you’re unsure, hang up and call the person on a number you already have. If the caller claims to be your bank, hang up and call back on a number you look up independently. 5. Check links before you tap, including links in QR codes Before opening a link in a text, email, or social media post, check the web address for misspellings or an unfamiliar domain. You can also copy it into the free Malwarebytes Scam Link Check for help assessing it. QR codes can hide suspicious links, too. Scammers sometimes place fake sticker overlays on top of legitimate QR codes in public spaces, and QR code phishing is morphing so fast that the FBI issued an alert in January about North Korean hackers using QR codes to target think tanks and government officials. Look for signs of tampering and check the web address your phone displays before opening it. If you’re not sure, don’t open the link. Instead, go directly to the organization’s official website or app. Scammers rely on speed and pressure, so the best defense is to slow down. If a message or call feels off, step away and check it through a channel you already trust. “One of the best cybersecurity suites on the planet.” According to CNET. Read their review →

items.title: Hackers Were Targeting Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
items.summary: A threat actor tried to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities four days before the flaws were publicly disclosed and patched, according to Amazon Threat Intelligence. The activity began on October 17, 2026, while the vulnerabilities were still under coordinated disclosure. The flaws, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and known together as PHP2Shell, can allow remote code execution on affected web servers. The early attempt was recorded by MadPot, Amazon’s network of honeypots—systems designed to attract and observe suspicious activity. It came from an IP address linked to a commercial anonymization service. AWS said it is not clear how the actor obtained information about the vulnerabilities before disclosure, or whether the attempt would have succeeded against a real server. Analysts from AWS also observed several more PHP2Shell attempts on October 21, before the public release of the fixes. The first proof-of-concept activity appeared around 02:00 UTC, about 12 hours before the disclosure window opened at 14:00 UTC. The activity used different payloads and anonymized infrastructure, which AWS said may indicate several actors. Additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared after disclosure, and AWS reported that PHP2Shell was being widely exploited. Hackers Were Targeting Critical PHP Vulnerabilities Days The vulnerabilities affect PHP’s handling of memory and request data. CVE-2026-109618 is tied to an out-of-memory condition that can leave internal data in an incomplete state. CVE-2026-109619 involves stale state that may remain in a long-running PHP worker and be used during a later request. In some cases, attackers may be able to use these flaws to run code remotely, without first logging in. The PHP security team released fixes on October 21. Patched versions include PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27 and 8.5.12. Older PHP branches may also need vendor-provided updates or an upgrade to a supported release. Teams should check the specific package or distribution they use, as some vendors may backport a fix without changing the version number shown by the upstream PHP project. Cybersecurity News previously covered the PHP team’s emergency patch warning , which urged administrators to prepare for the release. A later report detailed the emergency PHP2Shell security updates . The reports describe separate stages of the same story: the advance warning, followed by the patches for the two flaws. Why the early activity matters A patch release does not mark the start of risk. Attackers may learn about a weakness before public disclosure, as AWS’s October 17 observation suggests. After a fix is published, other attackers can also study the changes and develop working tools quickly. AWS said proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours of disclosure and urged defenders not to treat the public announcement date as the earliest possible date of exploitation. That means teams should review activity from before the patch date, not just investigate alerts generated afterward. AWS recommends starting the review from at least October 17. Relevant checks include web server logs, unusual process launches and unexpected file changes on PHP hosts. Administrators should also look for POST requests containing the string PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS in form uploads. Organizations should update PHP runtimes as soon as possible and confirm that production workers are running the fixed code. This includes checking web servers, containers and managed hosting environments, rather than relying only on the PHP version installed for command-line use. A restart or redeployment may be needed so long-running workers stop using the old runtime. If an immediate update is not possible, AWS suggests considering restrictions on multi-part file uploads. Such a change may affect normal application functions, so teams should assess the impact before applying it. AWS says configuration-only changes do not fully fix both vulnerabilities; upgrading to a fixed version is the complete remediation. For more context on reports of activity before the patch, see Cybersecurity News’ coverage of early PHP2Shell exploitation attempts . Another report covers the public PHP2Shell testing tool . Together, these reports underline why defenders should use multiple signals and avoid depending on a single CVE-specific detection rule. Indicators of comproise (IoCs):- IP address Observed date 103.216.220.92 October 17, 2026 31.223.184.166 October 21, 2026 37.19.200.5 October 21, 2026 134.209.159.64 October 21, 2026 103.114.163.188 October 21, 2026 95.217.98.37 October 21, 2026 Note: IP addresses and domains are intentionally defanged (e.g., [.] ) to prevent accidental resolution or hyperlinking. Re-fang only within controlled threat intelligence platforms such as MISP, VirusTotal, or your SIEM . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Exposed Refrigeration Systems Raise Global Cybersecurity Concerns
items.summary: Cybersecurity researchers at Forescout are drawing attention to the risks posed by exposed refrigeration control systems, warning that weaknesses in operational technology (OT) could have serious consequences for food supplies, business continuity and other temperature-sensitive operations. The warning comes following cyberattacks against French supermarkets in October 2026, which reportedly disrupted refrigeration systems at hundreds of stores. Attackers were able to interfere with cooling operations, resulting in temperature fluctuations, spoiled stock and significant disruption. The incidents have raised concerns about the security of internet-connected refrigeration equipment, particularly where older systems, exposed management interfaces and inadequate access controls leave operational technology vulnerable to interference. When Cyberattacks Have Physical Consequences Unlike conventional IT attacks, which frequently focus on stealing data or disrupting digital services, attacks against refrigeration controllers can directly affect physical processes. These systems are responsible for maintaining temperatures across supermarkets, food storage facilities and other environments where consistent cooling is essential. If attackers gain sufficient access, they may be able to manipulate temperature settings, interfere with defrost cycles or disrupt equipment operations. The consequences can extend beyond IT downtime to include damaged stock, financial losses and potential safety risks. The issue also extends beyond food retail. Refrigeration and temperature-control systems are used in healthcare, pharmaceuticals, manufacturing and logistics, making their security an important consideration across several industries. Internet Exposure Creates Opportunities for Attackers One of the central concerns is the accessibility of operational technology that was not originally designed to withstand direct exposure to the internet. Remote management capabilities allow engineers and third-party maintenance providers to monitor and adjust refrigeration equipment without visiting individual sites. However, these connections can introduce security weaknesses if they are poorly configured or inadequately protected. Research into industrial control systems has identified publicly accessible management interfaces, outdated firmware and weak authentication as recurring problems. In some cases, organisations may not have complete visibility of the equipment connected to their networks, particularly where systems have been installed and maintained by external contractors. Forescout Finds Nearly 13,000 Exposed Refrigeration Services Worldwide New research from Forescout’s Vedere Labs has identified 12,976 internet-exposed service observations across ten product groups, associated with 6,017 distinct public IP addresses in 99 countries and territories. The findings suggest that the weaknesses highlighted by the French supermarket attacks are part of a much wider global problem. The largest number of observations involved Copeland/Dixell XWEB services, with 7,075 recorded, followed by 4,697 Danfoss StoreView services. Researchers also identified 551 Copeland Site Supervisor services, 513 Carel pCOWeb services and 140 observations across six other product groups. Importantly, these figures represent exposed services rather than confirmed compromised devices. A single IP address may host multiple services, while one management interface may control several downstream systems. The researchers also found that 3,762 Danfoss StoreView service observations, representing 80% of the total, were running firmware older than version 4.3.1, making them potentially vulnerable to two previously disclosed security flaws. Hacktivists Have Targeted Refrigeration Before Forescout’s research suggests that attacks against refrigeration systems are not a new development. According to a technical bulletin published by Danfoss, hacktivist attacks in 2022 affected 16 Russian supermarkets and 40 stores in Israel. Forescout has also tracked more than 20 claimed attacks against refrigeration systems since January 2026, with pro-Russian hacktivist groups Z-Pentest Alliance and NoName057(16) among the most active. Targets have included supermarkets, wineries, fruit storage facilities and agricultural businesses across Europe. However, the researchers stress that the initial access methods and identities of those responsible for the recent French attacks have not been confirmed. Securing the Cold Chain Forescout is urging organisations to review how refrigeration management systems are connected to the internet and who is authorised to access them. Recommendations include removing publicly accessible management interfaces, replacing unsupported equipment, applying available security updates and introducing secure remote access for maintenance contractors. The researchers also recommend multifactor authentication, individual user accounts and continuous monitoring to identify suspicious changes to temperature settings, defrost schedules and alarms. The challenge is that attackers do not necessarily need to deploy malware to cause disruption. Once they gain sufficient access, they may be able to misuse legitimate management functions, making malicious activity harder to distinguish from routine maintenance. The research highlights a broader issue for operational technology security: organisations need visibility not only of connected devices, but also of who can access them, what changes they can make and how those changes affect physical operations. Read the full research here: Cold Chain, Open Control: Exposed Refrigeration Systems Reveal Global Risk
