Recommendations include removing publicly accessible management interfaces, replacing unsupported equipment, applying available security updates and introducing secure remote access for maintenance contractors.

The researchers also recommend multifactor authentication, individual user accounts and continuous monitoring to identify suspicious changes to temperature settings, defrost schedules and alarms.

The challenge is that attackers do not necessarily need to deploy malware to cause disruption. Once they gain sufficient access, they may be able to misuse legitimate management functions, making malicious activity harder to distinguish from routine maintenance.

The research highlights a broader issue for operational technology security: organisations need visibility not only of connected devices, but also of who can access them, what changes they can make and how those changes affect physical operations.

Read the full research here: Cold Chain, Open Control: Exposed Refrigeration Systems Reveal Global Risk

 

The post Exposed Refrigeration Systems Raise Global Cybersecurity Concerns appeared first on IT Security Guru.

You can find more information about Custom Rules on Azure WAF for Application Gateway here or for Azure Front Door here . items.summary_html:
Written in collaboration with Gunjan Jain​ and yuvalpery​ 

As described in our earlier blog, Addressing PHP2Shell CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: upgrade guidance and Azure WAF mitigations, we strongly recommend upgrading to a patched version of PHP as soon as possible. Upgrading PHP remains the recommended and complete remediation for these vulnerabilities. 

For customers who are unable to upgrade immediately, this guidance provides WAF custom rules that can help reduce exposure to selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for these vulnerabilities.  

WAF custom rules 

The following three custom rules can be considered based on your application configuration and traffic patterns. Because custom rules can affect legitimate application traffic, review the potential application impact and validate the rules before enabling enforcement. 

Restrict PHP session upload progress

PHP supports session upload progress for tracking file uploads. For applications that do not depend on this functionality, customers can use a custom rule to restrict multipart form requests containing PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS. 

The rule checks for multipart/form-data requests whose inspected request body contains the PHP session upload progress token. 

Custom rule definitions:

Azure Front Door WAF

{    "name": "BlockPhpSessionUploadProgress",    "priority": 100,    "enabledState": "Enabled",    "ruleType": "MatchRule",    "action": "Block",    "matchConditions": [      {         "matchVariable": "RequestHeader",         "selector": "Content-Type",         "operator": "Contains",         "negateCondition": false,         "transforms": ["Lowercase"],         "matchValue": ["multipart/form-data"]       },       {         "matchVariable": "RequestBody",         "operator": "Contains",         "negateCondition": false,         "matchValue": ["php_session_upload_progress"],         "transforms": ["Lowercase"]       }    ]  }

Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF 

{ "name": "BlockPhpSessionUploadProgress", "priority": 90, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Block", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "Contains", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "multipart/form-data" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "PostArgs" } ], "operator": "Contains", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "php_session_upload_progress" ], "transforms": [ "Lowercase" ] } ] }

This rule reduces exposure through the PHP session-upload-progress path but does not address all exploitation paths associated with the vulnerabilities. 

Potential application impact: Applications that legitimately use PHP session upload progress will also match this rule. A substring match may also detect the token when it appears as harmless text or in uploaded content exposed to inspection.

Limit deeply nested form parameters

Customers can use a custom rule to identify unusually deep parameter nesting in application/x-www-form-urlencoded requests. 

The proposed rule detects request field names containing 20 or more levels of bracket nesting after URL decoding. 

Because the 20-level threshold is an application policy choice rather than a vulnerability-defined boundary, legitimate applications using deeply nested parameters may also match this rule. 

Custom rule definitions:

Azure Front Door WAF: 

{    "name": "PhpFormNesting20",    "priority": 110,    "enabledState": "Enabled",    "ruleType": "MatchRule",    "action": "Log",    "matchConditions": [      {        "matchVariable": "RequestHeader",        "selector": "Content-Type",        "operator": "BeginsWith",        "negateCondition": false,        "transforms": [          "Trim",          "Lowercase"        ],        "matchValue": [          "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"        ]      },      {        "matchVariable": "RequestBody",        "operator": "RegEx",        "negateCondition": false,        "transforms": [          "UrlDecode"        ],        "matchValue": [          "(?:^|&)[^&=\\[]+(?:\\[[^&=\\]]*\\]){20}"        ]      }    ]  } 

Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF 

{ "name": "PhpFormNesting20", "priority": 91, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "BeginsWith", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" ], "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestBody" } ], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "(?:^|&)[^&=\\[]+(?:\\[[^&=\\]]*\\]){20}" ], "transforms": [ "UrlDecode" ] } ] }

Recommended deployment: Start with the rule in Log mode and review matches against legitimate application traffic. Consider moving the rule to Block only after validating application compatibility. 

Limit deeply nested multipart parameters

Customers can apply a similar control to multipart/form-data requests by detecting deeply nested field names. 

The proposed rule detects multipart field names containing 20 or more levels of nesting where the relevant request content is available to WAF inspection. 

As with deeply nested URL-encoded parameters, legitimate applications may use complex multipart field structures. 

Custom rule definitions:

Azure Front Door WAF

{    "name": "PhpMultipartNesting20",    "priority": 111,    "enabledState": "Enabled",    "ruleType": "MatchRule",    "action": "Log",    "matchConditions": [      {        "matchVariable": "RequestHeader",        "selector": "Content-Type",        "operator": "BeginsWith",        "negateCondition": false,        "transforms": [          "Trim",          "Lowercase"        ],        "matchValue": [          "multipart/form-data"        ]      },      {        "matchVariable": "RequestBody",        "operator": "RegEx",        "negateCondition": false,        "matchValue": [          "(?i)(?:^|\\r?\\n)content-disposition:[ \\t]*form-data[^\\r\\n]*;[ \\t]*name[ \\t]*=[ \\t]*(?:\"(?:\\\\[\"\\\\]|[^\"\\r\\n\\[])+(?:\\[(?:\\\\[\"\\\\]|[^\"\\r\\n\\]])*\\]){20}|[^ \\t\\r\\n;\"\\[]+(?:\\[[^ \\t\\r\\n;\"\\]]*\\]){20})"        ]      }    ]  } 

Application Gateway and Application Gateway for Container (AGC) WAF 

{ "name": "PhpMultipartNesting20", "priority": 92, "ruleType": "MatchRule", "action": "Log", "state": "Enabled", "matchConditions": [ { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "RequestHeaders", "selector": "Content-Type" } ], "operator": "BeginsWith", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "multipart/form-data" ], "transforms": [ "Trim", "Lowercase" ] }, { "matchVariables": [ { "variableName": "PostArgs" } ], "operator": "Regex", "negationConditon": false, "matchValues": [ "^[^\\[\\]]+(?:\\[[^\\]]*\\]){20}" ], "transforms": [] } ] }

This rule targets deeply nested multipart field names. It does not restrict every multipart upload or provide complete mitigation for the underlying vulnerabilities. 

Recommended deployment: Start in Log mode, review matching traffic, and consider moving to Block only after validating the impact on your application. 

Deployment and validation considerations

We recommend applying these custom rules only to affected PHP application domains and routes, including extensionless routes handled by PHP, rather than broadly applying them to unrelated applications. 

Before enabling enforcement: 

  • Review the potential impact on legitimate application traffic. 
  • Test each custom rule independently before deploying the rules together. 
  • Start applicable rules in Log mode and review legitimate matches. 
  • Verify the WAF policy scope and custom-rule precedence. 
  • After changing a rule to Block, validate both application behavior and the corresponding WAF events. 
  • Continue to prioritize upgrading PHP even when these controls are deployed. 

Custom rules may produce false positives, and WAF request-body inspection boundaries can affect coverage. An earlier terminal Allow rule in the WAF policy can also bypass subsequent custom-rule checks. 

The custom rules described above target selected request patterns associated with exploitation techniques for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They reduce selected attack surfaces but do not provide complete protection against either vulnerability. 

You can find more information about Custom Rules on Azure WAF for Application Gateway here or for Azure Front Door here.  

Upgrading to a patched version of PHP remains the recommended and complete remediation.

items.title: Where to Find Sysmon Logs on Windows and How to Export Them
items.summary: Sysmon writes to its own event log channel. In Event Viewer that’s Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational . On the command line it’s Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational, and on disk C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon%4Operational.evtx. To export it, run this from an elevated prompt: wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" C:\logs\sysmon.evtx If the channel doesn’t exist, Sysmon isn’t installed. On most machines it’s still a separate Sysinternals tool that someone has to deploy. Sysmon is the closest thing Windows has to a flight recorder. It captures process trees with full command lines and hashes, network connections per process, DNS queries, and file and registry changes. Prime Core has 12074 sigma rules written for Sysmon data, mapped to 645 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Here’s how to check that it’s running, export what it recorded, and investigate it in LogTotal. Get Started for Free Before you start Is it running? Check the service: sc query sysmon64 On 32-bit systems the service is called sysmon . You want STATE: RUNNING . What is it recording? Sysmon logs only what its configuration tells it to. Without a config file, you get a small default set built around process creation. Most of the value comes from a tuned config, such as SwiftOnSecurity’s or Olaf Hartong’s sysmon-modular. To see the current one, run sysmon64 -c (the binary lives in C:\Windows ). Save that output next to your export. Whoever analyzes the file will ask why there are no network events, and the config answers that. How far back does it go? Sysmon is chatty, and its channel has a size limit like any other log. Run wevtutil gl “Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational” and check maxSize . On a busy server, a default-sized log can cover surprisingly little time. You need an elevated prompt to export. Export the log In Event Viewer, right-click Operational under Sysmon and choose Save All Events As… , keeping the .evtx type. From the command line, you can filter while you export: :: last 24 hours wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" C:\logs\sysmon_24h.evtx /q:"*[System[TimeCreated[timediff(@SystemTime) <= 86400000]]]" :: process creation only wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational" C:\logs\sysmon_proc.evtx /q:"*[System[(EventID=1)]]" What to look for Event ID What it records Why you care 1 Process creation, with command line, hashes and parent The backbone of almost every investigation 3 Network connection by process Often filtered out in configs because of volume 10 One process opening another Access to lsass.exe is the classic credential-dumping signal (T1003.001) 11 File created Dropped payloads, staged archives 12,13,14 Registry changes Run keys and other persistence 22 DNS query by process Which process looked up that domain 4,16 Sysmon service state and config changed An attacker turning Sysmon off or neutering its config If the events simply stop at some point, look for event 16 or 4 just before the gap. Then check the System log for the Sysmon service being stopped. Upload and review in LogTotal LogTotal reads EVTX natively, so there’s nothing to convert. One thing to know first: LogTotal doesn’t sanitize EVTX files yet. Treat an EVTX upload as handing over the raw file. Use it freely for test machines, but for production hosts, get a yes from whoever owns data handling first. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows for Sysmon data, and how findings map to rules and ATT&CK techniques] When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix The specified channel could not be found Sysmon isn’t installed Check with sc query sysmon64 Channel exists but holds almost nothing No config, or a config that filters nearly everything Check sysmon64 -c Process events but no network events The config excludes event 3, which is common By design; check the config before assuming nothing happened Events stop at some point Sysmon stopped, uninstalled or reconfigured Look for events 4 and 16, and the System log Only the last few hours are there The log is full and overwriting Check maxSize; for history, use your SIEM Access is denied Prompt isn’t elevated Run as administrator FAQ Is Sysmon installed by default? On most machines, no. It’s a free Sysinternals download that you deploy and configure yourself. Microsoft has announced built-in Sysmon for newer Windows releases, so check what your builds actually ship with. Does the analyst need my Sysmon config? Not to read the events, but it explains the gaps. Send the sysmon64 -c output along with the export. Is there Sysmon for Linux? Yes. It writes to syslog instead of an EVTX channel; we’ll cover it in a separate guide.

items.title: New Serious PHP Vulnerabilities Released and Patched
items.summary: PHP maintainers have released two critical vulnerabilities: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately. Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs. The vulnerabilities: RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 ( GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 ( GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. Updating PHP is the only way to regain security. Do it now. More news . Good explanations .

PHP maintainers have released two critical vulnerabilities:

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately.

Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs.

The vulnerabilities:

  • RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.
  • RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

Updating PHP is the only way to regain security. Do it now.

More news.

Good explanations.

items.title: Hackers Planted Malware on Japanese Cloud Servers, Forcing the Provider to Shut Down Its Service
items.summary: Hackers planted malware in customer server environments at Japan’s Onamae.com Desktop Cloud, prompting the provider to begin shutting down servers across every service plan. The company listed 26,739 servers as potentially affected, raising concerns about stored data and login details. That figure describes the possible scope, not a confirmed count of infected systems. The provider confirmed the malicious programs on October 20, 2026, and began stopping customer servers from 4:00 a.m. Japan time on October 21. Its official incident notice said the shutdown aimed to prevent further damage. The notice gave no restart date, leaving customers without access while the investigation continued. Onamae identified the malware in some customer server environments and warned that information held inside those systems may have been viewed. However, its public findings do not name the malware, explain its functions, or describe how the attackers first gained access. The disclosure confirms an intrusion but leaves the attack chain unresolved. items.title: Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
items.summary: For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework . For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators. What a Korean user sees when they sign up The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: " By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy. " A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once: 모두 동의 (Agree to all) [필수] 서비스 약관 ([Required] Terms of Service) [필수] 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ([Required] Collection and use of personal information) [필수] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ([Required] Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas) [선택] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ([Optional] Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties) The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications). The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a form Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely. Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change. We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents. The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison: // Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code. export default { async fetch(request) { // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP. // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header. // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own. const country = request.cf?.country; if (country === "KR") { return renderSignUp({ locale: "ko-KR", consent: "itemized", // four separate items, three of them required socialLogin: false, // no path that skips the consent form }); } return renderSignUp({ locale: "en-US", consent: "combined", socialLogin: true }); }, }; What that does not show is why the country code is not the whole trigger. We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the use case is critical to meeting the objectives of a local requirement. A Korean resident traveling abroad, or behind a VPN or a mobile carrier's NAT, may not arrive with a Korean address. So IP-based geolocation decides which form appears by default, but the country a user selects at sign-up overrides that and carries the decision from there. The IP address tells us where a request came from; only the user can tell us where they reside. Keeping those two apart is what makes the consent meaningful rather than presumed. It is a small feature. It took a country-level product decision, and a change to the account creation path. What ISMS is and why it matters ISMS is a detailed, localized certification standard. It covers security policy, access control, authentication and permission management, encryption, incident response, risk management, and disaster recovery, all assessed against how personal data actually moves through an organization's systems, and against Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and its associated regulatory guidelines. Certification requires an independent audit by an auditor appointed by KISA, a governmental institution affiliated with the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), followed by review from a special committee. It is valid for three years, with an annual audit required to maintain it. The ISMS certification is primarily established under Article 47 of Korea's Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., with the certification criteria and procedure set out in its Enforcement Decree and in the public notification on ISMS certification issued by MSIT. What the audit examined Cloudflare is already certified against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018 and many other globally recognized frameworks. ISMS does not replace any of them. It is a localization of the same principles, layered with Korean regulatory requirements, and that changes what auditors look for and how they look for it. The controls in scope started with the review of data flows. We presented detailed data flow diagrams showing every path by which employees could access personal information that Cloudflare collects, processes, and stores. The flows themselves are not Korea-specific. What was different was the form the evidence had to take: the auditors were not willing to work from a narrative description of how data moves, they wanted diagrams they could read and interrogate. For each one, they examined every access control layer and tested its effectiveness, across our internal systems, our public-facing websites, event pages, and the Cloudflare dashboard, covering the full lifecycle of a user's data from first interaction through to destruction. Those diagrams are not published here due to confidentiality. The audit also scrutinized the language and terminology of our consent collection: the exact wording at sign-up, the structure of each notification, and whether the items were presented separately and clearly. That is the kind of detail the ISMS framework is designed to surface. Why the timeline ran to a year and a half Part of the answer is how audit cycles work. An ISMS audit covers a single annual period, and all evidence, documentation, and systems must reflect that period. Our preparation ran past one audit year and into the next, which meant retranslating updated policies for the new audit year, re-collecting and reassessing evidence, republishing an updated privacy policy, and absorbing formatting and design changes our marketing and website teams had introduced in the meantime. What the certificate covers KISA defines the certified scope as a service boundary rather than as an enumerated list of in-scope products. The Statement of Scope submitted to KISA describes that boundary in three parts: the organizational and operational perimeter : the Cloudflare entities, teams, and processes that operate the service; the infrastructure perimeter : the network and platform the certified service runs on; the information assets and personal information flows that fall inside the boundary under the ISMS control set. If a customer-consumed Cloudflare product is delivered through that certified service boundary, meaning it runs on the same certified platform, is operated by the same certified teams, and is governed by the same ISMS, it is covered by the certificate. The certificate is held by Cloudflare, Inc. That is a different shape from the reports most procurement teams work with. A SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate describes the system it covers and names the services included, so coverage is confirmed by finding the product in that list. The ISMS certificate carries no such list. Coverage follows the delivery path instead, whether or not a product is named anywhere. What this means for customers For organizations operating in Korea, this gives legal, security, and procurement teams a local assurance benchmark alongside Cloudflare's broader compliance portfolio. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 demonstrate a general security posture. ISMS reflects Korea-specific legal and regulatory expectations. That distinction matters in third-party risk reviews and in preparing for a team’s own compliance assessments. Cloudflare’s entry can be found on KISA's public register of certified organizations , which is the independent, verifiable confirmation to cite in a risk review. Broader privacy and data protection material sits on the Cloudflare Trust Hub . The question that usually stalls a vendor review of Cloudflare is whether a particular product in use is in scope. The certificate does not answer that by name, because it lists no products. It answers by boundary, meaning that the product is in scope if it is delivered through the certified service. For multinational teams managing security across regions, the certification confirms that Cloudflare's program has been reviewed against local requirements in one of Asia's most important digital markets, not just designed for global scale. Building a better Internet, for everyone ISMS is not a harder certification than the other assurance audits we go through. It is a more nuanced one. It is built around the regulatory needs of one specific region, and it asks for genuine investment in understanding and embedding those needs, rather than mapping them onto a common control framework. Going through it made Cloudflare more global, not less. It pushed us to think carefully about what it means to serve users in a specific local context, with local language, local consent expectations, and local data protection requirements, and to put that into how the product behaves rather than only into a document. That is consistent with what we are working toward: helping build a better Internet for everyone, not just in the regions where regulatory requirements are straightforward, but everywhere. To learn more about Cloudflare's compliance and assurance programs, visit our Trust Hub .

items.title: How do you verify AI coding agent output from any tool, not just one?
items.summary: Your developers are not committed to a single AI coding agent. Sonar's State of Code Developer Survey found that development teams juggle four different AI tools on average, and the state of the art shifts every few months. Teams move between agents, from Copilot to Claude Code to Cursor to Codex and on to whatever ships next. The models underneath those agents turn over too, often faster: a new model lands, developer preference follows it within weeks, and the agent in your IDE is reasoning on a different model than it was last quarter. Mobility and flexibility around tooling is a strength when it drives velocity. But it becomes a liability the moment your verification standard is tied to whichever agent happened to write the code. No one deliberately appoints the agent as the ultimate judge of quality. It's a role they assume gradually, accumulated through small, incremental steps over time. Every agent ships its own review step and its own signal that the work is done and the tests pass, already configured and already paid for. Add gating that varies by repository and the 35% of AI tool usage running through personal accounts, and the bar a change clears is inherited from the tool that produced it. Every tool checks its own work its own way, and code quality becomes a function of vendor selection rather than engineering principle. The useful question is how to verify AI coding agent output whichever agent produced it. Can an agent verify its own output? Up to a point. On a small, predictable codebase, an agent reviewing its own work does a reasonable job. The code is contained, the relevant call paths fit in context, and the mistakes tend to be shallow. That also describes most pilots, which is why self-review looks strong in evaluation and thinner in production. Scale and complexity set the boundary. On a large enterprise estate the conditions change: interconnected systems, stacks that mix legacy and frontier systems, dozens of teams committing across hundreds of repositories, and behavior that depends on code the agent never had in context. A clean result on a contained repo tells you very little about what holds up there. Three things stop holding at that scale: No segregation of duties. The agent that wrote the code brings the same context and assumptions when it judges the code, so a structural mistake made during generation reads as correct during review. No repeatable result. Review resting on reasoning alone gives different feedback on the same code from one run to the next, with no deterministic layer underneath to anchor it. No auditability. Review with nothing deterministic underneath leaves no repeatable pass/fail record to point to when compliance or a postmortem asks what happened. Independence comes from a separate methodology, applied by something other than the system under review. That is what holds up once the estate grows past the point where any single context window covers it. Human review does not rescue this. Research from the Wharton School (Shaw and Nave, 2026) describes a failure mode the authors call "cognitive surrender": participants followed the AI's advice 92.7% of the time when it was correct, and 79.8% of the time when the AI was confidently wrong. A safety net that defers to the thing it is supposed to be checking stops functioning as a safety net. Volume seals it. Agent pull requests routinely run 10x larger than human ones. Review by hand cannot scale to that volume, and any approach that depends on the generating system to catch its own mistakes scales no better. What tool-agnostic code verification requires Verification has to run separately from whatever generated the code. That is the core principle, and it has four load-bearing parts. An independent standard. Zero-trust, multilayered verification applies the same rigorous, repeatable, auditable checks to all code, whether a human, Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc, wrote it. One standard across every tool. Deterministic analysis. Deterministic code analysis catches the complex, hard-to-find issues in syntax, data flows, control flows, and structure that review by the generating agent misses. It returns the same result every time, which is what makes it auditable. Segregation of duties. Verification uses a different methodology than generation. items.summary_html:
Your developers are not committed to a single AI coding agent. Sonar's State of Code Developer Survey found that development teams juggle four different AI tools on average, and the state of the art shifts every few months.

Teams move between agents, from Copilot to Claude Code to Cursor to Codex and on to whatever ships next. The models underneath those agents turn over too, often faster: a new model lands, developer preference follows it within weeks, and the agent in your IDE is reasoning on a different model than it was last quarter. Mobility and flexibility around tooling is a strength when it drives velocity. But it becomes a liability the moment your verification standard is tied to whichever agent happened to write the code.

No one deliberately appoints the agent as the ultimate judge of quality. It's a role they assume gradually, accumulated through small, incremental steps over time. Every agent ships its own review step and its own signal that the work is done and the tests pass, already configured and already paid for. Add gating that varies by repository and the 35% of AI tool usage running through personal accounts, and the bar a change clears is inherited from the tool that produced it. Every tool checks its own work its own way, and code quality becomes a function of vendor selection rather than engineering principle.

The useful question is how to verify AI coding agent output whichever agent produced it.

Can an agent verify its own output?

Up to a point. On a small, predictable codebase, an agent reviewing its own work does a reasonable job. The code is contained, the relevant call paths fit in context, and the mistakes tend to be shallow. That also describes most pilots, which is why self-review looks strong in evaluation and thinner in production.

Scale and complexity set the boundary. On a large enterprise estate the conditions change: interconnected systems, stacks that mix legacy and frontier systems, dozens of teams committing across hundreds of repositories, and behavior that depends on code the agent never had in context. A clean result on a contained repo tells you very little about what holds up there.

Three things stop holding at that scale:

  • No segregation of duties. The agent that wrote the code brings the same context and assumptions when it judges the code, so a structural mistake made during generation reads as correct during review.
  • No repeatable result. Review resting on reasoning alone gives different feedback on the same code from one run to the next, with no deterministic layer underneath to anchor it.
  • No auditability. Review with nothing deterministic underneath leaves no repeatable pass/fail record to point to when compliance or a postmortem asks what happened.

Independence comes from a separate methodology, applied by something other than the system under review. That is what holds up once the estate grows past the point where any single context window covers it.

Human review does not rescue this. Research from the Wharton School (Shaw and Nave, 2026) describes a failure mode the authors call "cognitive surrender": participants followed the AI's advice 92.7% of the time when it was correct, and 79.8% of the time when the AI was confidently wrong. A safety net that defers to the thing it is supposed to be checking stops functioning as a safety net.

Volume seals it. Agent pull requests routinely run 10x larger than human ones. Review by hand cannot scale to that volume, and any approach that depends on the generating system to catch its own mistakes scales no better.

What tool-agnostic code verification requires

Verification has to run separately from whatever generated the code. That is the core principle, and it has four load-bearing parts.

  • An independent standard. Zero-trust, multilayered verification applies the same rigorous, repeatable, auditable checks to all code, whether a human, Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc, wrote it. One standard across every tool.
  • Deterministic analysis. Deterministic code analysis catches the complex, hard-to-find issues in syntax, data flows, control flows, and structure that review by the generating agent misses. It returns the same result every time, which is what makes it auditable.
  • Segregation of duties. Verification uses a different methodology than generation. That separation catches what a single generation pass structurally cannot.
  • Human accountability, enforced in CI. A quality gate in your CI/CD pipeline turns the standard into an enforced decision. Someone owns the pass, and something records it.

No single layer catches everything. A zero trust, multilayered framework combines deterministic algorithmic analysis for structure with context-aware reasoning for intent and business logic, so what one layer misses another catches, however the code was written.

Verification also has to live inside the loops developers already work in: the agentic loop where code gets written, the CI verification loop where it gets gated, and the code maintenance loop where it gets carried forward over years. A standard that arrives after all three have run gets routed around.

Where MCP fits: carrying verification into agent workflows

An independent standard earns its keep when it reaches developers where they already work, inside the agent and at the command line.

The Model Context Protocol is the interoperability mechanism that carries trusted code analysis signals into compatible agent workflows. It brings project context and Sonar's verification directly into the agent, so the standard travels to the tool.

SonarQube MCP Server is the connection that delivers the signal, and it relies on SonarQube to perform the underlying analysis. SonarQube is the independent verification layer that produces the result, and the signal is only as trustworthy as that analysis.

The distinction matters. Interoperability is what lets one standard span a multi-tool stack. The analysis behind it is what makes the standard worth trusting.

A practical workflow across agents

The same model works whether your team is using today's leading AI coding tools or whatever ships next quarter.

  1. Generate with whichever agent fits the task.
  2. Verify against a single independent standard through SonarQube MCP Server, so the agent gets deterministic feedback while it works, hours before PR time.
  3. Gate in CI, so every agent's output clears the same quality gate before it ships.
  4. Account for the result, with a human owning the merge and an auditable record behind it.

Change the agent, and the standard holds. That is the point.

What to verify before agent code ships

Agent-agnostic verification needs a concrete checklist. Before any agent's code ships, validate agentic code changes against five things:

  • Quality. Maintainability, complexity, and duplication, the properties that determine whether the next change is fast or painful.
  • Security. Vulnerabilities and insecure patterns caught at the source. In one study, autonomous frontier models left to fix vulnerabilities on their own failed 52% of the time and introduced a new bug or vulnerability 25% of the time. Remediation works when there is a verification layer behind it to confirm the fix actually landed.
  • Dependency risk. The provenance and known issues in your dependencies, verified as part of the same standard.
  • Maintainability. Structural drift that accumulates silently. Carnegie Mellon researchers measured a persistent 30% increase in static analysis warnings and a 41% increase in code complexity in projects that adopted an AI agent, a slowdown that outlasted the early velocity spike.
  • Build health. Whether the code actually builds and passes, verified before it reaches a human reviewer.

items.title: SonarQube container scanning is now in open beta
items.summary: The layer your code scans don’t see You already verify the code you write and the dependencies you import in SonarQube. The images you ship add another layer: operating system packages, language runtimes and libraries that never appear in your repository. Teams often check that layer in a separate tool and end up with a second set of findings to reconcile. Container scanning brings it natively into SonarQube. Risks in your images show up next to the risks in your code and dependencies, in the same workflow. Container scanning is included in SonarQube Advanced Security. Why scan the image? Securing your application runtime is as important as securing your dependencies. This week, two critical issues landed in the layer beneath application code: the PHP2Shell flaws in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, fixed Oct 21 ) and the compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys , which affects the certificate trust store your images and runtimes rely on. Neither is in your code or your declared dependencies. Both live in your images. Container scanning is built for that layer. It flags known exposure where a vendor advisory or CVE describes it, and it keeps checking images you have already analyzed. Below, we show how to check your images for PHP2Shell. How does SonarQube container scanning work? Scan. You run the Sonar container scanner CLI against an image, locally or in CI. Analyze. The scanner generates an SBOM for the image and sends it to SonarQube Cloud, which checks the components for known vulnerabilities and malicious packages. Review. Results appear in the scanner output and in SonarQube Cloud under Container images . Stay current. SonarQube Cloud re-checks analyzed images for newly published vulnerabilities, based on your organization’s re-analysis settings, so you do not need to re-scan an image to learn about new ones. For images based on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian 11 and higher, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Ubuntu and Alpine, vulnerability tracking includes vendor security advisories from those distributions. How do I get started with SonarQube container scanning? You need: a SonarQube Cloud organization with SonarQube Advanced Security; a SonarQube Cloud user token; the image available locally or in CI Download the scanner for Linux, macOS or Windows from the scanner download page , rename it to sonar-container-scanner and add it to your PATH then run as shown below. sonar-container-scanner --organization --token By default, the scanner exits with a failing code when it finds risks of high severity or above, so your pipeline can stop a risky image. Use --fail-on to change the threshold. docker build -t my-app:${BUILD_TAG} . sonar-container-scanner my-app:${BUILD_TAG} --fail-on high The container scanning documentation covers CI secrets, supported image inputs, caching and every option. How to check container images for PHP2Shell PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP runtime itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated 9.2 on CVSS v4.0). They let an attacker run code on a web server without logging in, and they affect PHP installations that serve web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php and php-cgi. Fixes shipped on October 21 in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Because the flaws are in PHP, not in your application code or its Composer packages, code analysis and dependency analysis will not flag them. In SonarQube, they show up through container scanning, as security advisories from the Linux distribution that packaged PHP in your image. Check your images in three steps Run the scanner on every image that runs PHP. If you scanned an image before October 21, run it again so the findings and severity are current. sonar-container-scanner my-php-app:latest --fail-on high In SonarQube Cloud, open Container images, select the image, and look for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 in its risks. They may appear under the distribution’s own advisory (for example a Debian or Ubuntu advisory), with the CVE listed alongside it. Update PHP. Rebuild the image on a patched base image or with the updated distribution package, then scan it again to confirm the risk is gone. What container scanning can and can’t see Detected: PHP installed from your distribution’s package manager (for example apt install php8.x on Debian or Ubuntu) on a supported base image, once that distribution has published its advisory. Debian and Ubuntu advisories are already available, and others are added as each distribution publishes them. Not detected: It does not detect PHP compiled from source including the official php images on Docker Hub and images built on them, such as wordpress, drupal and nextcloud. For these images, check the version inside the container with php -v and update to a fixed release. What do you see in SonarQube Cloud? Select Container images in the sidebar of your organization to see every image you have analyzed, with its tag, number of risks, most severe risk and when it was last analyzed. Open an image to see its versions and their risks, and manage them with the same workflow you use for dependency risks in your projects. To refresh results after an image itself changes, run the scanner again. Why use SonarQube for container scanning? SonarQube is the independent verification and governance platform for the code you write, the dependencies you import, and now the images you ship. It doesn’t depend on any one cloud, model or agent vendor. For container images, that means: One place for all of it. Image risks sit next to your code and dependency risks, in the same workflow. Checks where developers build. Run it locally or in CI, and stop a risky image before it ships. An inventory that stays current. Every image version you analyze is re-checked as new vulnerabilities are published. Container scanning is included with SonarQube Advanced Security at no additional cost. What is in the beta? In scope today: SonarQube Cloud, for organizations with SonarQube Advanced Security on the Team or Enterprise plan. Vulnerability tracking for images based on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian 11 and higher, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Ubuntu and Alpine. Scanning of images available locally, either on your machine or in the CI. This is a beta, and your feedback shapes what comes next. Try it today Read the container scanning docs and run your first scan on an image you already build.

The layer your code scans don’t see

You already verify the code you write and the dependencies you import in SonarQube. The images you ship add another layer: operating system packages, language runtimes and libraries that never appear in your repository. Teams often check that layer in a separate tool and end up with a second set of findings to reconcile. Container scanning brings it natively into SonarQube. Risks in your images show up next to the risks in your code and dependencies, in the same workflow. Container scanning is included in SonarQube Advanced Security. 

Why scan the image?

Securing your application runtime is as important as securing your dependencies. This week, two critical issues landed in the layer beneath application code: the PHP2Shell flaws in the PHP runtime (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, fixed Oct 21) and the compromise of eight eMudhra intermediate CA keys, which affects the certificate trust store your images and runtimes rely on. Neither is in your code or your declared dependencies. Both live in your images.

Container scanning is built for that layer. It flags known exposure where a vendor advisory or CVE describes it, and it keeps checking images you have already analyzed. Below, we show how to check your images for PHP2Shell.

How does SonarQube container scanning work?
  1. Scan. You run the Sonar container scanner CLI against an image, locally or in CI.
  2. Analyze. The scanner generates an SBOM for the image and sends it to SonarQube Cloud, which checks the components for known vulnerabilities and malicious packages.
  3. Review. Results appear in the scanner output and in SonarQube Cloud under Container images.
  4. Stay current. SonarQube Cloud re-checks analyzed images for newly published vulnerabilities, based on your organization’s re-analysis settings, so you do not need to re-scan an image to learn about new ones.

For images based on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian 11 and higher, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Ubuntu and Alpine, vulnerability tracking includes vendor security advisories from those distributions.

How do I get started with SonarQube container scanning?

You need:

  • a SonarQube Cloud organization with SonarQube Advanced Security;
  • a SonarQube Cloud user token;
  • the image available locally or in CI

Download the scanner for Linux, macOS or Windows from the scanner download page, rename it to sonar-container-scanner and add it to your PATH then run as shown below. 

sonar-container-scanner  --organization  --token


By default, the scanner exits with a failing code when it finds risks of high severity or above, so your pipeline can stop a risky image. Use --fail-on to change the threshold.

docker build -t my-app:${BUILD_TAG} .
sonar-container-scanner my-app:${BUILD_TAG} --fail-on high


The container scanning documentation covers CI secrets, supported image inputs, caching and every option.

How to check container images for PHP2Shell 

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP runtime itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both rated 9.2 on CVSS v4.0). They let an attacker run code on a web server without logging in, and they affect PHP installations that serve web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php and php-cgi. Fixes shipped on October 21 in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35.

Because the flaws are in PHP, not in your application code or its Composer packages, code analysis and dependency analysis will not flag them. In SonarQube, they show up through container scanning, as security advisories from the Linux distribution that packaged PHP in your image.

Check your images in three steps
  1. Run the scanner on every image that runs PHP. If you scanned an image before October 21, run it again so the findings and severity are current.
    sonar-container-scanner my-php-app:latest --fail-on high
  2. In SonarQube Cloud, open Container images, select the image, and look for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 in its risks. They may appear under the distribution’s own advisory (for example a Debian or Ubuntu advisory), with the CVE listed alongside it.
  3. Update PHP. Rebuild the image on a patched base image or with the updated distribution package, then scan it again to confirm the risk is gone.
What container scanning can and can’t see
  • Detected: PHP installed from your distribution’s package manager (for example apt install php8.x on Debian or Ubuntu) on a supported base image, once that distribution has published its advisory. Debian and Ubuntu advisories are already available, and others are added as each distribution publishes them.
  • Not detected: It does not detect PHP compiled from source including the official php images on Docker Hub and images built on them, such as wordpress, drupal and nextcloud. For these images, check the version inside the container with php -v and update to a fixed release.
What do you see in SonarQube Cloud?

Select Container images in the sidebar of your organization to see every image you have analyzed, with its tag, number of risks, most severe risk and when it was last analyzed. Open an image to see its versions and their risks, and manage them with the same workflow you use for dependency risks in your projects. To refresh results after an image itself changes, run the scanner again.

Why use SonarQube for container scanning?

SonarQube is the independent verification and governance platform for the code you write, the dependencies you import, and now the images you ship. It doesn’t depend on any one cloud, model or agent vendor. For container images, that means:

  • One place for all of it. Image risks sit next to your code and dependency risks, in the same workflow.
  • Checks where developers build. Run it locally or in CI, and stop a risky image before it ships.
  • An inventory that stays current. Every image version you analyze is re-checked as new vulnerabilities are published.

Container scanning is included with SonarQube Advanced Security at no additional cost.

What is in the beta?

In scope today:

  • SonarQube Cloud, for organizations with SonarQube Advanced Security on the Team or Enterprise plan.
  • Vulnerability tracking for images based on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, Debian 11 and higher, Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Ubuntu and Alpine.
  • Scanning of images available locally, either on your machine or in the CI.

This is a beta, and your feedback shapes what comes next.

Try it today

Read the container scanning docs and run your first scan on an image you already build.

items.title: How to Enable and Export PowerShell Script Block Logs
items.summary: PowerShell script block logs live in Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → PowerShell → Operational , as event 4104. They’re only complete if script block logging is turned on. To export them: wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" C:\logs\powershell.evtx PowerShell 7 is a separate product with a separate channel, PowerShellCore/Operational, and its own policy setting. If an attacker touched a Windows box, odds are PowerShell was involved. Script block logging records the code that actually ran, often after the obfuscation layers have been peeled off. Prime Core has 663 detection rules for PowerShell logs, mapped to 417 MITRE ATT&CK techniques. They cover malicious PowerShell use (T1059.001), obfuscation (T1027) and download cradles that pull in tools (T1105). Try LogTotal, free Before you start Is script block logging on? reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging" EnableScriptBlockLogging set to 0x1 means yes. If the key doesn’t exist, it’s off. Even then, Windows PowerShell 5.1 still logs script blocks it considers suspicious, as 4104 events at Warning level. So you may find some events. Just don’t mistake them for the full picture. Turning it on helps from now on, not for what already happened. Use the Group Policy setting Administrative Templates → Windows Components → Windows PowerShell → Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging , or set the registry value directly: reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging" /v EnableScriptBlockLogging /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f PowerShell 7 reads its own policy key under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\PowerShellCore. If it was installed from a zip rather than the MSI, its event channel may not be registered until you run RegisterManifest.ps1 from $PSHOME. Expect volume. Every script and module that runs ends up in the log. Raise the channel’s maximum size, or you’ll keep only a few hours. Expect secrets. Admin scripts sometimes carry passwords and API keys in plain text, and script block logging records them faithfully. Keep that in mind before this file goes anywhere, and read the LogTotal section below. Export the logs In Event Viewer, right-click Operational under PowerShell and choose Save All Events As… From the command line: :: script blocks only wevtutil epl "Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational" C:\logs\ps_4104.evtx /q:"*[System[(EventID=4104)]]" :: PowerShell 7 wevtutil epl "PowerShellCore/Operational" C:\logs\pwsh.evtx :: the classic "Windows PowerShell" log: engine start events with the host command line wevtutil epl "Windows PowerShell" C:\logs\windows_powershell.evtx That last one is easy to forget, and it’s worth grabbing. Event 400 records each engine start, including the engine version. An EngineVersion of 2.0 on a modern system usually means someone deliberately downgraded to dodge script block logging. Upload and review in LogTotal LogTotal reads EVTX natively. One thing to know first: LogTotal doesn’t sanitize EVTX files yet. [PROOF: confirm which formats the sanitize step covers today.] With PowerShell logs, that matters more than usual, because of the secrets mentioned above. Use EVTX uploads freely for test machines. For production hosts, get a yes from whoever owns data handling first. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. [PROOF: upload screen, size limit] Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows for PowerShell data] What this looks like on real data. We used [PROOF: sample source, e.g. a test VM with script block logging on, after running an encoded download cradle and a harmless AMSI-tampering test string]. LogTotal flagged [PROOF: actual findings]. [PROOF: link to the sample file] When it goes wrong Symptom Likely cause Fix No 4104 events at all Script block logging is off, and nothing looked suspicious Enable it for the future; check the Windows PowerShell log for what you can still get Only a handful of 4104 events, all Warning Logging is off; you’re seeing automatic suspicious-block logging Same as above PowerShellCore/Operational not found PowerShell 7 isn’t installed, or its manifest isn’t registered Run RegisterManifest.ps1 from $PSHOME 4104 text is unreadable ciphertext Protected Event Logging is on You need the decryption certificate Log covers only a few hours Default size, high volume Raise the channel’s maximum size FAQ Does script block logging catch obfuscated code? Largely, yes. It records script blocks as they’re compiled. When obfuscated code builds and runs the next stage, that stage gets logged as its own block, often in readable form. What’s the difference from transcription? Transcription writes text files of session input and output to a folder. Script block logging records the code itself in the event log. They complement each other, and both are worth having.

That last one is easy to forget, and it’s worth grabbing. Event 400 records each engine start, including the engine version. An EngineVersion of 2.0 on a modern system usually means someone deliberately downgraded to dodge script block logging.

Upload and review in LogTotal

LogTotal reads EVTX natively. One thing to know first: LogTotal doesn’t sanitize EVTX files yet. [PROOF: confirm which formats the sanitize step covers today.] With PowerShell logs, that matters more than usual, because of the secrets mentioned above. Use EVTX uploads freely for test machines. For production hosts, get a yes from whoever owns data handling first.

  1. Upload. Open logtotal.com and drop in the file. [PROOF: upload screen, size limit]
  2. Review. [PROOF: what the results screen shows for PowerShell data]

What this looks like on real data. We used [PROOF: sample source, e.g. a test VM with script block logging on, after running an encoded download cradle and a harmless AMSI-tampering test string]. LogTotal flagged [PROOF: actual findings]. [PROOF: link to the sample file] When it goes wrong SymptomLikely causeFixNo 4104 events at allScript block logging is off, and nothing looked suspiciousEnable it for the future; check the Windows PowerShell log for what you can still getOnly a handful of 4104 events, all WarningLogging is off; you’re seeing automatic suspicious-block loggingSame as abovePowerShellCore/Operational not foundPowerShell 7 isn’t installed, or its manifest isn’t registeredRun RegisterManifest.ps1 from $PSHOME4104 text is unreadable ciphertextProtected Event Logging is onYou need the decryption certificateLog covers only a few hoursDefault size, high volumeRaise the channel’s maximum size

FAQ

Does script block logging catch obfuscated code?

Largely, yes. It records script blocks as they’re compiled. When obfuscated code builds and runs the next stage, that stage gets logged as its own block, often in readable form.

What’s the difference from transcription?

Transcription writes text files of session input and output to a folder. Script block logging records the code itself in the event log. They complement each other, and both are worth having.

At least three organizations in the software, construction and wired communications equipment sectors were affected, according to Kaspersky’s investigation. The researchers say the operation’s earliest known evidence dates to July 2025. Analysts from Securelist identified the malware and named the activity Operation FlashHole. Their report describes Lazarus abusing CrossWeb EX, a financial security program used to access some South Korean banking and government websites. Securelist could not confirm exactly how the software was abused, but traced the chain to malicious code running under its process. items.summary_html:
North Korean-linked Lazarus hackers are using post-quantum cryptography in a malware delivery chain designed to conceal later-stage payloads from security tools.

The technique appeared in Operation FlashHole, a campaign targeting organizations in South Korea. Instead of relying on encryption alone to hide files on disk, the malware uses a modern key-establishment method to protect payloads sent from its command-and-control infrastructure.

The campaign’s infection chain combines phishing, trusted South Korean software, several malware families and code that runs mainly in memory.

At least three organizations in the software, construction and wired communications equipment sectors were affected, according to Kaspersky’s investigation. The researchers say the operation’s earliest known evidence dates to July 2025.

Analysts from Securelist identified the malware and named the activity Operation FlashHole. Their report describes Lazarus abusing CrossWeb EX, a financial security program used to access some South Korean banking and government websites.

Securelist could not confirm exactly how the software was abused, but traced the chain to malicious code running under its process.

This echoes earlier Lazarus activity involving South Korean security software and software supply chains. For more background, see this report on Lazarus malware in supply chains.

North Korean Hackers Use Post-Quantum Encryption

The campaign likely began with targeted phishing emails that directed victims to tailored websites, including fake résumé or interior-design pages.

Securelist found malicious links embedded in these sites and assessed that visiting them may have started the infection process. The researchers also noted signs that an image on one résumé page may have been generated using AI.

They could not confirm every step of the initial compromise, so the precise role of each lure remains an assessment rather than a proven account.

Operation FlashHole attack flow during initial compromise (Source – Securelist)

After initial access, the chain used legitimate Windows software and memory-based execution to limit the traces left on disk. The malware set included TechHub, TouchHub, TouchShift, ClientHub, LPEClient and Cubridge.

TechHub helped deliver later components, while other tools supported persistence, system profiling and payload delivery. Cubridge acted as a central operator, able to load separate modules and plugins instead of relying on one large backdoor.

This modular design matters because it can let attackers deploy only the capabilities needed on a particular device. Securelist describes tools that can collect system and process details, search files, and steal browser data such as stored passwords, cookies, bookmarks and browsing history.

Researchers also found that some components communicated through legitimate platforms such as GitHub, while others used compromised websites or Dropbox.

A previous Lazarus software vendor compromise shows why campaigns involving trusted software and supply chains can affect organizations beyond the first victim.

How the post-quantum encryption fits

The most notable change is in LPEClient, a Lazarus malware family used to profile infected computers and deliver further payloads. In this campaign, LPEClient obtains four ML-KEM-1024 public-key blocks from its command-and-control server.

It uses them to establish shared keys, then sends related ciphertexts back through ClientHub. The resulting keys help protect the next payload during delivery and decryption.

Appearance of the malicious websites (Source – Securelist)

ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism: it lets two parties establish a shared secret over a public channel, which can then be used with symmetric encryption. NIST standardized the method in FIPS 203 and lists ML-KEM-1024 as one of its parameter sets.

Its use does not mean the attackers have a quantum computer; the method is designed to resist attacks from future quantum computers.

Securelist reports that the malware uses the established keys with Threefish to decrypt a later payload, which is then loaded into memory. The report also describes techniques intended to interfere with security monitoring before that payload runs.

These details show why defenders should not treat post-quantum cryptography as a threat by itself: the concern is its use inside a broader chain that combines stealth, trusted software and staged malware delivery.

Organizations in South Korea should review the use and exposure of financial security software, keep it updated, and investigate unusual child processes or unexpected memory activity from trusted applications.

Security teams can also look for suspicious use of GitHub or Dropbox by systems that do not normally need those services, and correlate endpoint alerts with unusual web traffic. These checks are especially useful when malware runs largely in memory and leaves few files behind.

The wider lesson is that malware defenses need to examine behavior and context, not just known file signatures. Lazarus has combined targeted lures, legitimate software, browser-like network traffic and several layers of encryption.

Earlier reporting on Lazarus targeting drone companies offers another example of how the group uses tailored approaches against different sectors.

Securelist assesses with medium-to-high confidence that FlashHole is connected to the earlier Operation SyncHole campaign, based on similarities in targeting and malware.

items.title: Keeper Security Launches AI-Powered Phishing Protection to Block Credential Theft
items.summary: Keeper Security has introduced a new AI-powered phishing protection feature designed to prevent users from entering their credentials on fraudulent websites. Available through the Keeper Browser Extension, the new Phishing Protection capability uses a local AI engine to detect look-alike domains, spoofed websites and brand impersonation attempts. By identifying suspicious login pages directly in the browser, the feature aims to prevent credential theft before sensitive information reaches cybercriminals. The launch comes as credential-based attacks continue to pose a significant threat to organisations. According to the 2026 Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report, credential abuse was involved in nearly 40% of breaches. Meanwhile, cybercriminals are increasingly using generative AI to create convincing fraudulent websites and login portals that imitate legitimate services, making phishing attempts more difficult for users and traditional security tools to identify. Unlike conventional phishing detection tools that may rely on cloud-based analysis, Keeper’s new feature uses machine learning that operates entirely on the user’s device. Built on Keeper’s zero-knowledge security architecture, the technology analyses websites locally without sharing user data. “Phishing attacks are no longer simple email scams; they are highly automated, AI-driven operations designed to trick users into handing over sensitive credentials and information,” said Darren Guccione, CEO and Co-founder of Keeper Security. “When an adversary sets up a look-alike domain, form field or unofficial login portal, traditional security controls often fail to identify the threat until the damage is done. By embedding zero-knowledge AI into our browser extension, Keeper stops credential harvesting at the point of entry, giving individuals and organisations greater security and control.” Detecting Phishing Attempts at the Point of Entry Keeper’s Phishing Protection feature automatically examines web pages for characteristics commonly associated with credential-harvesting attacks. These include typosquatting techniques, where attackers use domains that closely resemble legitimate websites, as well as suspicious IP addresses, unusual URL structures and unauthorised websites requesting password information. When a potential threat is identified, the extension displays a warning explaining the suspicious activity and the specific indicators detected. Users can review the warning, dismiss it or disable Keeper on the affected website. They can also manage previously blocked sites and restore autofill functionality where appropriate. The feature is designed to provide an additional layer of protection against phishing attacks that evade existing email security gateways and web filtering technologies. Privacy and Administrative Control Keeper has also emphasised the privacy-focused design of the new capability, with its AI engine processing website information locally rather than transmitting sensitive data to external servers. “Security controls have to work at machine speed, and they cannot come at the expense of the zero-knowledge guarantees our customers depend on,” said Craig Lurey, CTO and Co-founder of Keeper Security. “We engineered this AI engine to execute entirely on the local device using the customer’s private key. It delivers continuous, proactive verification of web assets, ensuring that autofill is protected against sophisticated domain spoofing without creating a privacy trade-off.” The feature is optional and disabled by default. Enterprise IT administrators can enable and manage it centrally through the Keeper Admin Console, while individual users can configure their preferences directly within the browser extension. Keeper Phishing Protection is available now as an opt-in feature in version 18.2.0 of the Keeper Browser Extension.
