items.title: Node2Shell: From Brotli Data to Remote Code Execution
items.summary: Thales RED TEAM demonstrated remote code execution against the official vulnerable Node.js build, then confirmed that the fixed release rejects the same Brotli input. Executive summary Node2Shell is Imperva Red Team’s name for our analysis of CVE-2026-111497 , a High severity flaw in Node.js’s bundled Brotli decoder. Node.js says the out-of-bounds write can permit remote code execution and has released fixes for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Our standalone proof of concept ran code carried in a Brotli response or request body inside applications using the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image. It needed no debugger or instrumented binary. The same inputs were rejected by 24.22.1 . We tested Express 5.0.0–5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0–2.3.0, including the latest releases available at testing; execution took multiple attempts in our setup. Imperva has added WAF rules for CVE-2026-111497. Customers should update affected Node.js deployments to a fixed release. Overview A Node.js service can encounter Brotli on either side of an HTTP exchange. It may consume a compressed response from another server, or use middleware to decode an incoming request body. Both operations can send untrusted data into the native decoder bundled with Node.js. That shared path is where CVE-2026-111497 lives. We built a standalone proof of concept to see whether the flaw could lead to code execution in a Node.js application. In fresh containers running the official vulnerable Node.js image, the application ran code supplied with the Brotli data. We used a memory sanitizer separately to investigate the underlying bug and compared the results with the fixed release. The Node.js project disclosed the issue on October 21, 2026 . Its advisory credits Matteo Collina with reporting it and Antoine du Hamel with the fix. Our work is an independent validation of the impact and the released patch. Impact: From a decoder error to code execution In the working proof of concept, the test application had no code to create our marker file. After it received the Brotli data, the file appeared. Code carried in that data had run inside the target process. We reproduced this with the official Node.js 24.22.0 image in fresh Linux arm64 containers. The same inputs on Node.js 24.22.1 were rejected and created no marker. We also investigated the cause. A source comparison showed that the vulnerable decoder could continue past an invalid stream condition. In a separate sanitizer test, decoding that condition caused an out-of-bounds write. The sanitizer helped explain the flaw; it was not needed for the code-execution proof. We tested both a compressed response consumed by Node.js’s built-in fetch() and incoming Brotli bodies handled by configured request parsers. The table shows the Brotli-capable package ranges represented by our pinned endpoint tests: Application path Package range and tested configurations Node.js 24.22.0 Node.js 24.22.1 Consumed HTTP response Node.js built-in fetch() Supplied code ran; marker created Input rejected; no marker Incoming request body Express 5.0.0–5.3.0; tested 5.0.0 with body-parser 2.0.1, and 5.3.0 with body-parser 2.3.0 Supplied code ran with raw() and json() in both tested setups Input rejected; no marker; server stayed running Incoming request body body-parser 2.0.0–2.3.0; tested 2.0.0 standalone and 2.0.1/2.3.0 through Express Supplied code ran with raw() and json() in the tested setups Input rejected; no marker; server stayed running Express 5 documents Brotli decoding in its request-body parsers, and the body-parser release history records support beginning with 2.0.0. Express 5.3.0 and body-parser 2.3.0 were the latest releases when we tested on October 22, 2026. We reproduced execution at the listed versions; we did not individually test every intermediate release. The vulnerable code is in Node.js: these middleware versions identify paths that can invoke it. A bare Node.js HTTP server does not decode incoming Brotli bodies simply by receiving them. The proof did not succeed on every attempt. Our results establish code execution for the tested Linux arm64 build and application setups, and show how the fixed build handled the same inputs. We did not test every Node.js build or application. Technical deep dive: When invalid input looks incomplete A Brotli stream describes the block types available as decoding progresses. Our test input reached a block transition that the stream’s own structure made impossible. In the vulnerable decoder, that condition could look like a request for more input. Processing continued with an invalid internal state. Our separate sanitizer run showed that continuing from that state could write beyond an intended buffer. The upstream Brotli fix makes the decoder return a format error for the invalid transition and pass it to the caller. In our application tests, patched Node.js rejected the same inputs before code could run. Two tested routes into the native decoder. The patched runtime stops at the invalid-format check. The distinction matters for exposure. Express 5 and body-parser 2 can decompress incoming Brotli request bodies when their parsers are configured; they are routes into the vulnerable Node.js decoder, not the source of the flaw. On the response side, our test service consumed an external Brotli response with Node.js’s built-in fetch(). Both paths reach the same decoder. What defenders should do The priority is to replace affected Node.js runtimes. The project released fixes in 22.23.4 , 24.22.1, and 26.12.1 . Deploy these or newer fixed releases in each line, including in container images and other artifacts that bundle a Node binary. Move applications on unsupported Node.js lines to a supported release. Then map where untrusted Brotli data reaches that runtime. Review compressed responses consumed by services and incoming request bodies inflated by configured middleware. Check the Node.js version inside each deployed image or host; a package inventory can miss an older runtime bundled in a container. Where practical, temporarily limit untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths while updates roll out. Test changes against the application’s normal traffic. Complete remediation requires updating Node.js. Unexpected process exits during decompression and decoder errors may help prioritize investigation. Neither is a reliable stand-alone sign of exploitation; correlate them with the deployed runtime, application logs, and the source of the compressed data. Thales’s response and customer protection Thales Threat Research reproduced remote code execution through both a consumed Brotli response and configured request parsers, then confirmed that the released Node.js fix rejects the same inputs. That validation helps customers identify the services to update first: those running affected builds and decoding Brotli data from outside their trust boundary. Imperva has added dedicated WAF rules in response to CVE-2026-111497 and validated them to detect and block the exploitation attempts we were able to reproduce. Customers should update affected Node.js deployments to a fixed release. The runtime update remediates the decoder flaw. Our tests covered both an incoming request parser and a consumed HTTP response. In both cases the affected code is the Node.js decoder, so the runtime update addresses the shared cause. Closing thoughts In our tests, a Brotli response or request body made an application running the official Node.js 24.22.0 build execute code supplied with the data. No debugger or special build was involved. The fixed release rejected the same inputs. The proof took multiple attempts in our Linux arm64 setup, but the action for customers is clear: update Node.js wherever applications decode untrusted Brotli data, whether it arrives in an incoming request or a consumed response.

We tested Express 5.0.0–5.3.0 and body-parser 2.0.0–2.3.0, including the latest releases available at testing; execution took multiple attempts in our setup.

Imperva has added WAF rules for CVE-2026-111497. Customers should update affected Node.js deployments to a fixed release.

Overview

A Node.js service can encounter Brotli on either side of an HTTP exchange. It may consume a compressed response from another server, or use middleware to decode an incoming request body. Both operations can send untrusted data into the native decoder bundled with Node.js. That shared path is where CVE-2026-111497 lives.

We built a standalone proof of concept to see whether the flaw could lead to code execution in a Node.js application. In fresh containers running the official vulnerable Node.js image, the application ran code supplied with the Brotli data. We used a memory sanitizer separately to investigate the underlying bug and compared the results with the fixed release.

The Node.js project disclosed the issue on October 21, 2026. Its advisory credits Matteo Collina with reporting it and Antoine du Hamel with the fix. Our work is an independent validation of the impact and the released patch.

Impact: From a decoder error to code execution

In the working proof of concept, the test application had no code to create our marker file. After it received the Brotli data, the file appeared. Code carried in that data had run inside the target process. We reproduced this with the official Node.js 24.22.0 image in fresh Linux arm64 containers. The same inputs on Node.js 24.22.1 were rejected and created no marker.

We also investigated the cause. A source comparison showed that the vulnerable decoder could continue past an invalid stream condition. In a separate sanitizer test, decoding that condition caused an out-of-bounds write. The sanitizer helped explain the flaw; it was not needed for the code-execution proof.

We tested both a compressed response consumed by Node.js’s built-in fetch() and incoming Brotli bodies handled by configured request parsers. The table shows the Brotli-capable package ranges represented by our pinned endpoint tests:

Application path Package range and tested configurations Node.js 24.22.0 Node.js 24.22.1 Consumed HTTP response Node.js built-in fetch() Supplied code ran; marker created Input rejected; no marker Incoming request body Express 5.0.0–5.3.0; tested 5.0.0 with body-parser 2.0.1, and 5.3.0 with body-parser 2.3.0 Supplied code ran with raw() and json() in both tested setups Input rejected; no marker; server stayed running Incoming request body body-parser 2.0.0–2.3.0; tested 2.0.0 standalone and 2.0.1/2.3.0 through Express Supplied code ran with raw() and json() in the tested setups Input rejected; no marker; server stayed running

The vulnerable code is in Node.js: these middleware versions identify paths that can invoke it. A bare Node.js HTTP server does not decode incoming Brotli bodies simply by receiving them.

The proof did not succeed on every attempt. Our results establish code execution for the tested Linux arm64 build and application setups, and show how the fixed build handled the same inputs. We did not test every Node.js build or application.

Technical deep dive: When invalid input looks incomplete

A Brotli stream describes the block types available as decoding progresses. Our test input reached a block transition that the stream’s own structure made impossible. In the vulnerable decoder, that condition could look like a request for more input. Processing continued with an invalid internal state.

Our separate sanitizer run showed that continuing from that state could write beyond an intended buffer. The upstream Brotli fix makes the decoder return a format error for the invalid transition and pass it to the caller. In our application tests, patched Node.js rejected the same inputs before code could run.

Two tested routes into the native decoder. The patched runtime stops at the invalid-format check.

Then map where untrusted Brotli data reaches that runtime. Review compressed responses consumed by services and incoming request bodies inflated by configured middleware. Check the Node.js version inside each deployed image or host; a package inventory can miss an older runtime bundled in a container.

Where practical, temporarily limit untrusted Brotli traffic on affected paths while updates roll out. Test changes against the application’s normal traffic. Complete remediation requires updating Node.js.

Thales Threat Research reproduced remote code execution through both a consumed Brotli response and configured request parsers, then confirmed that the released Node.js fix rejects the same inputs. That validation helps customers identify the services to update first: those running affected builds and decoding Brotli data from outside their trust boundary.

Our tests covered both an incoming request parser and a consumed HTTP response. In both cases the affected code is the Node.js decoder, so the runtime update addresses the shared cause.

Closing thoughts

In our tests, a Brotli response or request body made an application running the official Node.js 24.22.0 build execute code supplied with the data. No debugger or special build was involved. The fixed release rejected the same inputs. The proof took multiple attempts in our Linux arm64 setup, but the action for customers is clear: update Node.js wherever applications decode untrusted Brotli data, whether it arrives in an incoming request or a consumed response.

items.title: A Hacker Tried to Turn an AI Chatbot Into a Tool for Attacking Other Servers
items.summary: An exposed artificial intelligence platform can give an intruder more than a place to send messages. If it connects to stored credentials, company data, or network tools, the platform may also provide a route toward those resources. A recent honeypot investigation shows how an attacker tried to use an AI agent to study real infrastructure and prepare further activity. The incident involved Flowise, an open-source platform for building AI workflows. In late August 2026, an unauthenticated Flowise honeypot received requests to inspect the service, list its workflows, and retrieve stored credentials. The honeypot was a decoy, not a live production system; it was designed to record activity without running real system commands or a real language model. Analysts from Sekoia’s Threat Detection & Research team identified the activity and documented how the intruder moved from basic checks to attempts to misuse the AI agent. Their report describes an operator who tried to obtain sensitive data and turn the chatbot into an assistant for examining other servers. The Sekoia investigation says the activity mainly abused Flowise features rather than relying on a software flaw. A Hacker Tried to Turn an AI Chatbot Into a Tool The attacker first checked whether the Flowise service was available and queried its version and node settings. They then requested lists of chatflows and credentials, followed by requests for details tied to specific credentials. Those steps could reveal AI service keys and database access details on a poorly protected real installation. The early activity lasted about three minutes, then stopped for just over two hours before a wider scan of the API routes. The report notes that the behavior resembled unauthenticated access associated with CVE-2024-31621, but says that particular flaw was not exploited in the honeypot. It was fixed in Flowise 1.6.6 and was included in the report only to describe the observed pattern. Separately, the Flowise vulnerability report covers risks tied to exposed Flowise installations and sensitive credentials. Flowise honeypot attack timeline (Source – Sekoia) After testing basic inference requests, the operator tried to rename an existing workflow and create a new one called “System Status.” The new workflow included an HTTP Request node aimed at an external server. If a similar workflow were executed in a live environment, it could make the Flowise server contact attacker-controlled infrastructure. Sekoia described this as misuse of a legitimate outbound request feature, rather than a confirmed software exploit. Prompts aimed at the AI agent The attacker also sent prompts designed to probe the agent’s capabilities. They asked it to reveal its system instructions, use tools, run commands, recall a planted access code, and disclose conversations from other users. These attempts are examples of prompt injection: instructions crafted to push an AI system away from its intended role or safeguards. The prompts also tried to reach data connected to a simulated finance chatflow. The attacker claimed to be conducting an authorized audit and asked the agent to query a database and summarize financial records. Sekoia says the operator later tried to get the agent to perform reconnaissance against a simulated internal host. Because the honeypot did not run a real model or execute system commands, the evidence shows attempts—not successful access to real records or systems. The activity then shifted toward a real target. The prompts included details about a Nightingale monitoring server, Redis data, and an online gambling platform operating across parts of Asia. iGaming app and website targeted (Source – Sekoia) The attacker asked for target analysis and guidance on weaknesses and access paths. Sekoia assessed that the information suggested a Chinese-speaking operator and an interest in the online gambling sector, but said there was not enough evidence to link the activity to a known group. This case is part of a wider concern about agents that combine natural-language prompts with tools, databases, or cloud permissions. A separate report on AI agents and cloud credentials describes how prompt injection can become more serious when an agent can reach services or secrets. Research on AI agent traps also examines how untrusted content can affect an agent’s decisions and memory. The key risk is not that a chatbot can answer questions. It is that an agent may be able to act on its answers by calling tools, making network requests, or reading connected data. A prompt alone should not grant access, but weak authentication, broad permissions, and unrestricted network paths can give an attacker more room to work. Organizations using Flowise or similar platforms should restrict administrative interfaces to authorized users and networks, review who can read or change workflows, and store only the credentials each agent needs. Teams should also limit outbound connections, monitor unusual requests to workflow and credential APIs, and require human approval before an agent takes actions with sensitive impact. Sekoia recommends strong authentication, strict permission boundaries, and monitoring for prompt injection and misuse of agent capabilities. items.title: CVE-2026-110264: Critical GitLab RCE Flaw Affects 12 Years of Releases
items.summary: GitLab has released urgent security updates addressing CVE-2026-110264, a maximum-severity vulnerability that could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable self-managed GitLab servers. The flaw carries a CVSS score of 10.0 and affects both GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). The vulnerability is particularly notable because the affected code dates back to GitLab 7.0, released in 2014. This leaves roughly 12 years of GitLab releases within the vulnerable range, although there is currently no evidence that attackers have been exploiting the weakness throughout that period. GitLab disclosed the issue and released patched versions on October 21, 2026. The vulnerability originates from an integer overflow triggered while GitLab compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Under certain conditions, an unauthenticated attacker could use that condition to execute arbitrary code on the underlying GitLab server. GitLab has intentionally withheld the complete exploitation path and specific prerequisites while administrators deploy patches. For organizations running self-managed GitLab infrastructure, the potential impact is severe. GitLab repositories frequently contain source code, CI/CD configuration, deployment secrets, access tokens, infrastructure definitions, and connections to production environments. Server-level compromise could therefore create opportunities for credential theft, repository manipulation, supply chain attacks, persistence, or lateral movement. Security teams looking for CVE-2026-110264 detection opportunities can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to strengthen visibility into vulnerability exploitation and related post-compromise behavior across SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake environments. Click Explore Detections to access relevant detection content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-110264 exploitation attempts, defenders should correlate GitLab application telemetry with process execution, abnormal server behavior, and GitLab’s newly released threat-detection logic. Security practitioners can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules and hunting queries, validate detection logic, generate relevant Attack Flows, and translate detection content across supported security platforms. Contact Sales CVE-2026-110264 analysis GitLab describes the vulnerability as an integer overflow in its regular expression compiler. Under certain conditions, compiling a specially crafted regular expression can lead to arbitrary code execution on the GitLab server without authentication. GitLab assigned the vulnerability the maximum CVSS v3.1 score of 10.0, with the vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H. This reflects a network-accessible vulnerability with low attack complexity, no required privileges, and no user interaction, with potentially high impact on confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Security researcher joaxcar discovered and reported the vulnerability through GitLab’s HackerOne bug bounty program. GitLab’s release notes also reference patches to Ruby regular-expression handling, while reporting indicates that the underlying affected engine is Onigmo, Ruby’s regular-expression implementation bundled into GitLab packages. CVE-2026-110264 affects GitLab CE and EE across an unusually broad range: GitLab 7.0 through versions before 18.11.13 GitLab 19.0 before 19.0.10 GitLab 19.1 before 19.1.9 GitLab 19.2 before 19.2.9 GitLab 19.3 before 19.3.6 GitLab 19.4 before 19.4.3 GitLab 19.5 before 19.5.1 GitLab backported the fix to 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, and 19.2.9 in addition to its normal supported patch branches because of the severity and unusually broad exposure. The long vulnerable window does not mean the flaw has been actively exploited since 2014. Rather, the vulnerable regular-expression functionality existed throughout releases dating back to GitLab 7.0. Neither GitLab nor the two supplied reports has confirmed exploitation in real-world attacks as of October 22, 2026. This vulnerability should also not be confused with CVE-2026-97229, another critical GitLab remote code execution flaw related to regular-expression processing that was patched earlier in October. That issue affected a narrower range of more recent releases. Installing the October 12 fixes for that vulnerability does not automatically protect systems from this newly disclosed flaw. Administrators who recently updated GitLab therefore need to verify their exact installed build rather than assuming a previous October security release provides sufficient protection. The currently available details for CVE-2026-110264 do not disclose the precise attacker-controlled input, endpoint, feature, or conditions required to reach the vulnerable regular-expression compiler. GitLab generally makes detailed security issues public 90 days after the release containing a fix, reducing the immediate availability of weaponizable technical information while customers patch. No public CVE-2026-110264 PoC has been disclosed in the supplied reports or GitLab advisory. Cybersecurity News specifically notes that GitLab has not published a public exploit, while the company has limited disclosure of the complete attack path. At the same time, the absence of a public proof of concept should not be interpreted as low risk. A remotely reachable, unauthenticated vulnerability with a CVSS 10.0 rating presents an attractive target, particularly because self-managed GitLab servers are frequently exposed to the internet. There are currently no campaign-specific CVE-2026-110264 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, payload hashes, or confirmed exploit request patterns because neither GitLab nor the cited security researchers have reported active exploitation. GitLab has, however, published two threat detections intended to identify possible exploitation attempts on self-managed installations: Onigmo native worker crash Org mode render error burst These detections are designed to identify suspicious behavior related to attempts to trigger the vulnerability. Their presence does not by itself confirm successful compromise and should be correlated with broader application and endpoint telemetry. Security teams should investigate unexpected GitLab application crashes, bursts of rendering errors, anomalous processes originating from GitLab or Ruby components, unexpected shell execution, newly created persistence mechanisms, and outbound connections from GitLab servers that deviate from normal operational patterns. CVE-2026-110264 mitigation GitLab strongly recommends that all organizations operating affected self-managed installations upgrade immediately. The fixed versions are: GitLab branch Fixed version 18.11 and earlier supported migration path 18.11.13 19.0 19.0.10 19.1 19.1.9 19.2 19.2.9 19.3 19.3.6 19.4 19.4.3 19.5 19.5.1 GitLab.com has already been updated. GitLab Dedicated tenants running internal versions 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0, or later already contain the necessary fixes and do not need to take action for this vulnerability. Self-managed customers should not delay remediation while waiting for additional exploitation details. GitLab has not published an alternative workaround that provides equivalent protection, making installation of the fixed release the reliable remediation path. Before upgrading, administrators should review GitLab’s upgrade documentation and account for database migrations. GitLab warns that single-node deployments may experience downtime while migrations complete, whereas properly configured multi-node environments can follow the vendor’s zero-downtime upgrade process. Versions 19.3.6 and 19.4.3 contain regular migrations, and 19.4.3 also includes a post-deploy migration. After patching, security teams should perform retrospective analysis rather than treating the update itself as proof that a server was never targeted. Review GitLab application logs for the two exploitation indicators published by GitLab and investigate suspicious activity preceding the upgrade. Defenders should also examine operating-system telemetry for: Unexpected child processes originating from GitLab, Ruby, or associated workers Shell or scripting interpreter execution under GitLab service accounts New SSH keys or administrative accounts Unexpected modifications to repositories or CI/CD pipelines Newly created scheduled jobs or persistence mechanisms Changes to runners, deploy tokens, personal access tokens, and project access tokens Unusual outbound connections from the GitLab server Unauthorized access to secrets stored in CI/CD variables Unexpected package, release, or repository modifications If compromise is suspected, organizations should isolate the server, preserve logs and forensic artifacts, rotate potentially exposed credentials and tokens, and validate the integrity of repositories and CI/CD workflows before returning the instance to production. Because GitLab installations often act as trusted infrastructure within software development pipelines, responders should also determine whether an attacker could have modified source code, artifacts, container images, infrastructure-as-code templates, or deployment workflows. A compromised GitLab server can create downstream supply chain risk even after the original server is remediated. Under certain conditions, an unauthenticated remote attacker could trigger the flaw and execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server. GitLab has not yet disclosed the complete input or application path required to reach the vulnerable code. When was CVE-2026-110264 first discovered? The vulnerability was reported to GitLab by security researcher joaxcar through the company’s HackerOne bug bounty program. GitLab publicly disclosed the issue and released patches on October 21, 2026. The vulnerable code itself had existed in GitLab releases since version 7.0 in 2014, but this does not mean the vulnerability had been known or exploited for the full 12-year period. Because GitLab can store source code, credentials, access tokens, CI/CD secrets, build artifacts, deployment configurations, and infrastructure definitions, server compromise could potentially result in sensitive data theft, repository tampering, persistence, credential compromise, lateral movement, or software supply chain attacks. GitLab’s CVSS assessment rates potential confidentiality, integrity, and availability impact as high. Can CVE-2026-110264 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Any self-managed GitLab CE or EE installation within the affected version ranges remains vulnerable until it is upgraded to a fixed release. After patching, review GitLab’s published “Onigmo native worker crash” and “Org mode render error burst” detections, examine historical application and endpoint telemetry for suspicious activity, and investigate unexpected process execution or configuration changes.   • Onigmo native worker crash
  • Org mode render error burst

These detections are designed to identify suspicious behavior related to attempts to trigger the vulnerability. Their presence does not by itself confirm successful compromise and should be correlated with broader application and endpoint telemetry.

GitLab branchFixed version18.11 and earlier supported migration path18.11.1319.019.0.1019.119.1.919.219.2.919.319.3.619.419.4.319.519.5.1

  • Shell or scripting interpreter execution under GitLab service accounts
  • New SSH keys or administrative accounts
  • Unexpected modifications to repositories or CI/CD pipelines
  • Newly created scheduled jobs or persistence mechanisms
  • Changes to runners, deploy tokens, personal access tokens, and project access tokens
  • Unusual outbound connections from the GitLab server

Unlock Android phones others can’t with XRY Pro

Android phones on recent security updates no longer have to be a dead end. XRY Pro now unlocks and extracts the latest Android devices.

  • Covers the phones you see every day

Enrich crypto wallets without leaving the case

More from every device with XRY and XRY Pro Full file system extraction from the newest Androids

items.title: CVE-2026-91403: Critical Oracle Java SE and GraalVM Flaw Enables Remote Attacks
items.summary: Oracle has issued an out-of-band Security Alert addressing CVE-2026-91403, a critical vulnerability affecting Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. The security issue resides in the Java Secure Socket Extension (JSSE) component and carries a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.1. The vulnerability is remotely exploitable without authentication. According to Oracle, an attacker with network access through multiple protocols can compromise vulnerable Java environments without providing credentials or requiring user interaction. Successful exploitation can expose critical data and enable unauthorized modification, creation, or deletion of information accessible to the affected Java runtime. Rapid7 classifies the flaw as critical and confirms the CVSS vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N. This means exploitation can occur over the network with low attack complexity, requires no privileges or victim interaction, and can have high confidentiality and integrity impact. The broad deployment of Java across enterprise web services, backend applications, middleware, APIs, and business-critical infrastructure increases the potential exposure. Organizations should therefore identify affected Java and GraalVM runtimes and prioritize Oracle’s Security Alert patches. Security teams looking for CVE-2026-91403 detection opportunities should monitor Java services for anomalous network interactions, unexpected certificate or TLS-related failures, suspicious child processes, and unusual access to sensitive application data. SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform can help security teams strengthen their defenses against emerging vulnerability exploitation with detection content mapped to MITRE ATT&CK® and available across multiple SIEM, EDR, and Data Lake environments. Click Explore Detections to access relevant SOC content and hunting logic. To Detect CVE-2026-91403 and associated post-exploitation behavior, defenders should combine Java application telemetry, network monitoring, endpoint visibility, and service-level logs. Security teams can also leverage Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into Sigma rules, generate hunting queries, validate detection logic, and translate detections across supported security platforms. Contact Sales CVE-2026-91403 analysis CVE-2026-91403 impacts the JSSE component used by Java applications to provide secure communications capabilities. Oracle describes the flaw as easily exploitable and confirms that attacks can originate remotely over multiple protocols without authentication. The vendor has not publicly disclosed the underlying programming error or complete exploitation sequence. Oracle’s vulnerability disclosure policy intentionally limits technical details that could facilitate weaponization while customers deploy patches. Therefore, claims about a specific malformed packet, certificate structure, API argument, or exploitation primitive should not be treated as confirmed unless Oracle publishes additional technical information. CVE-2026-91403 affects the following supported Oracle releases: Oracle Java SE 8u511 and 8u511-perf Oracle Java SE 11.0.33 Oracle Java SE 17.0.21 Oracle Java SE 21.0.13 Oracle Java SE 25.0.5 Oracle Java SE 27.0.1 Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21 Oracle GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13 Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20 Oracle also cautions that unsupported earlier releases were not tested but are likely to contain vulnerabilities addressed by the Security Alert. Organizations still operating unsupported Java branches should therefore not assume they are unaffected. The attack surface is broader than standalone Java desktop applications. Oracle specifically notes that exploitation can occur through APIs exposed by the vulnerable component, including situations in which a web service passes attacker-controlled data to those APIs. The vendor also states that the issue applies to Java deployments that execute untrusted code while relying on the Java sandbox for protection, including sandboxed Java Web Start applications and Java applets. The details for CVE-2026-91403 show particularly serious confidentiality and integrity consequences. Oracle rates both impacts as High while assigning no direct availability impact. A successful attacker could potentially gain unauthorized access to critical application data or modify, create, and delete information available to the compromised Java environment. That distinction is important for incident response. Organizations should not focus exclusively on service disruption. A vulnerable server may continue operating normally while sensitive information is accessed or application data is modified. At the time of publication, neither Rapid7 nor Oracle provides a public CVE-2026-91403 PoC or sufficient technical exploitation instructions to independently reproduce the vulnerability. Rapid7 also lists the issue as absent from the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 22, 2026. Likewise, no campaign-specific CVE-2026-91403 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, hashes, or payload signatures have been published in the primary sources. This limits the effectiveness of purely indicator-based hunting and makes behavioral visibility more important. Security teams should monitor Java-facing services for: Unexpected network requests reaching Java applications or web services Abnormal TLS or JSSE-related errors Changes to application data without corresponding legitimate activity Unexpected authentication or authorization anomalies Java processes initiating unusual outbound connections Unrecognized child processes launched by Java applications Modifications to files, configuration, or application resources Suspicious API requests immediately preceding abnormal data access Because the complete exploitation mechanics remain undisclosed, these behaviors cannot prove exploitation on their own. They should instead serve as investigation pivots when combined with vulnerability exposure and application-specific telemetry. CVE-2026-91403 mitigation Oracle released a dedicated Security Alert on October 21, 2026 rather than waiting for a later scheduled security cycle. Administrators should apply the patches referenced in Oracle’s patch availability documentation as quickly as operationally possible. Organizations should first inventory all Java installations, including runtimes bundled with commercial software, middleware products, application servers, containers, development environments, and third-party appliances. Java components embedded inside another product are often overlooked during vulnerability management because administrators may not realize that a separate JDK or JRE exists within the application directory. Priority should be given to systems that: Accept network connections from untrusted sources Expose Java-backed web services or APIs Process attacker-controlled input Handle sensitive business or customer data Run unsupported Java releases Use Java Web Start or other sandbox-dependent deployment models Oracle provides Security Alert patches only for versions covered under Premier Support or Extended Support. Earlier releases are not necessarily safe simply because they are absent from the affected-version table. Oracle explicitly recommends moving unsupported deployments to supported versions because older releases may also contain the vulnerability. If immediate patching is not possible, organizations should reduce exposure by restricting network access to affected services, limiting communication to trusted systems, and applying application-level access controls where feasible. These steps should be treated as temporary risk-reduction measures rather than replacements for the vendor update. Security teams should also review application and network logs retrospectively. Look for unexpected access to sensitive data, suspicious modifications, anomalous Java network activity, and unusual API requests that cannot be explained by legitimate business operations. If suspicious behavior is identified, responders should: Isolate the affected host where operationally possible. Preserve Java application, web-server, endpoint, and network logs. Review the integrity of sensitive application data. Identify credentials, secrets, and tokens accessible to the Java process. Rotate potentially exposed credentials. Search for unauthorized changes to application files and configuration. Examine outbound connections for signs of follow-on activity. Validate other Java systems with the same application configuration. Because confidentiality and integrity are the primary impacts identified by Oracle, incident response should include data-access and data-modification reviews even when there is no evidence of downtime. Organizations using SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform can strengthen behavioral monitoring around vulnerable Java services while patches are rolled out and continue hunting for post-compromise activity across their security stack. CVE-2026-91403 is a critical vulnerability in the JSSE component of Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM for JDK, and Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition. Oracle confirms that an unauthenticated attacker with network access can exploit the issue through multiple protocols. The vulnerable component can also be reached indirectly when a web service supplies attacker-controlled information to relevant APIs. Successful exploitation can expose critical data and allow unauthorized modification, creation, or deletion of information accessible to the affected Java environment. Oracle has not publicly disclosed the complete technical exploitation mechanism. When was CVE-2026-91403 first discovered? The precise discovery date has not been publicly disclosed. The CVE identifier was reserved on September 14, 2026, and Oracle publicly released its Security Alert on October 21, 2026. Oracle’s advisory does not credit an external researcher or organization for reporting the issue. What is the impact of CVE-2026-91403 on systems? Successful exploitation can result in unauthorized access to critical or complete application data and can allow attackers to create, modify, or delete information accessible through the affected Java environment. Oracle assigns High confidentiality and integrity impact while indicating no direct availability impact. The flaw scores 9.1 under CVSS v3.1 and requires neither authentication nor user interaction. Can CVE-2026-91403 still affect me in 2026? Yes. Systems running the affected Oracle Java SE or GraalVM releases remain exposed until the applicable security update is installed. Organizations should also evaluate older unsupported Java releases. Oracle states that these versions were not tested but may contain the same vulnerabilities and recommends migrating to supported software. How can I protect myself from CVE-2026-91403? Apply Oracle’s Security Alert patches and upgrade vulnerable Java and GraalVM installations according to the vendor’s patch availability guidance. Inventory Java runtimes throughout the environment, including copies embedded in third-party applications. Prioritize internet-facing services and applications processing untrusted data, restrict network exposure where immediate patching is impossible, and monitor Java services for suspicious network behavior and unauthorized access to sensitive data. If compromise is suspected, isolate affected systems, preserve forensic telemetry, review application data integrity, rotate potentially exposed secrets, and investigate related systems for signs of lateral or follow-on activity.

CVE-2026-91403 analysis

CVE-2026-91403 impacts the JSSE component used by Java applications to provide secure communications capabilities. Oracle describes the flaw as easily exploitable and confirms that attacks can originate remotely over multiple protocols without authentication.

The vendor has not publicly disclosed the underlying programming error or complete exploitation sequence. Oracle’s vulnerability disclosure policy intentionally limits technical details that could facilitate weaponization while customers deploy patches.   • Oracle Java SE 11.0.33
  • Oracle Java SE 17.0.21
  • Oracle Java SE 21.0.13
  • Oracle Java SE 25.0.5
  • Oracle Java SE 27.0.1
  • Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17.0.21
  • Oracle GraalVM for JDK 21.0.13
  • Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition 21.3.20

Oracle also cautions that unsupported earlier releases were not tested but are likely to contain vulnerabilities addressed by the Security Alert. Organizations still operating unsupported Java branches should therefore not assume they are unaffected.

The attack surface is broader than standalone Java desktop applications. Oracle specifically notes that exploitation can occur through APIs exposed by the vulnerable component, including situations in which a web service passes attacker-controlled data to those APIs.

The vendor also states that the issue applies to Java deployments that execute untrusted code while relying on the Java sandbox for protection, including sandboxed Java Web Start applications and Java applets.

The details for CVE-2026-91403 show particularly serious confidentiality and integrity consequences. Oracle rates both impacts as High while assigning no direct availability impact. A successful attacker could potentially gain unauthorized access to critical application data or modify, create, and delete information available to the compromised Java environment.

That distinction is important for incident response. Organizations should not focus exclusively on service disruption. A vulnerable server may continue operating normally while sensitive information is accessed or application data is modified.

At the time of publication, neither Rapid7 nor Oracle provides a public CVE-2026-91403 PoC or sufficient technical exploitation instructions to independently reproduce the vulnerability. Rapid7 also lists the issue as absent from the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of October 22, 2026.

Likewise, no campaign-specific CVE-2026-91403 IOCs such as malicious IP addresses, domains, hashes, or payload signatures have been published in the primary sources. This limits the effectiveness of purely indicator-based hunting and makes behavioral visibility more important.

Security teams should monitor Java-facing services for:

  • Unexpected network requests reaching Java applications or web services
  • Abnormal TLS or JSSE-related errors
  • Changes to application data without corresponding legitimate activity
  • Unexpected authentication or authorization anomalies
  • Java processes initiating unusual outbound connections
  • Unrecognized child processes launched by Java applications
  • Modifications to files, configuration, or application resources
  • Suspicious API requests immediately preceding abnormal data access

Because the complete exploitation mechanics remain undisclosed, these behaviors cannot prove exploitation on their own. They should instead serve as investigation pivots when combined with vulnerability exposure and application-specific telemetry.

CVE-2026-91403 mitigation

Oracle released a dedicated Security Alert on October 21, 2026 rather than waiting for a later scheduled security cycle. Administrators should apply the patches referenced in Oracle’s patch availability documentation as quickly as operationally possible.

Organizations should first inventory all Java installations, including runtimes bundled with commercial software, middleware products, application servers, containers, development environments, and third-party appliances. Java components embedded inside another product are often overlooked during vulnerability management because administrators may not realize that a separate JDK or JRE exists within the application directory.

Priority should be given to systems that:

  • Accept network connections from untrusted sources
  • Expose Java-backed web services or APIs
  • Process attacker-controlled input
  • Handle sensitive business or customer data
  • Run unsupported Java releases
  • Use Java Web Start or other sandbox-dependent deployment models

Oracle provides Security Alert patches only for versions covered under Premier Support or Extended Support. Earlier releases are not necessarily safe simply because they are absent from the affected-version table. Oracle explicitly recommends moving unsupported deployments to supported versions because older releases may also contain the vulnerability.

If immediate patching is not possible, organizations should reduce exposure by restricting network access to affected services, limiting communication to trusted systems, and applying application-level access controls where feasible. These steps should be treated as temporary risk-reduction measures rather than replacements for the vendor update.

Security teams should also review application and network logs retrospectively. Look for unexpected access to sensitive data, suspicious modifications, anomalous Java network activity, and unusual API requests that cannot be explained by legitimate business operations.

If suspicious behavior is identified, responders should:

  • Isolate the affected host where operationally possible.
  • Preserve Java application, web-server, endpoint, and network logs.
  • Review the integrity of sensitive application data.
  • Identify credentials, secrets, and tokens accessible to the Java process.
  • Rotate potentially exposed credentials.
  • Search for unauthorized changes to application files and configuration.
  • Examine outbound connections for signs of follow-on activity.
  • Validate other Java systems with the same application configuration.

Because confidentiality and integrity are the primary impacts identified by Oracle, incident response should include data-access and data-modification reviews even when there is no evidence of downtime.

items.title: Woman faces years in prison over a Cash App account she says she never opened
items.summary: A Cash App account opened in her name has left Amanda Smith facing criminal charges and potentially up to six years in prison. 404 Media reports that Smith says someone used her Social Security number (SSN) and date of birth to create an account that received money from a Facebook Marketplace scam. Allegedly, a buyer sent $1,000 for items that weren’t really for sale. A scammer had taken over someone else’s Facebook account and directed the buyer to pay a Cash App account in Smith’s name. Investigators obtained account information from Block, Cash App’s parent company. That information included Smith’s Social Security number and date of birth. Police subsequently arrested her in Pennsylvania over the alleged crime in Arkansas, a state she says she had never visited. She spent three nights in jail. But 404 Media’s review of account records found that several account details, including the address and network used, did not match her own. Smith also described a frustrating obstacle when she tried to investigate: “Cash App refused to provide me with any information about the account, because I couldn’t prove that I was the owner.” The account was associated with her closely enough to contribute to her arrest, yet she said she could not get information directly from the company. She later received account records through the criminal case. It’s a disturbing reminder that the consequences of identity theft can go well beyond an unfamiliar charge on your bank statement. You could also find yourself accused of a crime committed using your details. Breaches happen every day. Don’t be the last to know. SEE PLANS Smith suspects that information exposed in a data breach may have been used to impersonate her. When investigating, 404 Media found the phone number used for the account linked to an Amanda Smith in older breach data. They also found someone made a Venmo account using the same phone number but under another name entirely. The source of her Social Security number and date of birth hasn’t been established, and her case is ongoing. Her experience highlights why it matters to know which of your details have been exposed. How to protect yourself The practical lesson is to look beyond the headline that a company “lost customer data.” What matters is which information was exposed, because different exposures call for different responses. Our guide for how to handle being involved in a data breach recommends checking the affected company’s official information before deciding what to do next. The steps depend on the type of data that was stolen or leaked: Email addresses and phone numbers: Be alert for phishing messages and scam calls, including messages that refer to the breach. Passwords: Change the affected password and anywhere else you reused it. Enable multifactor authentication where available. Payment or banking details: Contact the relevant financial institution and review your accounts for unauthorized activity. Social Security numbers and other identifying information: Check your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts. In the US, you can freeze your credit for free with each of the three major credit bureaus: Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. This helps prevent new credit accounts being opened in your name, but does not prevent every type of identity misuse. If you discover an account opened in your name , contact the company’s fraud department through its official website and report the identity theft (in the US you can do that at IdentityTheft.gov ). Keep copies of your reports and correspondence, and ask for written confirmation when the fraudulent account is closed. A breach-checking service can help you identify known exposures linked to your information. Malwarebytes’ Digital Footprint Scan , for example, checks for exposures associated with your email address. What do cybercriminals know about you? items.title: New Android Malware Replaces Legitimate Banking Apps With Malicious Copies to Bypass Security Checks
items.summary: A newly identified Android banking Trojan called Hirudo takes an unusual route to financial fraud: it tries to remove a victim’s genuine banking app and install a modified copy in its place. The replacement keeps the bank app’s name and version, but contains extra code designed to interfere with security checks. Instead of relying only on fake login screens displayed over a real app, Hirudo’s operators try to make the banking app itself return answers that hide the malware’s presence. The campaign combines app replacement with credential theft and remote control of infected phones. Its operators can seek banking passwords, payment PINs, SMS messages and device-unlock details, while also viewing the screen and accessing the cameras. This makes Hirudo more than a fake banking app: it is a remote access Trojan, or RAT, built to help criminals gather information and act on a compromised device. Analysts from ThreatFabric identified the malware and reported that it has replacement copies prepared for eight Indonesian banking apps covering seven banks. The researchers also found a wider set of financial apps in Hirudo’s target list, suggesting the operators built a system that could be adapted beyond those banks. New Android Malware Replaces Legitimate Banking Apps Hirudo reaches users through apparently useful shopping and entertainment apps. ThreatFabric described lures themed around shopping, adult video and short dramas, including names such as Shopora, 1V1 X, ZoyaTV and KoiShort. The lure may show real-looking content, such as a storefront or video catalogue, while quietly checking whether the separate Hirudo payload is already installed. If it is not, the lure displays a fake update prompt and asks the user to install another app package. That second app carries the Trojan and needs its own permissions before its theft and remote-control features can work. The Hirudo fraud chain (Source – Threat Fabric) This two-app setup can make the first download appear less suspicious, while the false update persuades the user to install the more dangerous component. Once active, Hirudo uses Android’s Accessibility service to detect a targeted banking app and check its signing certificate. It then displays a false update message, opens the system uninstaller for the genuine app and downloads a bank-specific replacement. The replacement uses the same package name and version as the original, but it is signed with a public test key rather than the bank’s own key. Android will not accept it as an ordinary update over the bank-signed app, so Hirudo first tries to remove the genuine app. That step creates an important limit: the user may interrupt the uninstall or refuse to approve the replacement installation. Its remote-control features include live screen viewing over WebRTC and sessions using the phone’s front or rear camera. They should treat Accessibility and screenshot signals as supporting evidence, not as reliable proof that an app is safe, because Hirudo can tamper with both. Monitoring should also cover sensitive actions such as login, password recovery, adding a payment beneficiary and approving a transfer. The broader risk is clear: if malware can alter a banking app, signals generated only inside that app may be under an attacker’s control. A newly identified Android banking Trojan called Hirudo takes an unusual route to financial fraud: it tries to remove a victim’s genuine banking app and install a modified copy in its place.

The replacement keeps the bank app’s name and version, but contains extra code designed to interfere with security checks.

Instead of relying only on fake login screens displayed over a real app, Hirudo’s operators try to make the banking app itself return answers that hide the malware’s presence.

The campaign combines app replacement with credential theft and remote control of infected phones. Its operators can seek banking passwords, payment PINs, SMS messages and device-unlock details, while also viewing the screen and accessing the cameras.

This makes Hirudo more than a fake banking app: it is a remote access Trojan, or RAT, built to help criminals gather information and act on a compromised device.

items.title: Can LLMs Supercharge Geolocations? Our Tests Show Big Improvements But Humans Remain Key
items.summary: Sign up here to receive Bellingcat’s biggest investigations by email as soon as they are published . In September, the AI company Anthropic published a blog post that claimed its models were approaching “ superhuman capabilities for geolocating outdoor photos”. Anthropic made this claim by comparing its models’ performance to that of players of the popular online game GeoGuessr, which challenges users to geolocate Google Street View images. Bellingcat has been running its own benchmark tests on AI models since June 2025, right around the time when Large Language Models (LLMs) began to challenge reverse image searches for assisting with geolocation tasks. In our first round, GPT 4o-mini from OpenAI appeared to be the best tool for geolocating, a title which was taken by Google AI mode when we performed our second round of tests a few months later in August 2025. This time, we significantly upped the ante for the models, providing increasingly challenging photos and asking for only one set of coordinates. We tasked not only closed-weight models from Claude , Grok , Gemini , ChatGPT , and Mistral , but also open-weight models from Moonshot AI’s Kimi , commercial provider GeoSeer and the non-generative geolocation model GeoClip . In total, we fed each model 52 photos that had not been published anywhere on the internet before. The results showed that the current generation of models have markedly improved geolocation capabilities. Anthropic’s Opus and Fable, as well as Google’s recent Gemini 4 Argon model, performed the best on geolocation tasks, narrowing down locations from images faster than a human could under specific conditions. Preliminary tests of a set of agentic skills and tools being developed internally by Bellingcat also showed promising results in further improving the geolocation performance of generic-use AI agents. But crucially, the tests also showed why humans remain necessary for accurate and trustworthy geolocation work, as no models were foolproof. This is particularly important given the increased use of AI in military contexts. The Anthropic blog post focused specifically on geolocating photos for military and intelligence purposes such as targeting, a historically labour-intensive process requiring significant human expertise. While our tests showed some models performed extremely well at narrowing down results to the correct general area, none were close to being perfect at finding the exact spot a picture was taken. That accuracy is extremely important in geolocation, especially in military contexts where the cost of incorrect information can be life or death . It is also important for organisations like Bellingcat whose reputation relies on pinpoint factual accuracy. Our Methods To compare model results, we used two metrics built on the distance in kilometres between a prediction and the real location. GeoGuessr Score was used to assess whether models could systematically identify the general area, while the Mean Log Score (explained below) measured which models most accurately pinpointed the correct location in the final few kilometres. The GeoGuessr Score metric is based on the online game of the same name, whose scoring system Stanford University academics reverse-engineered in a 2024 study. This system rewards answers close to the general area an image was taken, but does not strongly distinguish between guesses close to the precise location. For example, an answer 200km from the correct location with more points than one 2,000km away. However, an answer 500m from where a picture was taken and another 5km away achieve a similar score. For real-world geolocations, that distance matters a great deal. For more precision, we introduced a custom metric that grades models higher if they narrow down the search in the last few kilometres. This metric, the Mean Log Score, assigns a value from 0 (completely inaccurate) to 100 (perfect model) and works on a logarithmic scale instead of a linear one like GeoGuessr score. Therefore, a 10-fold improvement in distance means the same whether it is from 5km to 500m or from 500km to 50km. You can compare both metrics here . Below are the model results sorted by either metric, showing how many photos each model geolocated within distance bands from the true location. Several models placed at least 10 out of the 52 photos correctly within one kilometre, and the top-performing models placed over 50 percent of the photos within 25 kilometres. NOTE: Geoseer-fast refused to answer on four of the 52 photos, claiming “This image is not suitable for geolocation”, while Mistral-large-4 refused once with “insufficient information in image to identify location”. Kimi-k2.6 also failed to provide a set of coordinates on one photo, and Gemini 4 Argon timed out repeatedly on one photo. Our Test To independently assess the models, we sought to give them very specific instructions and some images that were harder to geolocate than those provided in our past tests. The prompt asked for a single set of coordinates reflecting the photographer’s location. The purpose of restricting the response in this way was to prevent hedging, such as multiple guesses or confidence scores, and make the grading more uniform across different models. Models were allowed to use their providers’ built-in tools: search, code execution and page fetch. We capped their token output at 64,000 and ran each model under its default effort setting with a maximum time of 15 minutes per photo. If a model did not return coordinates on the first prompt, we also allowed a single rescue prompt asking it to do so using its previous reasoning and without using any tools. The images provided were unique, from around the world, not published on the internet before, scrubbed of metadata and provided without any context. They did not contain significant landmarks. We also included images in snowy, foggy and nighttime conditions. The results show that the LLMs tested could, in many circumstances, successfully narrow down a location much faster than a human can geolocate even without any context. This is not limited to Google Street View-style images. Take, for example, this image of vegetation and a very small part of a rooftop. An example of a photo used for testing, with annotation added after the test to highlight the only man-made object visible. Credit: Bellingcat. For an average person, identifying the country this photo was taken in without any context could take a significant amount of time. However, multiple models quickly narrowed it down to Kenya. You can navigate their answers in the map below. Notice how several correctly inferred enough vegetation details to narrow down the exact part of the world and the park itself, but also that for many, the final response was a best guess only. It is important to note that even though some models were correct, others were significantly off. The full model results for all 52 photos can be seen in the table below. Of the models tested, Gemini 4 Argon scored highest on the Mean Log Score, and Claude’s models (Opus and Fable) were at the top of the table regardless of the score metric. Even Claude Sonnet, the weakest of its lineup, consistently came close to the real location while being the fastest to answer across all models. This was followed by GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.1 Sol, as well as other Claude and Gemini models, and then the geolocation-specific model, GeoSeer Fast, which provided good results but also timed out frequently. We tested GeoSeer’s more competent Agent model, but it refused to answer on eight photos and regularly timed out. For secondary factors like time and cost, Claude also performed well on both metrics, and Gemini Argon, while much slower, came at a similar cost to Opus. Based on API rates, Argon and Opus models offered the best balance of accuracy and cost, especially compared to Fable and Grok. Grok was the most expensive option and had an underwhelming bottom-half performance. Meanwhile, GeoClip was freely available but only outperformed Claude Haiku. Model Limitations While we sought to analyse the most prominent models, there was one that we could not include as it has yet to be fully released. Support Bellingcat Your donations directly contribute to our ability to publish groundbreaking investigations and uncover wrongdoing around the world. Donate In its blog post , Anthropic claimed its Mythos model beats “even the strongest human baseline on median distance error, scoring 37.0km and 47.2km across 6,000 photos (placing 23.7 percent and 23.1 percent within 1km).“ But Nuno Moniz, Associate Research Professor at the Lucy Family Institute for Data & Society at the University of Notre Dame, told Bellingcat that “the median represents a strong simplification of what would be acceptable to compare AI-based system performance with regards to humans”. Anthropic compared its models to competitive GeoGuessr players and their success in identifying the location of Google Street View images. The entire set of test images was online and there was no guarantee the models were processing the imagery for the first time. While Anthropic has been relatively open about these methods, not all developers have been as forthcoming. It is therefore difficult to assess whether the same limitations will impact all other models, or whether there will be further caveats that we are simply not aware of. Moniz said that “the increasing availability of benchmarking tools and datasets has made it somewhat difficult to measure reliability in test results such as these”. Specifically, due to the ”uncertainty as to whether that data was included in its training”. This is why we ran our Bellingcat tests with non-published photos sourced from Bellingcat staff and the Bellingcat Volunteer Community. A further limitation of any models comparing performance to GeoGuessr scores is that the game uses images from Google Street View, which is limited to a select number of countries, and within these, a limited number of roads. Street View is also intentionally skewed to feature clear, high-quality photos taken during daytime that are useful for navigation, and users can pan around their view. There are also some well-known tricks that allow GeoGuessr players to bypass actual geolocation to correctly guess the location of photos: for example, Google is known to use a black car in Jordan and a white car in the UAE to capture imagery. While this wouldn’t necessarily impact model performance, it is a drawback of measuring against GeoGuessr score as the game has a set of workarounds that can bypass geolocation skill. Anthropic’s data consisted of thousands of social media photos of various scenes. Once again, though, these photos were online and may have featured in the model’s training data. Anthropic’s blog post contained four images as an example of this dataset. Images used as part of Anthropic’s dataset. Credit: Anthropic. The examples Anthropic shared are relatively easy to geolocate as they feature recognisable buildings and signs. But footage that requires geolocation often comes from regions where access is limited and which do not feature on social media or Street View. Specifically, in a military and intelligence context, footage often involves low-resolution material and intentionally obscured details recorded in remote or inaccessible areas. Context that could be found online can be uncertain or plain wrong, especially during a developing situation, such as the image below that Bellingcat investigators geolocated when verifying a US strike on a school in the city of Minab in Iran that killed at least 120 children earlier this year. An example of footage geolocated by Bellingcat. Screen shot from Mehr News. Anthropic researchers acknowledge this caveat, writing that it “does not as clearly emulate the task of precisely pinning down a location in near-real-time in a less populated battlefield setting; that is a task for future research.” As noted, it is also possible that similar caveats need to be applied to other models when seeking to understand and interpret any geolocation-related benchmarking. Supercharged Models In parallel to the above models, we also tested a set of agentic skills and tools being developed internally by Bellingcat. These are researcher-informed instructions and code that can equip generic-use AI agents to augment their geolocation ability. For instance, we designed skills such as allowing it to download Environmental Systems Research Institute (ESRI ) satellite imagery tiles. We also designed another skill that enabled direct access to data from Bellingcat’s OpenStreetMaps search tool , which aims to assist geolocation efforts by comparing items identified in imagery (like the position of a pylon compared to a nearby railway line) to OpenStreetMaps data. GeoSleuth is a similar project that has already been published, which we used for comparison. We picked Claude’s Opus 5.5 model to run both skills customisations because of its strong performance and reasonable pricing, and ran all the photos through the supercharged models under the same conditions – except that they had no timeout enforced as the supercharged models required more time to utilise their extra skills. The different timeout conditions and expanded toolset do not allow for a direct comparison of the customised models to the previous off-the-shelf models’ results, even if they both outperformed the barebones Opus model they were based on, and all other models on GeoGuessr Score, with only Argon ranking above Bellingcat’s agent in Mean Log Score . Still, this test allows us to showcase why skill customisations can bring value. Take the following photo. An image captured at the Global Campus of Human Rights in Venice. Credit: Bellingcat. While in this instance the supercharged models got the exact spot there were other instances where they did not, as the results in the table above show. This again emphasises that even with extra skill sets added these models were still far from infallible. While in this instance the supercharged models got the exact spot, there were other instances where they did not, as the results in the table above shows. This again emphasises that even with extra skill sets added, these models were still far from infallible. Tests Conclusions Despite increased model improvement, our analysis shows that important caveats remain and it is important to keep a human in the loop when seeking to guarantee a geolocation is precise and correct. Our tests show that the coordinates models provide as answers are rarely an exact match, even with supercharged models. Invariably, even the best models, with the best tools, can confidently claim a wrong position. Anthropic says its Mythos model was able to pinpoint less than a quarter of its social media photos dataset within a 1km radius. But narrowing down a location is rarely the trickiest part of geolocation work. A large part of important geolocation work is in the final stretch: finding specific coordinates from a general area. This level of specificity is needed because a general area is not a match. Matching features and perspective are necessary for an accurate geolocation, and in many cases that is done on very low-quality images or even by cross-referencing multiple sources. This level of precision is essential for investigations where it matters what building a person could be found at, what lines of sight individuals might have had, or what impact an air strike might have led to. Since LLMs can still confidently get things wrong, as our analysis shows, all results still have to be verified independently. Strong human geolocation skills therefore remain crucial, as the more one understands about geolocations, the better one can verify or take to completion an automated result. Though it can speed up geolocation work significantly, especially in narrowing down an area of interest, AI models remain a useful assistant rather than a tool we can blindly delegate geolocations to. Bellingcat is a non-profit and the ability to carry out our work is dependent on the kind support of individual donors. If you would like to support our work, you can do so here . You can also subscribe to our Newsletter and follow us on Bluesky here , Instagram here , Reddit here and YouTube here .
