items.title: Delivery bots accused of illegally scanning customers
items.summary: Two Chicago customers say robots delivering their groceries and takeout scanned their faces and hands without consent, stored the data alongside their names and addresses, and used the recordings to train AI . Their separate lawsuits accuse delivery robot operators Coco Robotics and Serve Robotics of violating Illinois’ biometric privacy law. Both companies dispute the claims. The plaintiffs filed the cases in the Circuit Court of Cook County, Illinois, alleging that the robots used their cameras along with light detection and ranging (LiDAR) sensors to scan them. LiDAR uses laser pulses to build a detailed 3D map of a robot’s surroundings. The lawsuits allege that, at close range, these sensors capture facial geometry in enough detail to support facial recognition. Mitchell Breidinger ordered DoorDash groceries in September 2025. A Coco robot, operated by Coco Robotics, made the delivery. To collect it, he had to stand within about a meter of the robot’s cameras and LiDAR sensor while he entered a PIN code in the DoorDash app, and a Coco remote pilot watched the live video, according to the complaint . Barry Schain filed a similar complaint against Serve Robotics, which sent one of its robots to deliver his Uber Eats order. The complaint against Cyan Robotics (the California-based company that does business as Coco Robotics) states that the robots record detailed 360-degree LiDAR data on the urban environments that they navigate. Coco has never said that it blurs, downsamples, or removes human faces or hands from that LiDAR data, the complaint adds. It also says the company: “gives no notice before a robot records a person, identifies no specific purpose or retention period for the data, obtains no written release, and has published no retention or destruction schedule.” Those who are scanned by Coco robots have no account to close with the robotics company and don’t get to choose whether they are served by a robot, the complaint points out. Cyan uses the data that the robots collect to train its AI, the complaint says, adding that it also has data-sharing partnerships with companies including ChatGPT creator OpenAI. Schain, who most recently took a delivery from a Serve robot on October 4, makes similar claims in his complaint. The company fulfills food delivery orders for both Grubhub and Uber Eats, it says, noting (unlike the complaint against Cyan) that these robots also collect audio. Serve Robotics licenses video and LiDAR data to third parties for model training, the complaint says, citing Serve’s own filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Both companies have pushed back, according to reports . Coco said it has not collected biometric data in Chicago, that the suit “fundamentally misunderstands our technology” and that “the data we share is navigational data used to make sidewalks safer for all users.” It called the case “frivolous.” Coco said that it doesn’t share data from the beginning and end of delivery runs. Serve said that the robot systems are “not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles.” Whether the data the robots capture qualifies as biometric information under BIPA is central to the lawsuits. Illinois’ biometric law Illinois’ biometric privacy law gives people the right to sue companies over the unlawful collection and use of their biometric data. Under that law, biometric identifiers include scans of hand and face geometry. Companies must tell people in writing what biometric information they’re collecting, what they’ll use it for, and how long they’ll keep it. They must also get each person’s written consent and publish a schedule for destroying the data, and they must not sell or otherwise profit from it. These class action suits were not delivered in a vacuum. Chicago residents had already mounted a petition against the delivery robots, citing collisions, interference with emergency vehicles, and concerns about potential surveillance. More than 4,550 Chicagoans have signed it, the petition says. Both suits were filed by the same Chicago law firm, Almeida Law Group. Each seeks $1,000 per class member for negligent violations or $5,000 for intentional or reckless ones. Each complaint says its proposed class “includes many thousands of persons.” Browse like no one’s watching. “gives no notice before a robot records a person, identifies no specific purpose or retention period for the data, obtains no written release, and has published no retention or destruction schedule.”

Those who are scanned by Coco robots have no account to close with the robotics company and don’t get to choose whether they are served by a robot, the complaint points out.

Cyan uses the data that the robots collect to train its AI, the complaint says, adding that it also has data-sharing partnerships with companies including ChatGPT creator OpenAI.

Schain, who most recently took a delivery from a Serve robot on October 4, makes similar claims in his complaint. The company fulfills food delivery orders for both Grubhub and Uber Eats, it says, noting (unlike the complaint against Cyan) that these robots also collect audio.

Serve Robotics licenses video and LiDAR data to third parties for model training, the complaint says, citing Serve’s own filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Both companies have pushed back, according to reports.

Coco said it has not collected biometric data in Chicago, that the suit “fundamentally misunderstands our technology” and that “the data we share is navigational data used to make sidewalks safer for all users.” It called the case “frivolous.” Coco said that it doesn’t share data from the beginning and end of delivery runs. Serve said that the robot systems are “not designed to identify individuals or create biometric profiles.”

Whether the data the robots capture qualifies as biometric information under BIPA is central to the lawsuits.

Illinois’ biometric law

Illinois’ biometric privacy law gives people the right to sue companies over the unlawful collection and use of their biometric data.

Under that law, biometric identifiers include scans of hand and face geometry. Companies must tell people in writing what biometric information they’re collecting, what they’ll use it for, and how long they’ll keep it. They must also get each person’s written consent and publish a schedule for destroying the data, and they must not sell or otherwise profit from it.

These class action suits were not delivered in a vacuum. Chicago residents had already mounted a petition against the delivery robots, citing collisions, interference with emergency vehicles, and concerns about potential surveillance. More than 4,550 Chicagoans have signed it, the petition says.

Both suits were filed by the same Chicago law firm, Almeida Law Group. Each seeks $1,000 per class member for negligent violations or $5,000 for intentional or reckless ones. Each complaint says its proposed class “includes many thousands of persons.”

items.title: Fortinet Urges Customers to Patch Critical Flaws Affecting FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer
items.summary: Fortinet has urged customers to prioritize security updates for FortiOS, FortiManager, and FortiAnalyzer scheduled for October 22, 2026. The coordinated release addresses critical and high-severity vulnerabilities, including flaws found through AI-assisted security testing. The company said customers should address internet-facing devices first. In an October 21 announcement , Fortinet Chief Information Security Officer Carl Windsor warned customers against treating these fixes as routine maintenance. The update follows security releases for FortiMail and FortiAuthenticator, extending the patching effort across several key products. Fortinet said its testing program uses advanced AI models to examine code paths, protocol handling, and configuration logic. The company thanked Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceX for their work with its security teams. The concern extends beyond finding new bugs. Fortinet warned that attackers can use AI to compare patched and older software, identify changed code, and build exploits within hours or days. This process, known as patch diffing, can expose weaknesses before customers finish upgrading. AI may also help attackers combine lower-severity flaws into a more serious attack chain. However, the announcement does not provide individual CVE identifiers, CVSS scores, or detailed attack conditions for this release. It also does not report active exploitation of these newly addressed flaws. Its earlier testing report also stressed human review. Security analysts validate AI findings and test whether they are exploitable, helping separate real vulnerabilities from false alarms and recommend product security improvements. Affected Versions and Required Updates FortiOS customers should move to version 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.13, or 7.2.14, depending on their current branch. Affected releases span 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.12, and 7.2.0–7.2.13. FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer share the same minimum fixed releases: 8.0.2, 7.6.8, 7.4.12, and 7.2.13. Their affected versions cover 8.0.0–8.0.1, 7.6.0–7.6.7, 7.4.0–7.4.11, and 7.2.0–7.2.12. Fortinet lists October 22 availability for all these updates. For FortiMail, the fixed versions are 8.0.2, 7.6.7, and 7.4.9. Customers running affected FortiMail 7.2 releases must move to the 7.4 branch or later. FortiAuthenticator users should install 8.0.4 or 6.6.11, depending on their branch. Product Release Branch Affected Versions Patched Version or Required Upgrade FortiOS 8.0 8.0.0–8.0.1 8.0.2 or later FortiOS 7.6 7.6.0–7.6.7 7.6.8 or later FortiOS 7.4 7.4.0–7.4.12 7.4.13 or later FortiOS 7.2 7.2.0–7.2.13 7.2.14 or later FortiManager 8.0 8.0.0–8.0.1 8.0.2 or later FortiManager 7.6 7.6.0–7.6.7 7.6.8 or later FortiManager 7.4 7.4.0–7.4.11 7.4.12 or later FortiManager 7.2 7.2.0–7.2.12 7.2.13 or later FortiAnalyzer 8.0 8.0.0–8.0.1 8.0.2 or later FortiAnalyzer 7.6 7.6.0–7.6.7 7.6.8 or later FortiAnalyzer 7.4 7.4.0–7.4.11 7.4.12 or later FortiAnalyzer 7.2 7.2.0–7.2.12 7.2.13 or later FortiMail 8.0 8.0.0–8.0.1 8.0.2 or later FortiMail 7.6 7.6.0–7.6.6 7.6.7 or later FortiMail 7.4 7.4.0–7.4.8 7.4.9 or later FortiMail 7.2 7.2.0–7.2.9 Upgrade to the 7.4 branch or later FortiAuthenticator 8.0 8.0.0–8.0.3 8.0.4 or later FortiAuthenticator 6.6 6.6.0–6.6.10 6.6.11 or later Fortinet plans to publish public advisories on its PSIRT page on November 10. Its notice says FortiSASE will receive automatic updates before the coordinated release. FortiManager Cloud updates may require manual action, while public cloud updates follow the relevant cloud provider’s release process. The gap between firmware availability and full public disclosure gives customers time to upgrade before detailed advisories appear. It does not mean exposed devices can safely wait until November. Fortinet explicitly asks customers to act when the updates become available, rather than delay for technical details. PHP and Node.js Add Patching Pressure The warning comes alongside separate PHP and Node.js security releases. These are distinct issues, not confirmed components of the Fortinet vulnerabilities. PHP released emergency patches on October 21 for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, known as PHP2Shell. Both can allow remote code execution without authentication. One involves memory exhaustion leaving incomplete request data, while the other involves stale request state surviving after memory is freed. Cybersecurity News’s PHP2Shell coverage explains the risks across different server setups. Fixed PHP releases are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. The PHP Foundation also described how AI-assisted research contributed to investigating these weaknesses. Separately, the Node.js security update addresses ten vulnerabilities, including four rated high severity. CVE-2026-111497 affects Brotli decompression and can allow code execution through an out-of-bounds memory write. Other high-severity fixes address TLS hostname verification bypasses and DNS name truncation. The affected supported branches are 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x. Fortinet recommends identifying exposed systems, backing up configurations, and scheduling urgent maintenance windows for October 22–23. Teams should review logs for unusual administrator access and unauthorized configuration changes before and after patching. Where upgrades cannot happen immediately, administrators should restrict HTTPS and SSH management to trusted addresses, remove FortiManager administration from the public internet, and enforce multifactor authentication with unique passwords. These controls reduce exposure but do not replace installing the security updates. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. Integrate TI Feeds with data from 16K SOCs .

items.title: Samsung and Vizio Smart TVs Still Send Tracking-Like Traffic After Users Turn It Off
items.summary: Samsung and Vizio smart TVs kept sending traffic consistent with automatic content recognition (ACR) even after researchers turned off the feature in the privacy settings. The findings raise questions about whether smart TV privacy controls stop viewing-related data flows, while also clarifying an important limit. Encrypted traffic prevented researchers from confirming exactly what these devices transmitted. The Watching the Watchers study examined 12 commercial televisions from ten manufacturers across eight operating systems representing roughly 95% of the U.S. smart TV market. Researchers ran 5,943 automated experiments, comparing network activity with automatic content recognition enabled and disabled. Samsung TV Tracking After Users Turn It Off ACR identifies screen content using short audio or video samples, or digital fingerprints derived from them. Providers compare these signals against known content to identify programs. Viewing records can support audience measurement, targeted advertising, and data sharing. The testbed (Source: Watchingthewatchers) Samsung, Vizio TVs Continue Tracking After Opt-Out The feature can monitor content beyond streaming apps, including antenna broadcasts and HDMI devices. Earlier Cyber Security News coverage of smart TV tracking described how ACR can operate even when a television serves mainly as an external display. For the new analysis, researchers captured network packets. At the same time, televisions played controlled content through antenna inputs, HDMI connections, streaming services, and screen mirroring. Each viewing scenario was repeated with ACR enabled and after opting out. Samsung’s Tizen television showed ACR-consistent traffic in all 30 opted-out tests involving its built-in streaming service. Similar traffic appeared in 41 of 60 antenna tests, 18 of 30 HDMI tests, and six of 30 Tubi tests. Finding: opting out (Source: Watchingthewatchers) Vizio’s SmartCast television continued contacting its identified Amazon Kinesis ACR endpoint in every opted-out run for the affected scenarios. Researchers observed no decrease when the feature was disabled. These findings do not prove that Samsung or Vizio continued recording viewing histories. Most ACR traffic was encrypted, so researchers relied on destinations, timing, volume, and other network patterns. They could not determine what information reached company servers or whether companies stored it. Opt-outs worked in the tested LG webOS, Sony Google TV, Amazon Fire TV, and VIDAA systems. Roku’s setting did not cover its own streaming service, a restriction disclosed on the tested TCL television but not the Roku-branded model. The research paper also describes risks beyond uncertain encrypted traffic. VIDAA transmitted ACR messages over MQTT without encryption, exposing device identifiers, app names, input sources, and audio fingerprints. LG webOS stops ACR traffic without sound; Sony Google TV stops on a black screen (Source: Watchingthewatchers) An unauthenticated server exposed more than 57 million detection results linked to over one million televisions. VIDAA subsequently added login requirements, according to the researchers, but transmissions remained unencrypted. Separately, Vizio’s WatchFree+ service placed readable program or channel information in network names visible through DNS requests and TLS server-name information. This could reveal viewing choices to network observers even with ACR disabled. Researchers recommend disconnecting the television from the internet or blocking identified ACR endpoints. Their published blocklist did not disrupt viewing in tested scenarios, but it does not stop the WatchFree+ title leak. Smart TV risks also extend beyond ACR. Separate research into proxy-enabled television apps highlights why app permissions and bundled services deserve scrutiny. These findings apply to the tested devices and firmware, not every television from these brands. Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: The Keys Are in the Browser: Secret Exposure Across AI-Built Websites
items.summary: Cyble scanned 1.3M+ newly registered domains and found AI-built sites leaking live secrets to the browser: OpenAI keys, Stripe keys, and database tokens. Spinning up a website no longer takes a developer. A prompt to an AI app-builder returns a working, styled, deployable site in minutes, and when one template works, the same operator clones it across a dozen domains before launch. That is also how secrets end up in plain sight. Over a month, Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) scanned more than 1.3 million newly registered domains, identified the ones built by AI app-builders, and read their public front-end code for exposed credentials. We built our own classifiers to spot AI-generated websites as they are registered, paired with a scanner that pulls exposed keys and credentials straight from their public code. On 35 of the 22,306 AI-built sites we identified, a genuinely private secret was sitting in the browser: live OpenAI keys, Stripe secret keys, backend database tokens, and, in several cases, a single credential cloned across a whole fleet of domains. Thirty-five is a small number, since counting every key-shaped string on an AI-built site is easy and misleading, as most are meant to be in the browser; a single reCAPTCHA key appeared on thousands of sites. We kept only the credentials that are never supposed to leave a server. Those are the findings below. This report walks through the two leak patterns we observed, what appears exposed, what an attacker can do with these keys, and how to shut down the exposure. AI-built Websites are leaking the keys that power them An AI-built site generates its content with a Large Language Model (LLM), and the key to that model often ships in the page the visitor downloads. That is the plainest pattern we found, and the most on-the-nose. Five AI-built sites carried live OpenAI API keys in their client-side code, sixteen distinct keys across them, and four of the five are confirmed AI-generated. One AI-writing site stands out on its own: it shipped twelve different OpenAI keys, one per content category, as plain values in its bundle. Figure 1 shows a single entry, with the key masked. Figure 1 – Live OpenAI keys embedded as plain values in an AI-writing site’s JavaScript (key masked by CRIL). A handful of sites, but each key is sensitive to exposure. An OpenAI secret key is a billing credential: anyone who reads the page can spend the owner’s balance, exhaust the rate limit, or run the bill up until someone notices and revokes it. Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit. Clone-and-leak: one secret across a whole fleet An AI builder makes the hundredth site as cheap as the first, so an operator clones a working template across many domains, and whatever secret sat in the template now sits on every copy. We saw this in two shapes. A Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet. Thirteen near-identical domains, each a short word (ask, call, chat, get, hello, hey, hi, its, join, let, meet, my, see), glued to one brand, all served the same client bundle, and all embedded the same live Slack incoming-webhook URL. Figure 2 shows the URL in the shipped bundle, masked. Figure 2 – One Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet, in each site’s shipped bundle (secret and workspace IDs masked). Anyone who can read the page can post messages to the operator’s Slack workspace via that webhook. That works for spam, for phishing aimed at the operator’s own staff, or for flooding a channel. One Stripe secret key across four domains and two brands. A single Stripe secret key appeared on four domains under two separate brand names. The same sk_live_ value across all four points to one operator, or one shared Stripe account, behind every site. Figure 3 shows the assignment. Figure 3 – The same live Stripe secret key reused across four domains under two brands. A Stripe secret key provides full API access to the account, including the ability to create charges, issue refunds, and read customer and payout records. That one key exposes the operator’s whole payment account on every domain in the fleet. The 13-domain Slack fleet runs on Bubble , a no-code and AI app builder, as confirmed by Bubble’s x-bubble-perf response header and client markers. Bubble serves each app from a dynamic.js bundle, and any value a developer places in a client-accessible field ships inside that bundle in plain text. The Stripe cluster runs on a Next.js build instead, which shows that the pattern spans builders rather than tracing to a single platform. What else is exposed Four AI-built sites exposed a Supabase service role JSON Web Token (JWT) on their front ends. A service-role token bypasses row-level security and grants full read and write to the project database. In terms of impact, it sits at the top of the set because it opens the entire backend rather than a single service. Most of the remaining secret-looking strings on AI-built sites carry no/minimal exposure. 3,824 sites shipped browser-safe values: reCAPTCHA site keys, Stripe publishable keys, Supabase anon keys, builder telemetry tokens. 2,172 sites carried Google API keys, which matter only if they are unrestricted. 1,461 sites exposed a Supabase or Firebase backend address, which is a real exposure only when that backend’s rules are open. Filtering those out is why the confirmed count is 35, not several thousand. Table 1 breaks the 35 down by type. The values stay withheld, and a few sites appear under more than one row. Exposure Sites What an attacker gains OpenAI API key 5 Spend the owner’s balance, exhaust quota, run up the bill Shared Slack webhook 13 Post arbitrary messages into the operator’s workspace Stripe secret key 6 Full API access: charges, refunds, customer and payout data Supabase service-role JWT 4 Full read/write to the backend database, bypassing access rules AWS access key 5 Cloud account access, scope set by the paired secret GitHub token / Google OAuth secret 2 Source-control or identity-provider access Table 1 – Confirmed private-credential exposures across 22,306 AI-built sites, by type. What an attacker can do with these Every credential in Table 1 is a working key to a live account. An attacker reads a public web page, copies a value, and calls an API. Here is what that buys them, key by key. OpenAI and other LLM keys: Run inference on the victim’s account until the bill or rate limit stops them. On a metered account, that is direct financial loss; on a funded one, it is a free, anonymous model endpoint that the attacker can point at anything, billed to the victim and running under their quota and identity. Stripe secret key; Drive the victim’s payment account through Stripe’s own API: create and refund charges, push the account toward fraud, and pull the customer list, email addresses, and payout history. One key is a money problem and a data-breach problem at once. Supabase service-role token: Read and write the entire production database, past whatever row-level security the app configured. That means stealing every user record, altering or deleting data, and planting content the app will serve back to its own visitors. Slack incoming webhook: Post into the operator’s own Slack as if from inside. Flooding a channel is a nuisance case; the real risk is internal phishing. AWS access key: With the paired secret and enough permission, reach into the owner’s cloud: spin up resources (crypto-mining is the usual first move), read storage buckets, or pivot further in. GitHub token or OAuth secret: Read or push to the owner’s source repositories or misuse their identity integration. One exposure counts many times over. When the key sits on a cloned fleet, it is live on every domain in that fleet, so an attacker who finds it on one site has compromised all of them. Conclusion AI app-builders made it almost free to publish a website, and just as free to clone one, and most of what they produce is worth nothing to steal. The exceptions are what we went looking for. A small, steady set of these sites hand over the key that runs them, and when an operator copies one site across a fleet, the leak rides along to every domain. Against the millions of domains registered each month, the number is tiny, but every hit is a live account an attacker can reach and exploit just by opening the page. If you build on these tools, read your own shipped code before you publish it. If you defend an organization, assume your keys may surface on sites you never built and look for them. Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web , deep web , and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats . Our Recommendations For developers and AI-builder users: Keep every secret key (OpenAI sk-, Stripe sk_live_, a Supabase service-role token) in a server-side function or backend workflow, never in a client-accessible field. Use only the browser-safe variants on the front end, publishable and anon keys, and enforce access with Supabase row-level security, Firebase rules, and API key restrictions. Rotate any key that has ever sat on the client side, and treat it as already compromised. Read your own page source before you ship, and search it for sk-, sk_live_, service_role, and hooks.slack.com. If you find them, so can anyone. For SOCs and defenders: Monitor public code and newly registered domains for your own keys and webhooks; don’t just paste sites. items.summary_html:
Cyble scanned 1.3M+ newly registered domains and found AI-built sites leaking live secrets to the browser: OpenAI keys, Stripe keys, and database tokens.

Spinning up a website no longer takes a developer. A prompt to an AI app-builder returns a working, styled, deployable site in minutes, and when one template works, the same operator clones it across a dozen domains before launch. That is also how secrets end up in plain sight.

Over a month, Cyble Research and Intelligence Labs (CRIL) scanned more than 1.3 million newly registered domains, identified the ones built by AI app-builders, and read their public front-end code for exposed credentials. We built our own classifiers to spot AI-generated websites as they are registered, paired with a scanner that pulls exposed keys and credentials straight from their public code. On 35 of the 22,306 AI-built sites we identified, a genuinely private secret was sitting in the browser: live OpenAI keys, Stripe secret keys, backend database tokens, and, in several cases, a single credential cloned across a whole fleet of domains.

Thirty-five is a small number, since counting every key-shaped string on an AI-built site is easy and misleading, as most are meant to be in the browser; a single reCAPTCHA key appeared on thousands of sites. We kept only the credentials that are never supposed to leave a server. Those are the findings below.

This report walks through the two leak patterns we observed, what appears exposed, what an attacker can do with these keys, and how to shut down the exposure.

AI-built Websites are leaking the keys that power them

An AI-built site generates its content with a Large Language Model (LLM), and the key to that model often ships in the page the visitor downloads. That is the plainest pattern we found, and the most on-the-nose.

Five AI-built sites carried live OpenAI API keys in their client-side code, sixteen distinct keys across them, and four of the five are confirmed AI-generated. One AI-writing site stands out on its own: it shipped twelve different OpenAI keys, one per content category, as plain values in its bundle. Figure 1 shows a single entry, with the key masked.

Figure 1 – Live OpenAI keys embedded as plain values in an AI-writing site’s JavaScript (key masked by CRIL).

A handful of sites, but each key is sensitive to exposure. An OpenAI secret key is a billing credential: anyone who reads the page can spend the owner’s balance, exhaust the rate limit, or run the bill up until someone notices and revokes it. Twelve keys in one bundle are twelve live credentials shipped at once, and five sites like this are five accounts an attacker can exploit.

Clone-and-leak: one secret across a whole fleet

An AI builder makes the hundredth site as cheap as the first, so an operator clones a working template across many domains, and whatever secret sat in the template now sits on every copy. We saw this in two shapes.

A Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet. Thirteen near-identical domains, each a short word (ask, call, chat, get, hello, hey, hi, its, join, let, meet, my, see), glued to one brand, all served the same client bundle, and all embedded the same live Slack incoming-webhook URL. Figure 2 shows the URL in the shipped bundle, masked.

Figure 2 – One Slack webhook shared across a 13-domain fleet, in each site’s shipped bundle (secret and workspace IDs masked).

Anyone who can read the page can post messages to the operator’s Slack workspace via that webhook. That works for spam, for phishing aimed at the operator’s own staff, or for flooding a channel.

One Stripe secret key across four domains and two brands. A single Stripe secret key appeared on four domains under two separate brand names. The same sk_live_ value across all four points to one operator, or one shared Stripe account, behind every site. Figure 3 shows the assignment.

Figure 3 – The same live Stripe secret key reused across four domains under two brands.

A Stripe secret key provides full API access to the account, including the ability to create charges, issue refunds, and read customer and payout records. That one key exposes the operator’s whole payment account on every domain in the fleet.

The 13-domain Slack fleet runs on Bubble, a no-code and AI app builder, as confirmed by Bubble’s x-bubble-perf response header and client markers. Bubble serves each app from a dynamic.js bundle, and any value a developer places in a client-accessible field ships inside that bundle in plain text. The Stripe cluster runs on a Next.js build instead, which shows that the pattern spans builders rather than tracing to a single platform.

What else is exposed

Four AI-built sites exposed a Supabase service role JSON Web Token (JWT) on their front ends. A service-role token bypasses row-level security and grants full read and write to the project database. In terms of impact, it sits at the top of the set because it opens the entire backend rather than a single service.

Most of the remaining secret-looking strings on AI-built sites carry no/minimal exposure.

  • 3,824 sites shipped browser-safe values: reCAPTCHA site keys, Stripe publishable keys, Supabase anon keys, builder telemetry tokens.

  • 2,172 sites carried Google API keys, which matter only if they are unrestricted.

  • 1,461 sites exposed a Supabase or Firebase backend address, which is a real exposure only when that backend’s rules are open.

Filtering those out is why the confirmed count is 35, not several thousand. Table 1 breaks the 35 down by type. The values stay withheld, and a few sites appear under more than one row.

Exposure Sites What an attacker gains OpenAI API key 5 Spend the owner’s balance, exhaust quota, run up the bill Shared Slack webhook 13 Post arbitrary messages into the operator’s workspace Stripe secret key 6 Full API access: charges, refunds, customer and payout data Supabase service-role JWT 4 Full read/write to the backend database, bypassing access rules AWS access key 5 Cloud account access, scope set by the paired secret GitHub token / Google OAuth secret 2 Source-control or identity-provider access

Table 1 – Confirmed private-credential exposures across 22,306 AI-built sites, by type.

What an attacker can do with these

Every credential in Table 1 is a working key to a live account. An attacker reads a public web page, copies a value, and calls an API. Here is what that buys them, key by key.

  • OpenAI and other LLM keys: Run inference on the victim’s account until the bill or rate limit stops them. On a metered account, that is direct financial loss; on a funded one, it is a free, anonymous model endpoint that the attacker can point at anything, billed to the victim and running under their quota and identity.

  • Stripe secret key; Drive the victim’s payment account through Stripe’s own API: create and refund charges, push the account toward fraud, and pull the customer list, email addresses, and payout history. One key is a money problem and a data-breach problem at once.

  • Supabase service-role token: Read and write the entire production database, past whatever row-level security the app configured. That means stealing every user record, altering or deleting data, and planting content the app will serve back to its own visitors.

  • Slack incoming webhook:  Post into the operator’s own Slack as if from inside. Flooding a channel is a nuisance case; the real risk is internal phishing.

  • AWS access key: With the paired secret and enough permission, reach into the owner’s cloud: spin up resources (crypto-mining is the usual first move), read storage buckets, or pivot further in.

  • GitHub token or OAuth secret: Read or push to the owner’s source repositories or misuse their identity integration.

One exposure counts many times over. When the key sits on a cloned fleet, it is live on every domain in that fleet, so an attacker who finds it on one site has compromised all of them.

Conclusion

AI app-builders made it almost free to publish a website, and just as free to clone one, and most of what they produce is worth nothing to steal.

The exceptions are what we went looking for. A small, steady set of these sites hand over the key that runs them, and when an operator copies one site across a fleet, the leak rides along to every domain.

Against the millions of domains registered each month, the number is tiny, but every hit is a live account an attacker can reach and exploit just by opening the page.

If you build on these tools, read your own shipped code before you publish it. If you defend an organization, assume your keys may surface on sites you never built and look for them.

Cyble’s Threat Intelligence Platforms continuously monitor emerging threats, infrastructure, and activity across the dark web, deep web, and open sources. This proactive intelligence empowers organizations with early detection, impersonation, infrastructure mapping, and attribution insights. Altogether, these capabilities provide a critical head start in mitigating and responding to evolving cyber threats.

Our Recommendations

For developers and AI-builder users:

  • Keep every secret key (OpenAI sk-, Stripe sk_live_, a Supabase service-role token) in a server-side function or backend workflow, never in a client-accessible field.

  • Use only the browser-safe variants on the front end, publishable and anon keys, and enforce access with Supabase row-level security, Firebase rules, and API key restrictions.

  • Rotate any key that has ever sat on the client side, and treat it as already compromised.

  • Read your own page source before you ship, and search it for sk-, sk_live_, service_role, and hooks.slack.com. If you find them, so can anyone.

For SOCs and defenders:

  • Monitor public code and newly registered domains for your own keys and webhooks; don’t just paste sites.

  • Treat a secret found on one domain of a template fleet as exposed on all of them, and scope the response to the fleet, not the domain.

The post The Keys Are in the Browser: Secret Exposure Across AI-Built Websites appeared first on Cyble.

items.title: Hackers Actively Exploiting Siemens Software Center Flaw in ClickFix Malware Attacks
items.summary: Hackers are exploiting a DLL side-loading flaw in Siemens Software Center to run malware through a trusted, signed application. Tracked as CVE-2026-110936, the weakness affects versions before 4.0.9.8. Siemens has confirmed active exploitation and released a fix, and existing installations will receive the update the next time the application starts. Siemens published security advisory SSA-580366 on October 15 and added a reference to active exploitation on October 19. According to the company’s campaign details, attackers distributed a genuine Siemens executable alongside malicious files outside official channels. Siemens said it was unaware of any breach involving its systems, products, or update channel. The attackers used Siemens Software Center version 3.5.8.7 to deliver their malware. The executable retained its valid digital signature and was not modified. Instead, attackers placed malicious DLL files beside it, exploiting how the vulnerable application searched for supporting libraries. Siemens Software Center Flaw Exploited According to Siemens , DLL side-loading occurs when an application loads an untrusted library from its folder without proper validation, allowing malicious code to execute with the application’s privileges due to an uncontrolled search path. This makes the executable’s location and behavior important. A valid signature on SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe does not establish that neighboring DLLs are safe. Defenders who check only the genuine executable’s fingerprint could miss the files responsible for the infection. The activity is linked to the Romulus multi-platform ClickFix campaign. ClickFix tricks users into running commands through fake verification or repair prompts. Previous reporting on the ROMULUS ClickFix platform described hidden PowerShell scripts, modified installers, and malicious libraries loaded through legitimate software. Cyber Security News has also covered ClickFix attacks using Python tunnels , where trusted executables, nearby malicious DLLs, and scheduled tasks formed part of the infection chain. These cases show why signed software still requires behavioral checks. Siemens identified 96.62.218[.]59 and wizardexpensive[.]com as payload-hosting and command-and-control infrastructure. Both were active when its campaign notice was published. Another address, 2.27.248[.]127, previously distributed the malicious AllMyBasic.msi bundle but was no longer serving files. Earlier downloads still require investigation. Warning signs include Siemens Software Center appearing in startup apps or Task Scheduler on computers where users never installed it. Indicators of Compromise Type Indicator Purpose / Detection IP 96.62.218[.]59 Active C2 / payload host Domain wizardexpensive[.]com Active C2 / payload host IP 2.27.248[.]127 Inactive; historical MSI host SHA-256 (MSI) f4d7c5321bb0d1bda439304a753bcf9b467b98ca53c7e9493b9c2c3451092e4a Malicious installer SHA-256 (DLL) 3fdcc7d7d049a89711fb31fb236940a1c5a09d899143ffd20c3c41fb1f2cf491 Malicious DLL Directory %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\SM Software Provisioning Service\ Malware installation folder Files activate.bak , statinfosta.DB Suspicious beside SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe File path %LOCALAPPDATA%\FTSuite\ftc.uml Infection-related artifact Execution msiexec launching SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe from %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\ Suspicious process activity Persistence Unexpected startup entry or scheduled task Potential persistence mechanism Investigators should check for a folder named SM Software Provisioning Service under AppData\Local\Programs and unexpected execution of SiemensSoftwareCenter.exe from that location, particularly when launched by msiexec. Other reported traces include activate.bak or statinfosta.DB beside the executable and an FTSuite folder containing ftc. uml under AppData\Local. Connections to the reported infrastructure should trigger further investigation rather than being treated as harmless software-update traffic. Users should install Siemens Software Center 4.0.9.8 or later. Starting an existing installation triggers its automatic update. Downloads should come from the official Siemens Software Center page, not third-party bundles. Defenders should block the listed infrastructure, review historical logs, and isolate compromised systems. Stop the malicious process, remove startup entries and scheduled tasks, then reset affected passwords through the incident response process. Users should never paste commands from webpages into Run or PowerShell. A genuine “I am not a robot” check does not require running a command on the computer. items.title: Railway Security Incident: Hackers May Have Accessed Customer Environment Variables
items.summary: Railway has disclosed a security incident in which an unauthorized third party may have accessed customer environment variables, including some decrypted values. The cloud platform warned that the affected data could contain API keys, database passwords, and private registry credentials, and urged all customers to replace stored secrets. The company published its security disclosure on October 21, 2026, after detecting unusual activity in systems that store these variables. Its initial findings suggest that only some users may be affected. However, Railway has not released an affected account count, identified the attacker, or explained how access was gained. Railway Security Incident Environment variables hold settings that applications need during builds and normal operation. Railway’s documentation explains that these values can include configuration details and secrets supplied to services. This makes the storage system a sensitive target because stolen credentials could give attackers access to connected services beyond Railway itself. The key distinction is that Railway reported possible access to encrypted variables and, for some, decrypted contents. This does not establish that attackers broke the encryption. The notice does not explain how readable values may have been obtained, leaving that part of the investigation unresolved. Railway believes the incident forms part of a recent series of attacks against platform companies aimed at compromising AI inference providers. These providers run AI models in response to user requests. Railway said it notified upstream providers and asked them to revoke keys proactively, but did not identify those providers. The suspected focus on AI access reflects a wider credential theft risk. Cybersecurity News previously covered an LLMjacking attack involving a leaked AWS key , where stolen access was used to run paid AI models at the victim’s expense. Railway has not confirmed that similar misuse occurred in this incident. Related reporting on AI agents exposing API keys and cloud secrets also shows why secret handling matters across modern development tools. That report describes exposure through configuration files, command output, and model context. It is background on credential risk, not evidence of how attackers entered Railway’s systems in this case. Deployments Paused as Credential Resets Continue Railway paused deployments during its investigation, preventing customers from releasing new application versions. Its incident status page confirmed that builds remained unavailable at 02:19 UTC on October 22. The restriction also affects recovery because some credential changes require services to be redeployed before applications can use the replacement values. The company also began rotating all Railway storage bucket credentials as a precaution. Replacement credentials will appear automatically in customer dashboards. However, Railway said applications cannot be redeployed to pick up those credentials until builds return, creating an additional recovery hurdle for customers with services that depend on storage buckets. Railway recommends immediately rotating all secrets stored as environment variables, including API keys and private registry credentials, and checking connected service logs for unusual activity. Customers should not wait for confirmation that their account was affected. The company has published guides covering database passwords, AI provider usage, cloud access, and GitHub activity. Railway said it will email customers directly as affected accounts are confirmed. The investigation remains ongoing, with the full scope still unclear. items.title: 12-Year-Old GitLab Vulnerability Allows Remote Code Execution on Self-Managed Server
items.summary: GitLab has released urgent security updates for a critical vulnerability that could let attackers run code on self-managed servers without logging in. Tracked as CVE-2026-110264, the flaw carries the maximum CVSS score of 10.0 and affects both GitLab Community Edition and Enterprise Edition. The company published the fixes on October 21, 2026. The affected code reaches back to GitLab 7.0, released in 2014, giving the vulnerability a roughly 12-year history. That does not mean attackers have been using it for 12 years. GitLab’s advisory describes the risk but does not report confirmed attacks or provide a public exploit. GitLab Remote Code Execution Flaw According to GitLab’s official security advisory , the vulnerability involves an integer overflow when the server compiles a specially crafted regular expression. Regular expressions are patterns used to match text. Under certain conditions, processing an attacker-controlled pattern could allow arbitrary code to run on the server. GitLab’s CVSS assessment describes a network-based attack with low complexity, no account privileges, and no required user interaction. It rates the possible impact on data privacy, data integrity, and service availability as high. However, the company has not disclosed the full conditions needed to reach the vulnerable code. GitLab credited security researcher joaxcar with reporting the issue through its HackerOne bug bounty program. Its release notes also list Ruby regular-expression patches, providing further context about the affected software layer without revealing a complete attack path. Administrators should not assume the flaw requires access to a particular project or feature unless GitLab confirms that restriction. CVE ID Severity CVSS Score Affected Edition Vulnerability and Potential Impact CVE-2026-110264 Critical 10.0 CE and EE An integer overflow while compiling a specially crafted regular expression could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on the GitLab server. CVE-2026-15723 High 8.2 CE and EE Improper input handling during OmniAuth-to-LDAP account linking could let an authenticated attacker take over an LDAP-backed account when SAML and LDAP auto-linking are enabled. CVE-2026-112212 High 7.5 CE and EE Cache poisoning in OAuth/OIDC discovery responses could let an unauthenticated attacker redirect certain authentication flows to an attacker-controlled server. CVE-2026-12664 Medium 6.8 CE and EE Missing GraphQL scope checks could allow a user with a read_api token to retrieve a project’s incoming email address and create work items beyond the token’s intended permissions. CVE-2026-16255 Medium 5.9 EE Incomplete SAML/LDAP membership-lock enforcement could allow authenticated users to grant or accept memberships outside identity-provider controls through requests created before the lock was enabled. CVE-2026-105777 Medium 4.3 CE and EE Improper filtering of internal response headers could expose sensitive internal server credentials under certain conditions. CVE-2026-13319 Medium 4.3 CE and EE Missing authorization checks in the group milestones API could let authenticated users read milestone details and project paths from private projects without membership. CVE-2026-112378 Medium 4.3 EE Insufficient server-side billing checks could allow authenticated users to access paid AI features without a valid subscription. CVE-2026-105711 Low 3.5 CE and EE Incorrect caching of merge request titles could expose confidential issue titles to authenticated users without project membership. CVE-2026-14288 Low 3.1 EE Improper access control during approval-rule synchronization could allow authenticated users to bypass required merge request approvals on protected branches. CVE-2026-112326 Low 3.1 EE Incorrect cleanup during error handling could allow users with read-only permissions to permanently delete existing vulnerability records. CVE-2026-103515 Low 2.7 EE Incomplete enforcement of a Duo administrator lock could allow group Owners to re-enable AI-backed data transfers to a third-party service through Amazon Q settings. Affected Versions and Available Fixes The vulnerability affects GitLab CE and EE versions starting with 7.0. GitLab has fixed it in versions 18.11.13, 19.0.10, 19.1.9, 19.2.9, 19.3.6, 19.4.3, and 19.5.1. Earlier releases within those branches remain affected. The company extended the fix to four older branches beyond its standard patch releases. Self-managed customers should upgrade immediately. GitLab.com already runs patched software. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0, or later already include the fixes and require no action, according to the notice. GitLab also says that when an advisory does not name a specific deployment type, all deployment types are affected. This issue should not be confused with the earlier GitLab code execution vulnerability patched on October 12. That separate flaw, CVE-2026-97229, also involved regular-expression handling but affected a different version range. Installing that earlier update does not address this newly disclosed vulnerability. GitLab has published two detection guides for self-managed environments, named “Onigmo native worker crash” and “Org mode render error burst.” These resources are intended to help security teams identify possible exploitation attempts. Their publication is not evidence that attacks have occurred, and the release notice does not establish either signal as proof of a successful compromise. The patch release addresses 12 vulnerabilities overall. Another serious issue, CVE-2026-15723, carries a CVSS score of 8.2. When OmniAuth SAML and LDAP auto-linking are both enabled, an authenticated attacker could take over an existing LDAP-backed account without the victim’s involvement. CVE-2026-112212, rated 7.5, concerns poisoned OAuth and OpenID Connect discovery responses that could redirect certain flows to an attacker-controlled server. These fixes follow other recent GitLab security updates, including a separate AI Gateway remote command execution vulnerability . Those reports concern different components and attack requirements, making accurate version checks more useful than assuming one GitLab update covers every related product. Administrators should review GitLab’s upgrade instructions before deployment. The notice warns that database migrations can affect the process, with downtime for single-node installations and zero-downtime procedures available for suitable multi-node setups. Versions 19.3.6 and 19.4.3 include regular migrations. GitLab normally makes detailed security issues public 90 days after patching, so teams should not delay updates while waiting for full technical details. The GitLab fixes arrive alongside security updates for Node.js and PHP, adding to the patching workload for teams running web applications and development services. Cyber Security News reports that Node.js released security updates addressing ten vulnerabilities across its 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x branches, with patched versions listed as 26.12.1, 24.22.1, and 22.23.4. Meanwhile, PHP issued emergency patches for PHP2Shell , a pair of critical memory-handling flaws tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. items.title: GoDaddy Revoking 404,607 TLS Certificates Following Compliance Failures
items.summary: GoDaddy launched a mass revocation of 404,607 SSL/TLS certificates after finding that issued certificates did not match its published certificate policies. The company missed its required revocation deadline, creating a second compliance issue. An updated customer notice says the incorrectly issued certificates were revoked on October 21, 2026. The incident affects certificates issued under GoDaddy and Starfield certificate chains. Customers still using an affected certificate may face browser security warnings or website access problems until they install a replacement, according to GoDaddy’s customer guidance . Receiving a replacement alone does not confirm that the website is using it. GoDaddy Revoking 404,607 TLS Certificates According to the original incident report , a third party flagged differences between issued certificates and the profiles described in Starfield’s Certificate Policy and Certification Practice Statement, known as CP/CPS. These documents set out the rules the certificate authority follows when issuing certificates. The differences involved certificate policy information, including policy object identifiers, or OIDs, and CPS URI policy qualifiers. These fields identify certificate policies and reference the authority’s published practices. The issued certificates did not match the documented profiles. The reports describe a compliance failure, not a confirmed theft of private keys. GoDaddy stopped certificate issuance after confirming the report. Its investigation uncovered additional differences across affected profiles. The company corrected and published its documentation before resuming issuance. Further checks found similar problems in the older Starfield G2 chain, which was no longer actively issuing certificates. Domain validated certificates made up most of the affected population. Starfield R1 DV accounted for 208,896 certificates, while Starfield G2 DV accounted for 187,159. Smaller numbers of organization validated and extended validation certificates were also affected across the GoDaddy and Starfield chains. GoDaddy Missed the Revocation Deadline The delayed revocation report cites Section 4.9.1.1 of the TLS Baseline Requirements. For the stated policy violation, affected certificates should be revoked within 24 hours and must be revoked within five days, except for short-lived subscriber certificates. The specified revocation reason is “superseded.” GoDaddy began contacting subscribers on October 14. Its outreach included customers holding large certificate inventories and organizations providing government, financial, and health services. However, only 170,566 certificates had been revoked when the October 18 deadline passed at 23:45 UTC. By 05:29 UTC on October 19, the revoked total had reached 227,422. GoDaddy said dedicated teams were handling customer contact, replacement, revocation, and progress tracking through email, SMS, and phone calls. Its later customer notice states that the incorrectly issued certificates were revoked on October 21. Affected administrators should review the SSL certificate section of their GoDaddy account and follow any replacement notice. GoDaddy warns that an updated certificate can exist in the account while the domain continues serving the old certificate. Customers receiving an installation alert should download and install the replacement immediately. The case echoes earlier DigiCert certificate revocations following a DNS validation error , although the underlying failures differ. It also highlights the operational concerns covered in Cybersecurity News’ report on certificate mismanagement . Update defenses against new malware as soon as it appears. items.title: Using AWS WAF to apply mitigations for PHP2Shell RCE vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619)
items.summary: On October 21, 2026, the PHP project released emergency fixes for two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in the PHP core runtime, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 and collectively named PHP2Shell. Both are rated 9.2 (Critical) under CVSS v4.0, and both allow an unauthenticated attacker to run code on a vulnerable server. The fixed releases are PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. But patching a fleet takes time: you need to inventory where PHP runs, schedule maintenance windows and test applications against the new builds. This post shows you how to use AWS Web Application Firewall ( AWS WAF ) to help reduce exposure to the confirmed attack paths during that window. You’ll learn which request patterns to block, how to write the rules in AWS WAFv2, how to deploy them without breaking legitimate traffic and where its protection ends, so you don’t develop a false sense of safety. For how Amazon threat intelligence detected PHP2Shell exploitation before public disclosure, see Amazon Threat Intelligence identifies PHP2Shell exploitation prior to public disclosure in MadPot . For AWS service status and the AWS WAF rule that AWS recommends, see AWS Security Bulletin 2026-143-AWS . IMPORTANT: Patching is the only complete fix, and you should upgrade PHP as your first priority. The vulnerabilities in brief Both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities are unauthenticated RCE issues rooted in how PHP handles multipart/form-data request processing (the request format browsers use for file uploads) before your application code runs, which is why the AWS WAF rules in this post focus on multipart traffic, request body size, and the session upload progress field. At a high level, CVE-2026-109618 corrupts memory when PHP runs out of memory mid-request, and CVE-2026-109619 lets one request leave behind stale data that a later request on the same worker process reuses. For the root-cause analysis, affected versions, and PHP’s own guidance, see the official PHP advisories and release announcement: CVE-2026-109618 (out-of-memory corruption) – PHP advisory GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w CVE-2026-109619 (stale global state) – PHP advisory GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp PHP security release announcement, October 21, 2026 Where AWS WAF fits in your response AWS WAF is a defense-in-depth control in this situation, not a replacement for the PHP upgrade. The PHP advisories are explicit: updating to a patched release is the only complete mitigation. One of the two vulnerabilities is largely outside the reach of any web application firewall, as explained later. Treat the rules in this post as mitigating controls that help reduce exposure while you patch, then remove them or keep them as supporting controls after you’ve patched. AWS WAF inspects HTTP requests at the edge. It doesn’t parse the internal structure of a multipart body, and it has no visibility into PHP worker memory or server-side configuration. The following table maps each attack element to whether AWS WAF can help mitigate it. Attack element AWS WAF coverage Session upload progress field in a multipart POST ( PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS , the form field that turns on PHP’s upload-tracking feature) Yes. A targeted rule can block requests carrying that field. Multipart upload path ( multipart/form-data , the request type used for file uploads and the entry point for both vulnerabilities) Yes, if the application has no legitimate multipart uploads. Block multipart/form-data. Out-of-memory condition from an oversized body Partial. Cap the request body size. Doesn’t catch header amplification (many small part headers that cost far more memory to represent than their size on the wire) that stays under the cap. Repeated attempts against the same worker (the reused PHP process that handles many requests) Yes. A rate-based rule blunts the volume an exploit needs. fatal_error_backtraces producer (a PHP 8.5 setting that stores crash-trace state across a request) No. This is a server configuration setting ( fatal_error_backtraces=0 ). Invalid or deprecated INI diagnostics as a consumer (warnings PHP raises when applying bad configuration settings) No. This path runs server-side, not over client HTTP. Where an application does not accept multipart uploads, an edge rule that blocks multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application, plus the session-upload-progress trigger, which is a defense-in-depth control during the patch window. If your application does use multipart uploads, AWS WAF reduces risk but does not close the vulnerability, because header amplification (a few kilobytes of part headers that expand into far more memory inside PHP) stays within size limits and the firewall cannot parse the headers inside individual body parts. In that case, prioritize the PHP upgrade and apply the server-side mitigations described later. Implementing the AWS WAF rules The rules below are AWS WAFv2 JSON, deploy each of them on the WAF protection pack (web ACL) associated with the Amazon CloudFront distribution, Application Load Balancer, or Amazon API Gateway stage in front of your PHP workloads. IMPORTANT: Before implementing any changes, ensure that your WAFv2 logging is setup in line with AWS WAF Logging guidance. Start every rule in Count mode, confirm it does not match legitimate traffic, then switch to Block. Request body inspection limits AWS WAF inspects a bounded portion of the request body. On Application Load Balancer and AWS AppSync the limit is a fixed 8 KB. For AWS services such as CloudFront and API Gateway, the default is 16 KB and you can raise it to 32, 48, or 64 KB through the web ACL AssociationConfig as seen below. Any part of the body beyond the inspection limit counts as oversize. Choose the limit that fits the rules you deploy, because a body-size rule can only enforce a cap up to the inspected size. aws wafv2 update-web-acl ... --association-config \ 'RequestBody={CLOUDFRONT={DefaultSizeInspectionLimit=KB_16}}' AWS WAF Rule This rule targets both CVEs by blocking a request only when all three conditions in its AndStatement are true at once: The method is exactly POST – matched on the HTTP method, no transformation. A PHP session identifier is present (the nested OrStatement , so either sub-condition satisfies this leg): PHPSESSID appears as a cookie key (exact match on the key, scanning all cookies), or PHPSESSID appears anywhere in the request body (contains match). The body contains PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS – the form field that activates PHP’s session upload progress feature. Pair the rule with session.upload_progress.enabled=0 on the server, which turns the feature off. { "Name": "PHP2Shell", "Priority": 0, "Statement": { "AndStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "POST", "FieldToMatch": { "Method": {} }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "OrStatement": { "Statements": [ { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Cookies": { "MatchPattern": { "All": {} }, "MatchScope": "KEY", "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "EXACTLY" } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHPSESSID", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, { "ByteMatchStatement": { "SearchString": "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS", "FieldToMatch": { "Body": { "OversizeHandling": "CONTINUE" } }, "TextTransformations": [ { "Priority": 0, "Type": "NONE" } ], "PositionalConstraint": "CONTAINS" } } ] } }, "Action": { "Block": {} }, "VisibilityConfig": { "SampledRequestsEnabled": true, "CloudWatchMetricsEnabled": true, "MetricName": "PHP2Shell" } } Additional WAF Rules to consider Block multipart requests when the application has no uploads NOTE: This rule, if implemented in Block mode, will break applications that require file uploads. If your application does not require file uploads, then blocking multipart/form-data removes the multipart out-of-memory path that works against any application for both CVEs at the edge.
